messages.content: I want to make Golden Cheese Yeast Bread, but I'd like to go slowly. What should I set out before I start mixing?

Set out 6 cups all-purpose flour, 2 cups shredded Cheddar cheese, 3 tablespoons sugar, and 2 (.25 ounce) packages active dry yeast. You'll also need the milk and egg called for when you start beating the dough together.
I've got the flour and Cheddar on the counter. Should all 6 cups of flour go into the bowl right away?
No—start with only 3 cups of the flour in a large mixing bowl. Add the shredded Cheddar, sugar, yeast, and salt, then give those dry ingredients a good mix.
The cheese is mixed through the flour now. Does it matter if the yeast touches the salt?
Just stir everything together evenly so the yeast, salt, sugar, cheese, and flour are distributed. Once the milk and egg go in, the mixture will start coming together more smoothly.
Okay, I'm ready with the milk and egg. What texture am I looking for after beating?
Add the milk and egg to the bowl and beat on low speed until the mixture looks smooth, with no dry pockets clinging to the sides.
It's smooth but still more like a thick batter than dough. Do I add the rest of the flour all at once?
Add the remaining flour gradually, stirring in just enough to form a soft dough. You may not need to dump it in all at once; stop when it holds together and feels soft rather than wet.
The dough is soft and a little tacky. Should I flour the counter heavily before kneading?
Lightly flour the surface, then turn the dough out onto it. Use enough flour to prevent sticking, but avoid working in so much that the dough becomes stiff.
I'm kneading now. How long should I keep going, and how will I know it's ready?
Knead until the dough is smooth and elastic, about 6-8 minutes. It should feel springy, pull together cleanly, and look more even on the surface.
I'm making Cawl Traditional Welsh Broth today. What's the best place to start? I've got a large pot out but want to make sure I start with the right amounts.
Absolutely. For this broth, measure 2 quarts water into the large pot. You'll also need 12 ounces beef shank ready to go in once the water is boiling.
The water is measured, and the beef shank is still in the fridge. What vegetables should I prep before heating the pot?
Prep 2 large onions, chopped, and 2 large carrots, sliced. Keep them nearby so the ingredients are organized as you work through the broth.
Onions are chopped and the carrots are sliced. Should I add those now, or get the water boiling first?
Begin by bringing the 2 quarts water to a boil in the large pot. Hold the beef shank and vegetables aside while the water comes up to temperature.
The pot is boiling steadily. Do I lower the heat before adding the beef shank?
Place the 12 ounces beef shank into the boiling water, then reduce the heat so it simmers gently. Let it simmer for 1 1/2 hours.
It's simmering now. How gentle should it look during that time?
Aim for small, steady bubbles rather than a hard boil. That keeps the beef shank cooking evenly while the broth develops over the full 1 1/2 hours.
The timer is done and the broth is hot. What do I do before putting it away?
Take the pot off the heat and let the broth cool, then leave it to cool overnight as directed.
It cooled overnight. The meat looks firm now—how should I handle it?
Lift the meat out of the broth, trim off any gristle, and cut the meat into medium sized pieces. Set the pieces aside for the next stage of the cawl.
Canadian Cedar Planked Salmon is on deck today. What should I do first? I've got the grill available, but I want to make sure I start early enough.
Absolutely. This one needs planning because the untreated cedar plank should be submerged in water for about 12 hours, or overnight, before it goes near the grill.
Good to know. What size plank am I looking for, and how much salmon does the recipe use?
Use a 24x8x1 inch untreated cedar plank, and plan on 6 salmon fillets that are 4 ounces each.
I have the plank and the fillets. What else should be on the counter before I start?
You'll need 1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil and 1 large red onion, chopped. Keep coarse salt nearby too, since it's used when the plank goes on the grill.
For soaking the plank, does it just sit in a sink or tub of water?
Yes. Fully submerge the untreated cedar plank in water so the whole board is covered. If it wants to float, weigh it down with something clean and heavy enough to keep it under.
The plank has soaked overnight. Should I oil the fish yet or get the grill going first?
Get the outdoor grill preheated for high heat first. While it heats, you can keep the salmon, olive oil, and chopped red onion ready so assembly is easy once the plank is prepared.
When the grill is hot, do I put the salmon on right away?
Place the prepared cedar plank on the hot grill first, then sprinkle it with coarse salt. Give yourself a moment to make sure it's sitting securely on the grates before adding anything else.
Any quick check before I start loading the plank with the salmon?

Make sure the plank is the soaked untreated cedar board, the grill is at high heat, and your 6 salmon fillets, 1/2 cup olive oil, and chopped red onion are within reach. From there, you're set up to continue with the recipe on the salted plank.
I'm starting Chocolate Cheesecake II; can you walk me through the setup? I'm starting by clearing space and want to make sure I have the crust ingredients right.
Absolutely. For this part, set out 1 1/2 cups chocolate cookie crumbs, 2 tablespoons white sugar, 1/4 cup melted butter, and 1/4 cup semisweet chocolate chips.
I've got the crumbs and sugar measured. Should the oven be on before I melt the butter?
Yes, go ahead and heat the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), so it's ready when the crust is in the pan.
Oven is heating. I'm using a 9 inch springform pan—does it need anything before the crumbs go in?
Lightly grease the 9 inch springform pan, especially the bottom and where the sides meet the base, so the crust releases more cleanly.
Pan is greased. My butter is melted now; what texture am I looking for when I mix the crumbs?
In a small bowl, stir together the 1 1/2 cups chocolate cookie crumbs, 2 tablespoons sugar, and the melted 1/4 cup butter. The mixture should look evenly moistened and sandy, with no dry pockets.
It's damp and crumbly, not paste-like. Do I add the 1/4 cup semisweet chocolate chips to that bowl too?
Keep the 1/4 cup semisweet chocolate chips measured and ready, but for this crust step, only the crumbs, sugar, and melted butter are mixed together.
Got it. How far up the sides should I press the crust without making it uneven?
Press the crumb mixture firmly across the bottom of the prepared pan, then work it about 1 1/2 inch up the sides. Use the bottom of a measuring cup or your fingers to even it out.
The crust is pressed in, but the corner where the bottom meets the side looks thicker. Should I fix that?

Yes, gently redistribute a little from that thick corner and press again so the base and the 1 1/2 inch side wall are fairly even. Once it's compact and level, this stage is ready for the next part of the cheesecake.
Cabbage Kielbasa Supper is what I'm cooking today. Can you keep me on track? I've got cabbage on the counter but want to make sure I prep it right.
Absolutely. Shred enough cabbage to make 8 cups, and have a 5-qt. slow cooker ready because it will be quite full at the start.
The cabbage is shredded. I also have potatoes—how should I cut them for this?
Use 3 medium potatoes and cut them into 1/2 inch cubes so they cook evenly with the cabbage.
Potatoes are cubed. I'm checking the onion and seasoning before I load the cooker.
Chop 1 medium onion, then add it with the cabbage and potatoes. Season with 1 3/4 teaspoons salt and pepper.
Everything is chopped. Should I layer it or just mix the vegetables together in the crock?
Combine the cabbage, potatoes, onion, salt, and pepper directly in the 5-qt. slow cooker. A gentle toss is enough; it doesn't need to be perfectly mixed.
The vegetables are in and the crock is nearly full. Do I add the liquid before the sausage?
Yes. Pour the broth over all the vegetables so it can work its way down as the cabbage cooks.
Broth is in. The sausage is sliced in pieces—does it get stirred through or stay on top?
Place the sausage on top. The slow cooker may look packed, but the cabbage will cook down as it heats.
Lid is on now. How long should I leave it, and what should I check before serving?
Cook it on low for 8-9 hours, until the vegetables are tender and the sausage is heated through.
Can you help me get started on Elizabeths Extreme Chocolate Lovers Cake? I want to make sure I have the dry ingredients measured correctly.
Absolutely. For this cake, measure out 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour and 2 teaspoons baking soda. Keep them handy, since they'll be sifted together soon.
I've got the flour and baking soda out. Is there anything small I'm likely to miss before I start heating the oven?
Yes—add 1/2 teaspoon salt to your lineup. You'll also need 6 (1 ounce) squares unsweetened chocolate, chopped, so it's ready when the recipe calls for it.
The chocolate is chopped and the salt is measured. What should I do with the oven and pans?
Go ahead and heat the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). While it heats, get out 2 round 9 inch pans.
I found the 9 inch pans. Do they just need greasing, or should I prep them another way?
Grease and flour both of the 2 pans. Try to coat the bottoms and sides evenly so the cake layers release cleanly later.
The pans are coated. Should I mix the chocolate in with the dry ingredients now?
Not yet. For this stage, focus on the dry mixture: sift together the flour, baking soda, and salt.
I'm sifting now. What texture am I looking for when it's done?
It should look evenly combined and lighter, with no obvious clumps of flour, baking soda, or salt left in the bowl.
That's done. Do I use the sifted mixture right away, or keep it somewhere while I handle the next part?
Set the sifted dry mixture aside for now. Keep the chopped unsweetened chocolate nearby, and your greased and floured pans should be ready once the batter comes together.
I'm about to start Buffalo Chicken Wings I. Can you talk me through the prep? I'm setting up the fryer area now.
Absolutely. Put together the main items before you heat anything: 24 chicken wings and 2 quarts vegetable oil for deep frying. You'll also want a large skillet or deep fryer ready.
The wings are out and I have the oil. What sauce ingredients should I keep nearby?
Keep 4 tablespoons butter, 1 tablespoon distilled white vinegar, hot sauce, salt, and pepper within reach. The butter, vinegar, and hot sauce will become the coating after the wings cook.
I'm using a deep fryer. How long should the wings be in the oil?
Fry the chicken wings in the vegetable oil until they're done, about 10 minutes. Work safely around the hot oil and avoid crowding if your fryer needs batches.
They've been frying and look cooked through. What do I do when I pull them out?
Remove the chicken from the oil and let it drain. If you were using a skillet, you'd also remove and drain off the oil; either way, reserve the cooked wings while you make the sauce.
The wings are draining. Should I clean out the skillet before making the sauce?
Yes, make sure the oil is drained away before using the skillet for the sauce. Then melt the 4 tablespoons butter in the skillet over gentle heat.
The butter is melted. When do the vinegar and hot sauce go in?
Add the 1 tablespoon distilled white vinegar and the hot sauce to the melted butter, then stir so the sauce comes together.
The sauce is mixed. How should I season and serve the wings?
Season the sauce or coated wings with salt and pepper to taste, then toss the reserved fried wings in the butter-vinegar-hot sauce mixture until they're well coated. Serve them while hot.
I'm about to start Gelatin Fruit Salad. Can you talk me through the prep? I've got a saucepan out but haven't opened anything yet.

Absolutely. Set out 1 cup applesauce, 2 (3 ounce) packages cherry gelatin, 1 (12 ounce) can lemon-lime soda, and 1 (8 ounce) can crushed pineapple. Keep the pineapple undrained because the juice goes in too.
I found the applesauce and both gelatin boxes. Should the soda be cold before I add it?
Cold is fine. You won't heat the soda directly; it gets stirred in after the hot applesauce has dissolved the gelatin.
Okay, the pineapple can says crushed and it's 8 ounce. I'll leave the juice in. What do I do at the stove?
Pour the 1 cup applesauce into the saucepan and bring it to a boil over the stove. Stir occasionally so it heats evenly and doesn't scorch on the bottom.
The applesauce is bubbling now. Do I keep the burner on while adding the gelatin?
Take the saucepan off the heat first. Then stir in both 3 ounce packages of cherry gelatin until the granules are fully dissolved and the mixture looks smooth.
It's dissolved and smells very cherry. Should I pour the soda in all at once?
Add the 12 ounce can of lemon-lime soda slowly so it doesn't foam over. Stir gently as you pour.
The foam settled. When does the pineapple go in?
Stir in the 8 ounce can of crushed pineapple now, including all the liquid from the can. Mix just until the fruit is evenly distributed.
It's mixed. I have a serving bowl ready—how long should it sit?
Pour it into the bowl, cover it, and refrigerate until firm. Once it's set, it's ready to serve chilled.
I'm making Diegos Special Beef Stew today. What's the best place to start? I've got the slow cooker out but want to start it correctly.
Absolutely. For this part of the stew, set out 1 pound cubed beef stew meat, 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour, 2 tablespoons olive oil, and 2 teaspoons butter.
The beef is still in its package. Should I season it yet, or does the flour come before anything else?
For this recipe, start by putting the cubed beef and the flour into a resealable plastic bag. No extra seasoning is listed in these steps.
Okay, the beef and flour are in the bag. How coated should it be?
Seal the bag well, then shake it until the flour is spread evenly over the beef cubes. You're looking for a light, even coating rather than clumps.
The coating looks even. I have a skillet ready—do I use the butter with the oil right away?
The listed cooking step uses the 2 tablespoons olive oil in the skillet. Heat the oil over medium heat before adding the floured beef.
Medium heat is on. Should I crowd all the beef into the pan, or work in batches?
Brown the beef on all sides in the skillet. If the pan seems crowded, use batches so the pieces can brown instead of steaming.
Some pieces are browning faster than others. What texture or color am I aiming for?
Aim for browned surfaces on all sides of the beef cubes. They don't need to cook through in the skillet; this step is just to build color before the slow cooker.
The beef is browned. Where does it go now?
Transfer the browned beef to the slow cooker. Scrape it in carefully so you keep those coated, browned pieces together for the stew.
I'm ready to cook Flax and Sunflower Seed Bread. What should be ready before I begin? I've got the pan out and want to load it correctly.
Absolutely. Start by setting out 1 1/3 cups water, 2 tablespoons softened butter, 3 tablespoons honey, and 1 1/2 cups bread flour. Keep the sunflower seeds nearby, but don't put them in the pan yet.
The water is measured, and the butter is soft. Should the honey go in with the liquids?

Use the order your bread machine manufacturer recommends. If your machine calls for liquids first, the water and honey can go in before the flour, with the softened butter added as directed for your model.
Mine says liquids first, then dry ingredients. I'll add the water, honey, and butter, then the bread flour.
That matches the recipe's guidance: place all ingredients except the sunflower seeds into the bread machine pan in the manufacturer's recommended order.
Everything except the sunflower seeds is in the pan. The flour is sitting on top and the pan is locked in.
Great. Select the basic white cycle on the bread machine, then press start.
It's running now. The kneading has started, but I haven't heard any alert yet.
Let it keep kneading. The sunflower seeds should be added only when the machine's alert sounds during the knead cycle.
The alert just beeped. I have the sunflower seeds ready by the lid.
Open the lid briefly and add the sunflower seeds now, then close the lid so the machine can continue the cycle.
Seeds are in, and the dough is pulling together around the paddle. Do I need to do anything else while it bakes?

No extra recipe step is needed after the sunflower seeds go in. Let the basic white cycle continue through kneading, rising, and baking, then remove the loaf when your bread machine indicates it's done.
I have Garden Party Salad planned for today. What should I set up first? I've got my mixing bowls out but want to be sure I start in the right place.
Absolutely. Set out a small bowl for the dressing and a larger bowl for tossing the salad later. For the dressing, measure 1/4 cup vegetable oil and 1/4 cup orange marmalade.
Oil and marmalade are measured. Does the dressing need anything creamy or tangy?
Yes. Add 3 tablespoons cider vinegar for tang and 3 tablespoons mayonnaise to make it creamy.
They're all in the small bowl. Should I stir gently or really whisk it?
Whisk it until the dressing looks smooth and the marmalade, mayonnaise, oil, and vinegar are fully blended. Then put the bowl in the refrigerator to chill.
The dressing is chilling. Do I prep the salad part right away or wait?
Wait until just before serving to assemble it, so the salad stays fresh and the almonds keep their texture.
We're getting close to serving. I have chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley ready—what bowl should I use?
Use the large bowl now. Combine the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley in it, leaving enough room to toss everything without spilling.
Everything is in the large bowl. The dressing has thickened a little in the fridge; is that okay?
That's fine. Give the chilled dressing a quick whisk to loosen it, then pour it over the chicken mixture.
Dressing is on. How thoroughly should I toss it before putting it on the table?
Toss until the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley are lightly and evenly coated. Serve it right away after tossing.
I'm about to start Garlic Butter. Can you talk me through the prep? I've got a small mixing bowl out and the butter is softening.
Absolutely. You'll want 1 cup butter, softened enough to mash easily, plus 1 tablespoon minced garlic. If the butter gives when pressed with a spoon, it's ready to mix.
The butter is soft and I measured the minced garlic. What else should I put on the counter?
Set out 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese and 1 tablespoon garlic salt. You'll also be seasoning with Italian seasoning, pepper, and paprika.
Should I melt the butter or keep it softened for this?
Keep it softened, not melted. Add the softened butter, minced garlic, and grated Parmesan to the small bowl, then mash and stir until the garlic and cheese are evenly worked through.
It's mixed, but it looks a little chunky from the Parmesan. Is that okay?
Yes, a little texture from the Parmesan is fine. Scrape down the sides of the bowl so the butter mixture is gathered together before you season it.
Ready for seasoning. How much goes in now?
Stir in the 1 tablespoon garlic salt, then add Italian seasoning, pepper, and paprika to season the butter. Mix until the seasonings are spread evenly through the whole bowl.
The color looks lightly speckled and it smells strong. Should I keep mixing?
Mix just until there are no plain streaks of butter left. Overmixing isn't a big issue here, but once everything looks evenly combined, you can stop.
How should I serve or store it after mixing?
You can use it right away on bread, vegetables, or cooked meat. For storage, spoon it into a small container, smooth the top, cover it, and refrigerate until firm.
Help me stay organized for Apple Cranberry Crisp 2. What comes first? I've got the apples out but want to make sure I don't miss anything.
Absolutely. For the fruit mixture, you'll need 2 pounds Granny Smith apples, peeled, cored, and thinly sliced, plus 3/4 cup cranberries.
The apples are sliced and the cranberries are measured. What should I set beside the bowl next?
Add 1/4 cup white sugar and 3 teaspoons ground cinnamon to your prep area. The directions also call for nutmeg when mixing the fruit, so keep that nearby too.
Got it. What pan and oven temperature should I use?
get the oven warming to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). While it heats, butter an 8 inch square baking dish.
The oven is heating and the dish is buttered. Should the fruit go straight into the pan or get mixed first?
Mix it first in a large bowl: combine the sliced Granny Smith apples, cranberries, white sugar, cinnamon, and nutmeg until the fruit is evenly coated.
The apples look coated, but there's a little sugar and spice at the bottom of the bowl. Is that okay?
Yes, that's fine. Give it one more gentle toss so the spices are distributed, then scrape the fruit and any sugar-spice mixture into the buttered dish.
Should I pack the apples down or leave them loose?
Spread them evenly into the baking dish. You can lightly level the top, but don't press hard; the fruit should sit evenly so it cooks at the same rate.
The fruit is in the dish. What do I do with the same bowl now?
Use that same bowl to combine the oats, flour, and brown sugar for the crisp topping. Once those are mixed, you'll be ready to add the topping over the fruit.
I pulled up Early Morning Oven Roasted New Potatoes. Can you guide the first few moves? I've got the potatoes on the counter but haven't started cutting yet.
Absolutely. You'll need 1 1/2 pounds of new potatoes cut into wedges, plus 4 tablespoons of butter. Go ahead and wedge the potatoes so they're all fairly similar in size for even coating.
The potatoes are cut into wedges. I'm checking the seasonings before I turn anything on—what should be out?
Set out 2 teaspoons fresh rosemary, along with salt and pepper to taste. If the rosemary is in sprigs, chop it finely so it disperses well in the butter.
Rosemary is chopped, and I have salt and pepper ready. Should I start with the oven or the skillet?
Start by preheating the oven to 450 degrees F, which is 230 degrees C. While it heats, keep the potato wedges nearby so they're ready to coat.
Oven is heating. I've got a skillet on the stove—how hot should it be before the butter goes in?
Use a hot skillet, then add the 4 tablespoons butter and let it melt. Keep an eye on it so it melts smoothly rather than browning too much.
The butter is melted and still looking golden. Do the herbs go in right away?
Yes. Stir in the 2 teaspoons fresh rosemary, then season with salt and pepper to taste. Give it a quick stir so the rosemary perfumes the butter.
It smells good. I'm worried about some wedges getting more butter than others—what's the best way to coat them?
Add the potato wedges to the melted butter mixture and turn them until they're evenly coated. Use a spatula or tongs to lift from the bottom so the rosemary and seasoning cling to all sides.
They're glossy and coated now. Should I do anything else before moving them along?

Spread the coated potatoes in an even layer so they aren't piled up. The recipe's key prep is complete: potatoes cut into wedges, butter melted with rosemary, salt, and pepper, then the wedges coated evenly.

source_seed.recipe_title: Early Morning Oven Roasted New Potatoes

messages.content: Buffalo Chicken Wings I is on deck today. What should I do first? I've got the wings out and want to do it in the right order.
Absolutely. Set up 24 chicken wings and 2 quarts vegetable oil for deep frying. Use a large skillet or a deep fryer, and make sure you have a safe spot ready for draining the cooked wings.
I'm using a deep fryer. Before I heat the oil, what do I need for the sauce?
For the sauce, keep 4 tablespoons butter and 1 tablespoon distilled white vinegar nearby, along with hot sauce. You'll also season it with salt and pepper to taste at the end.
Oil is heating now. How long should the wings cook once they go in?
Fry the chicken wings in the hot vegetable oil until they're done, about 10 minutes. Don't crowd them if your fryer is small; cook in batches if needed so they fry evenly.
They've been frying and look crisp. What should I do when I pull them out?
Lift the wings out carefully and let them drain. Then remove the oil from the skillet or fryer area as needed, reserving the cooked chicken wings for the sauce.
The wings are drained. I'm switching back to the skillet for the sauce—what goes in first?
Melt the butter in the skillet. Once it's melted, stir in the distilled white vinegar and hot sauce so they come together into a coating sauce.
Should the wings go into that sauce, or is it more of a drizzle?
Toss the reserved fried wings in the skillet with the butter, vinegar, and hot sauce mixture so they get coated all over.
They're coated now. What's the final seasoning before I serve them?
Season the wings with salt and pepper to taste, then serve them hot while the coating is glossy and the skin is still crisp.
Can you help me put together Easy Bake Oven Cookie Mix? I've got a medium bowl out and want to make sure I measure everything right.
Absolutely. Measure 1 1/2 cups quick-cooking oats into the bowl, then add 3/4 cup all-purpose flour.
The oats and flour are in. I'm packing the brown sugar now—how much goes in, and is there anything tiny I might miss?
Add 3/4 cup packed brown sugar, and don't forget 1/4 teaspoon baking soda. Stir those together with the oats and flour until the dry mix looks evenly combined.
It's mixed, but the brown sugar made a few small clumps. Should I break those up before adding anything else?
Yes, press out any brown sugar clumps with the spoon or your fingers so the oats, flour, baking soda, and sugar are evenly distributed.
That looks better. I see shortening in the directions, but I don't see an amount here—how should I handle it?
Use the shortening called for by your recipe source, then cut it into the dry mixture with a pastry cutter, fork, or two knives. Work it in until the mixture starts to look like coarse cornmeal.
I'm using a fork. Some bits are still pea-sized and sticking to the oats.
Keep pressing and scraping the fork through the bowl. The goal is that there should be no lumps of shortening left, just a crumbly, cornmeal-like texture throughout.
Okay, it's crumbly now and I don't see obvious shortening lumps. Do I bake it right away or store it?
For this mix, portion it for storage: measure 1/2 cup of the mixture into each re-sealable bag or container.
Should I pack the 1/2 cup tightly into the bags, or leave it loose?
Leave each 1/2 cup portion loose rather than compressed, seal the bags or containers well, and label them as Easy Bake Oven Cookie Mix so they're ready to use later.

While it softens, keep the chicken station separate and ready.

messages.content: I'm starting Grand Marnier Chicken and want to keep the counter organized before I open the chicken. I have the cutting board, mallet, shallow dish, and a small skillet ready.

If you're adding onion here, slice it very thin and soften it gently before any liquid goes into that skillet. For the recipe prep, set out 4 skinless, boneless chicken breast halves, 1 cup milk, 1 cup dry bread crumbs, and 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese, and keep the raw-chicken area separate from the coating area.
The skillet is on low. I haven't opened the chicken yet; should I pour the milk into the dish now or wait?
Wait on the milk for a moment. Slice and lightly pound the chicken first, then the flattened fillets can go into the dish and the milk can be poured over them.
The part I'm unsure about is cutting the breasts horizontally into thirds. They're thick and slippery.
Work with 1 breast at a time. Lay it flat, steady it with your palm, and keep the knife parallel to the board, using gentle sawing strokes so each breast becomes 3 thin pieces.
The onion strips in the skillet are soft now and that sharp smell is gone; getting them started early was right for this. I'm ready to put the chicken on the board.
Great. Keep the skillet gentle while you focus on the chicken, and slice all 4 breasts the same way so you end up with 12 thin fillets.
I've cut them all, and I do have 12 pieces. A couple are thicker on one side and a few edges look ragged.
That's okay. Lightly pound each piece, with extra taps on the thicker ends, just until the fillets are more even; don't hit so hard that the ragged edges tear further.
Should I cover the chicken before using the mallet, or is it fine directly on the board?
Cover it if you can, using plastic wrap or parchment. It keeps the mallet cleaner and helps prevent little bits of raw chicken from spreading around.
The pieces are flatter now. I measured 1 cup milk, and I'm wondering if the Parmesan or crumbs go into that milk.
Keep the milk plain. Arrange the flattened chicken in the shallow dish and pour the 1 cup milk over the fillets.
The dish is pretty crowded, so the milk touches most of the chicken but doesn't fully cover every edge.
Turn the fillets once or twice so both sides get moistened, then spread them as evenly as the dish allows. Start a timer for 10 minutes once they're all coated with milk.
Timer is set for 10 minutes. I still have the bread crumbs and Parmesan sitting in their containers.
Use a clean separate dish for the coating. Add 1 cup dry bread crumbs and 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese there, away from the raw-chicken board and milk dish.
While the chicken soaks, I want to wash the knife, board, and mallet. Is there any reason to mix the coating first?
Go ahead and clean first. Wash anything that touched raw chicken, then wash your hands well before returning to the bread crumb and Parmesan dish.
Cleanup is done and there are a few minutes left. Should the coating be stirred together now or left in layers?
Stir the bread crumbs and Parmesan together evenly now. When the 10 minutes are up, the milk-soaked chicken will be ready to move into that clean coating dish.

Chop 1 medium onion and 1 green bell pepper, peel and thinly slice 1 large carrot, keep the garlic close by, and measure out 2 tablespoons vegetable oil.
original_cues.support_feedback_cue: The oil is glossy now. I like that you're keeping the spicy things as a small bowl accent; that's exactly what I wanted for this soup. How soft should the vegetables get?
original_cues.support_user_cue: I'm about to start Fast and Delicious Black Bean Soup. I have a large pot, the blender, and a cutting board ready—how should I stage the first few ingredients?

messages.content: I'm starting Fast and Delicious Black Bean Soup and have the pot, blender, knife, and cutting board out. Can you help me organize the vegetables and the first cooking steps?

Keep the black bean soup base mild, and set any chili oil, hot sauce, pepper flakes, jalapeno, or cayenne aside as a tiny bowl-side accent. Chop 1 medium onion and 1 green bell pepper, peel and thinly slice 1 large carrot, keep the garlic ready, and measure 2 tablespoons vegetable oil for the pot.
Onion and green pepper are chopped, the carrot is sliced thin, and the garlic is ready. I also have the beans and broth nearby—does the blender come into play before the pot does?
The blender can wait. Start in the large pot with the oil and vegetables, then stir in 1 can of black beans and the chicken broth; the remaining can of beans gets pureed smooth afterward.
Okay, I'll leave the blender jar empty for now. Should the oil go into a cold pot, or do I heat the pot first?
Add the 2 tablespoons vegetable oil to the large pot, then put it over medium heat. Give it a minute or so until the oil looks shiny and moves easily across the bottom when you tilt the pot.

The oil is shimmering now. I like that you kept the heat from the spicy stuff as a little bowl accent; that's exactly what I wanted for this soup. How tender should the onion, pepper, carrot, and garlic get?

Add the onion, green bell pepper, carrot, and garlic to the pot. Cook them for 5 minutes over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the onion turns translucent, the pepper softens, the carrot slices bend a little, and the garlic smells mellow instead of sharp.
They're in and sizzling softly. Some onion pieces are sticking to the spoon, and the carrots are mostly lying flat on the bottom.
Use short, steady strokes with the spoon and scrape along the bottom of the pot. You want the vegetables to soften without letting the onion or garlic brown too much.
I'm at about 3 minutes. The pepper is slumping, but the pan looks a little dry around the edges—should I splash in broth now?
If nothing is scorching, hold off until the vegetables have had the full 5 minutes. Keep the heat at medium and keep nudging the mixture around so the aromatics soften before the liquid goes in.
The 5 minutes are done. The onion is clear at the edges, the garlic smells gentler, and the carrot slices bend when I press them. What should I add next?
Stir in 1 can of black beans and the chicken broth. As the broth hits the hot pot, scrape the bottom so the softened onion, bell pepper, carrot, and garlic release into the soup.
The broth and 1 can of beans are mixed into the vegetables. The second can of black beans is still unopened next to the blender—do I puree that by itself?
Yes. Put the remaining can of black beans into the blender and puree until smooth, with no large pieces of bean left.
The puree is smooth but thick, and a lot of it is clinging to the sides of the blender jar. How do I get it into the soup without losing a bunch?
Scrape it out with a spoon or spatula, then stir it into the pot through the center and around the edges. The broth should loosen the puree and make the soup look darker and fuller.
It's mostly blended in now, but I can see a few darker swirls and the soup is thicker. I'm also thinking ahead to serving it gently—how should I finish the bowls?

Keep the heat at medium and stir from the bottom until the color evens out; turning it higher can make the thicker soup catch. Ladle the soup as a mild base, then add just a small spoonful, thin drizzle, or tiny pinch of chili oil, hot sauce, pepper flakes, jalapeno, or cayenne to one side of each bowl so the spice stays easy to control.

messages.content: I'm making Baked Fish and Rice 2 and want to keep the timing straight. Can you talk me through it while I prep?
Absolutely. Set your oven to 375 degrees F, or 190 degrees C, and grease an 11-in. baking dish. You'll start with 1 1/2 cups boiling chicken broth and 1/2 cup uncooked long grain rice.
Oven is heating and the dish is greased. Should the broth already be boiling before it goes in?
Yes, use the chicken broth while it's boiling so the rice starts cooking properly in the dish. Pour it in with the uncooked long grain rice.
Rice and hot broth are in the baking dish. I have Italian seasoning and garlic powder out too.
Stir in 1/4 teaspoon Italian seasoning and 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder, making sure the rice is spread fairly evenly across the bottom.
It's mixed and level. Do I put anything else in before it bakes?
Not yet. Cover the baking dish and bake it at 375 degrees F for 10 minutes.
The covered rice mixture has baked for 10 minutes. It looks partly absorbed but still moist.
That's fine for this stage. Add the broccoli, Parmesan cheese, and half of the onions over the rice mixture.
Broccoli, Parmesan, and half the onions are in. Should I stir them down into the rice or leave them on top?
Gently distribute them so they sit evenly with the rice mixture; no need to mash or overwork it. Keep the surface ready for the fish.
Okay, the top is even. I've got the fish fillets and paprika ready—how should I arrange them?
Lay the fish fillets on top of the rice mixture in a single layer, then sprinkle them with paprika. That completes the recipe's listed assembly.

Keep any sweet drizzle or topping on the outer rim of the bruschetta, not across the center. Set out 10 slices of Italian bread, 2 1/2 teaspoons olive oil, 4 vine-ripened tomatoes, and 1 teaspoon chopped fresh basil.
The bread is on the counter and the tomatoes are still by the sink. Should I prep the baking sheet first?
Yes. Use a medium baking sheet, and make sure it is ready for the bread to sit in a single layer.
I've got the sheet out. I'm wondering whether the broiler should start heating while I wash the tomatoes.
Go ahead and preheat the broiler now. While it heats, wash the 4 vine-ripened tomatoes so they have a moment to dry before dicing.
I like keeping the sweet finish just on the rim here; that's exactly what I wanted. Once the tomatoes are drying, how should I place the bread?
Lay the 10 slices of Italian bread flat on the medium baking sheet in one layer. If a couple need to sit at a slight angle to fit, that is fine as long as they do not overlap much.
They're all on the sheet with a little space between them. How careful do I need to be with the oil?
Use the full 2 1/2 teaspoons olive oil for all the slices together. Brush a light coat over the tops so each piece gets some oil without becoming soggy.
The oil is brushed on. Should I deal with the tomatoes before the bread goes anywhere near the heat?
Yes, dice the 4 vine-ripened tomatoes now. Aim for small, spoonable pieces so they will sit neatly on the bread.
The tomatoes are diced, and there's a lot of juice on the board. Do I mix the basil into that?

Add the 1 teaspoon chopped fresh basil to the diced tomatoes, or keep it separate to scatter over the top right before serving. If the tomatoes are very juicy, use a spoon so you can control how much liquid lands on the bread.
Good point. I'm keeping the tomato pieces in a bowl and leaving most of the juice behind. Anything else before topping?
Check that the bread slices are still in one layer and evenly brushed with olive oil. Keep the tomato-basil mixture close by so you can spoon it on without soaking the bread.
Everything is lined up: bread on the sheet, tomatoes diced, basil ready, and the broiler heating. How should I finish the tray for serving?
Spoon the diced tomato and basil over the oiled bread slices in tidy portions. If you add a sweet accent, keep it around the outer edge, then serve the bruschetta when the pieces look ready to plate.

messages.content: I'm getting ready to make Chocolate Covered Pretzels and I want the chocolate dipping part organized before I turn on the stove. What should I set out?

For the briny add-ins, mince any pickle, caper, olive, or pepperoncini very finely and stir them into the warm chocolate mixture so they come through as tiny bursts instead of topping the pretzels. Lay out wax paper for cooling, open the 2 (10 ounce) packages of pretzels, and keep your dipping space close to the double boiler.
Wax paper is on the counter, and I've got the pretzels in a wide bowl. What goes into the double boiler?

Add 2 cups semisweet chocolate chips and 1 tablespoon heavy whipping cream to the top of the double boiler. Keep the water below at a gentle heat so the chocolate melts over low heat rather than getting harsh or grainy.
Should I wait for the chips to melt a little before adding the cream, or do they go in together?
Put the chocolate chips and heavy whipping cream in together. Stir constantly with a heatproof spatula as they warm so the cream blends evenly into the melting chocolate.
I like having the little briny pieces mixed through the coating; that's exactly what I wanted instead of scattering them on top. The chips are just starting to slump now.
Perfect. Keep stirring slowly and scraping the bottom and sides of the bowl until the chocolate and cream turn smooth, glossy, and fully combined.
It's glossy now, but I'm not sure how thin it should be for dipping the pretzels quickly.
It should look fluid and very warm, loose enough to coat a pretzel without clumping. If it is still moving easily when you stir, start dipping before it has a chance to thicken.
I'm using twist pretzels. Do I drop a bunch in at once or handle them separately?
Dip them 1 at a time so each pretzel gets coated quickly and you can keep the shape neat. Slide each one into the chocolate, lift it out, and let the extra chocolate drip back into the bowl.
Would a fork work better than tongs for lifting them out?
A fork is usually easier for this. Let the pretzel sit on the fork, tap the fork lightly on the bowl's edge, then transfer the pretzel to the wax paper without dragging it.
The first sheet is filling up and a few are close together. Will they stick as they cool?
They can stick if the chocolate touches while setting, so leave a little space between them on the wax paper. Once they are placed, avoid moving them until the coating cools and firms.
I've still got more pretzels left, and the chocolate is getting a little thicker around the edges. Should I stop?

Keep the double boiler on low and stir the edges back into the center to keep the mixture warm and smooth. Finish dipping the remaining pretzels, then let all of them rest on the wax paper until the chocolate is firm to the touch before serving or storing with wax paper between layers.
I'm making Baked Pork Chops Low Fat Version and want someone to talk me through it while I prep.
Absolutely. Set out 6 center cut pork chops and trim off any visible fat if that hasn't been done yet. You'll also need 1 teaspoon garlic powder for seasoning.
The chops are trimmed, and the garlic powder is on the counter. What other seasoning should I grab?
Grab 1/2 teaspoon seasoning salt. The recipe also calls for 1 egg, beaten with the egg substitute mixture, so have a small bowl ready for that.
Got it. Should I start heating the oven before I rinse the pork?
Yes, go ahead and set the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), so it's ready when the chops are coated.
Oven is heating. I'm at the sink with the pork chops now—what should they look like before seasoning?
Rinse the pork chops, then pat them dry really well with paper towels. Once the surface isn't wet, season them with the garlic powder and seasoning salt to taste.
They're dry and seasoned. I have the egg bowl nearby, but I'm not sure how to set up the coating area.

Put the beaten egg and egg substitute mixture in the small bowl. Arrange your coating station so the pork can go from flour, into the egg mixture, and then into the bread crumbs without a lot of backtracking.
So flour first, then egg, then crumbs? I want the coating to stay light.
Exactly. Dredge each pork chop lightly in flour, dip it in the egg mixture, then coat it liberally with bread crumbs so the outside is evenly covered.
All 6 chops are breaded. Anything I should check before they go in the oven?

Make sure the oven has reached 350 degrees F, the chops are evenly coated, and there aren't heavy clumps of flour left on them. Then they're ready to bake according to the recipe's next cooking direction.

For the garlic and scallion, slice them very thin and soften them gently before any liquid goes into the bread machine pan. Measure the bread ingredients so you can keep the amounts straight: 1 cup water, 1 1/2 tablespoons white wine vinegar, 3 tablespoons olive oil, and 1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper.
The garlic clove is small and the scallion is trimmed. How thin are we talking—coins, slivers, or a mince?
Go for thin slivers or very fine rings rather than a chunky mince. They should soften quickly and disappear into the loaf more evenly.
I have a tiny skillet heating. Should I use fresh oil from the bottle or borrow from the measured olive oil?
Borrow a small splash from the measured 3 tablespoons olive oil. That way the oil in the skillet and the oil you add later still equal 3 tablespoons total.
The slices are in the skillet now and they smell sharp but good. How much color is okay?
Keep them pale. Pull them off once they look glossy, flexible, and fragrant, before the garlic starts browning.
I like how the thin slices softened so quickly; that works better for this bread than dropping the garlic and scallion in raw.
Yes, that soft stage will fold into the dough more smoothly. Let the skillet cool for a minute so the aromatics are warm, not hot.
They've cooled a little, and there's oil clinging to the pan. Do I scrape everything into the bread machine pan now?
Scrape in the garlic, scallion, and every bit of that oil you can get. Then you can start adding the measured liquids in the order your machine recommends.
My bread machine booklet says liquid first. Which one should hit the pan before the vinegar?
Pour in the 1 cup water first. After that, add the 1 1/2 tablespoons white wine vinegar.
Water and vinegar are in. I still have some of the 3 tablespoons olive oil in the measuring cup.
Add the remaining measured olive oil from the cup. Between what softened the garlic and scallion and what you're pouring now, the pan should get the full 3 tablespoons.
The cayenne is measured, but it looks like almost nothing on the spoon. Is 1/8 teaspoon really all that goes in?
Yes, use just 1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper for this recipe. Sprinkle it into the pan with the liquids and softened aromatics.
Everything from this part is in the pan, and I wiped the outside dry. Anything to check before I lower it into the machine?
Make sure the kneading paddle is seated, the pan rim is clean, and the outside is dry. Set the pan into the bread machine and lock it firmly in place.
It's locked in and the display is asking for a cycle. Which setting should I choose?
Select the Basic or White cycle, then press Start. Once it begins mixing, take a quick look to confirm the pan is secure, then let the machine run.
I'm making Garden Party Salad for a small lunch. Can you guide me through it without rushing?
Absolutely. Start by setting out the dressing ingredients you have listed: 1/4 cup vegetable oil, 1/4 cup orange marmalade, 3 tablespoons cider vinegar, and 3 tablespoons mayonnaise.
Those are on the counter. Should I use a mixing bowl or something smaller for the dressing?
Use a small bowl if you have one. Add the oil, orange marmalade, cider vinegar, and mayonnaise to it so you can whisk them together cleanly.
The marmalade is a little thick. Do I need to warm it first?
You can whisk it as-is; just keep going until the mixture looks smooth. The mayonnaise and vinegar will help loosen the marmalade as it blends.
Okay, the dressing is smooth now. What should happen before I assemble the salad?
Chill the dressing after whisking. Cover the bowl and put it in the refrigerator until you're close to serving time.
I'm serving soon, and I have the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley ready. What size bowl should I use?
Use a large bowl so there's room to toss without spilling. Put the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley in that bowl together.
Should I add the dressing all at once or in portions?
Since the recipe says to add the dressing just before serving and toss, pour it over the mixture close to the table time, then toss until everything is lightly coated.
The salad is coated and looks good. Any final serving advice?
Serve it right away while the dressing is freshly tossed through the chicken, raisins, almonds, and parsley. If the bowl edges got messy, wipe them before bringing it out.
I'm making chicken pot pie ix and want to get the stovetop prep going smoothly. Can you talk me through it?
Absolutely. Start by getting your ingredients within reach: 1 pound skinless, boneless chicken breast halves, cubed; 1 cup sliced carrots; 1 cup frozen green peas; and 1/2 cup sliced celery.
The chicken is cubed, and I have the carrots, peas, and celery measured. Should the oven be on already?
Yes, set the oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C), so it is heating while you handle the saucepan step.
Oven is heating. What size pan should I use for the chicken and vegetables?
Use a saucepan large enough to hold the cubed chicken, carrots, peas, and celery with room for water to cover everything.
I have them all in the saucepan. Do I add anything besides water at this point?
For this part, just add enough water to cover the chicken and vegetables.
The water is covering everything. How long should it boil?
Bring it to a boil and let it boil for 15 minutes. Keep an eye on the water level so the mixture stays covered while it cooks.
It has boiled for 15 minutes, and the chicken looks cooked through. What do I do with the liquid?
Remove the saucepan from the heat, then drain the chicken and vegetables.
Drained. Should I leave the mixture in the pan or move it somewhere else while the oven finishes heating?
Set the drained chicken, carrots, peas, and celery aside for the next part of the pot pie. The required prep for this section is complete.

Reserve a small ladleful of gravy for serving, and spoon it only onto slices that need a little loosening. Set out a large bowl, a 10x15 inch jellyroll pan, waxed paper, 3 pounds ground beef, 17 finely crushed saltine crackers, 1/2 cup milk, 1 1/2 teaspoons garlic powder, plus onion powder, salt, and pepper.
I have the jellyroll pan out, but I haven't lined it yet. Should I do that before crushing the crackers?
Yes, line the 10x15 inch pan with waxed paper now while everything is dry. Press the paper into the corners and let a bit hang over the edges so it's easier to manage later.
The paper is down, though it has some creases along one long side. Is that going to make the meat stick weirdly?
It should be fine. Flatten the biggest crease with your palm, then leave it alone; once the beef mixture is pressed firmly into the pan, it will hold the paper in place.
That gravy idea is exactly what I wanted; I like that the slices won't end up weighed down. I'm opening the beef now and dropping it into the bowl in chunks.
Keep the chunks loose in the bowl so the crackers and milk can work through them. Sprinkle the 17 finely crushed saltines over the beef rather than dumping them all in one spot.
Some cracker crumbs are powdery, but a few pieces are more like flakes. Do I need them completely uniform?
They don't need to be perfect. If you see any obvious large bits, crush those once more; small flakes will disappear into the 3 pounds of beef as you mix.
Okay, the crumbs are on top. Should the 1/2 cup milk go in slowly, or can I pour it over everything?
Pour the 1/2 cup milk in a thin drizzle across the surface. That helps moisten the crumbs evenly before you start bringing the beef together.
The milk slipped down the side of the bowl, and the top still looks a little dry. Should I mash it hard with my hands?
Use a folding motion instead of mashing. Lift the beef from the bottom, turn it over the crumbs, and repeat until you no longer see dry cracker patches.
It's sticky and mostly combined. I haven't added the garlic powder or the other seasonings yet.
Sprinkle in 1 1/2 teaspoons garlic powder now, then dust the surface with onion powder, salt, and pepper. Spread them broadly over the mixture so you don't get one heavily seasoned pocket.
I'm mixing it in, but I'm trying not to overwork the beef. What should it look like when I stop?
Stop when the seasoning looks evenly distributed and the beef, cracker crumbs, and milk are blended. It should look cohesive, not kneaded smooth.
The mixture looks even. How do I get it into the lined pan without making the edges thin?

Move it over in several large handfuls, placing them down the center of the waxed-paper-lined pan first. Spread outward to the corners, then press the raised areas down until the layer is even across the 10x15 inch pan.

Keep the serving plate to 2 thin sauce stripes, and put the remaining sauce in a small dipping dish so the churros stay uncovered. For the dough base, set out 1 cup water, 2 1/2 tablespoons white sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons vegetable oil, and have the flour nearby for after the mixture boils.
Does the vegetable oil go into the saucepan with the water and sugar, or does it get added later?
Add it right away. The 1 cup water, 2 1/2 tablespoons white sugar, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil all go into the small saucepan before it heats.
The oil is sitting in little patches on the surface. Should I try to whisk it smooth before turning on the heat?
You don't need to force it smooth. Put the saucepan over medium heat and stir gently as it warms so the sugar and salt dissolve.
It's steaming now, and I see bubbles around the edges, but the center isn't really rolling yet.
Let it go a bit longer. You're looking for a real boil across the liquid, then take the saucepan off the heat right away.
If it starts bubbling hard, should I lower the heat first or just move it off the burner?
Move it off the burner once it reaches that boil. The flour goes in after the pan is off the heat, while the liquid is still hot.

I like the 2 thin sauce stripes on the plate; that works better for this because the churros can stay crisp instead of getting buried under sauce. The pan is off the heat now—how should I work in the flour?
Add the flour to the hot liquid off the heat and stir firmly. Scrape the sides and bottom of the pan as you mix until it comes together into one dough ball with no dry flour showing.
It turned thick almost immediately and is clinging to the spoon. I was expecting something more like batter.
That thick texture is what you want here. Churro dough should pull together into a cohesive ball, not stay pourable.
Can that dough sit in the saucepan for a few minutes while I bring the frying oil up?
Yes, a short wait is fine while you heat the frying oil. Use a deep-fryer or deep skillet and bring the oil to 375 degrees F, or 190 degrees C, before adding dough.
I'm using a deep skillet, and the thermometer tends to jump around. How close to 375 do I need to keep it?
Aim to stay as close to 375 degrees F, 190 degrees C, as you can. If the temperature drops after adding dough, wait for it to climb back before starting another batch.
Can I pipe a few churro strips onto parchment while the oil catches up, or should I wait?
You can pipe a few pieces ahead so they're ready, but don't slide them into the skillet until the oil is back at temperature. Oil that's too cool can make them greasy.
Once they're fried, do they go straight onto the plate with the sauce stripes, or should I drain them somewhere first?
Drain them briefly first so excess oil comes off. Then arrange them on the plate with the 2 thin sauce stripes and keep the extra sauce in the small dish for dipping.
I'm making Flavorful Rice Dressing 2 and have a large bowl and skillet out. Can you guide me through it?
Absolutely. Tear up 7 slices of day-old bread and add them to the large bowl, then add 1 cup torn corn bread as well.
The breads are in the bowl. Should the water go in before I heat the skillet?

Pull 1 (12 ounce) package of refrigerated biscuit dough and 1 (8 ounce) package of corn bread mix. You'll also want 1 cup diced onion and 1 cup diced celery ready for the pot later.

At this stage, focus on making the flavored butter mixture thoroughly combined. Keep the drained escargots ready nearby for assembling the vol au vent.

That's the prep the recipe gives: oven at 400 degrees F/200 degrees C, escargots drained, rinsed, and drained again, and the butter mixture mixed thoroughly. You're ready to move on to assembly.

Yes, press out excess air, seal the bag tightly, and set it on a plate or in a shallow dish in case of leaks.

Keep them mostly in one line down the center of each crepe, using 1 sliced banana per crepe.

Roll each crepe gently around the banana-filled center, keeping the seam tucked underneath when you set it down.

Warm the skillet over medium heat, then place the rolled crepes in it seam-side down so they hold their shape.

Let the crepes warm for about 90 seconds, just enough to soften the filling and take the chill off. Move them to plates and add the pressurized whipped cream right before serving.

Absolutely. Set out 1 (8 ounce) package of softened cream cheese and 1/2 cup softened butter so they're easy to beat together.

You'll need 2 cups all-purpose flour and 1 cup white sugar. Keep the flour near your mixing bowl and the sugar near a saucepan for later.

Soft is fine. Shape it into a ball, cover it, and chill it for 2 hours so it firms up.

You can clean the mixing bowl. Keep the 1 cup white sugar handy, along with milk and a saucepan for the cooking step.

Put the sugar and milk in a saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the milk boils and the sugar is dissolved.
