For the chicken pieces, brown them in the skillet, then use a sheet pan or broiler finish and let them rest uncovered briefly before serving. Start by clearing space for 4 pounds of dark meat chicken pieces, 1 tablespoon vegetable oil, 5 cloves crushed garlic, and 1/2 cup all-purpose flour.
The chicken is still wrapped, and I have the oil nearby. Should I measure the flour and garlic now?
Yes. Put the 1/2 cup all-purpose flour in a shallow dish so it is ready for dredging, and keep the 5 cloves crushed garlic in a small bowl because you will use only 1/2 of it at first.
Okay, flour is in a shallow dish and the garlic is split in two small piles. What should happen with the flour?
Season the flour with poultry seasoning and mix it evenly through the 1/2 cup of flour so every piece of chicken gets coated the same way.
I like that browning-and-uncovered-rest move here; it works better for this dish. My skillet is on the stove now—do I heat it before coating the chicken?
Heat the large skillet first, then add the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil. Give the oil a moment to shimmer before anything else goes in.
The oil is shimmering. Do I add all the garlic or just the portion we set aside?
Add 1/2 of the crushed garlic to the skillet now. Stir it briefly so it scents the oil without letting it burn.
It smells garlicky already. Should I start dredging while that cooks?
Yes, dredge the dark meat chicken pieces in the seasoned flour. Shake off excess flour before each piece goes into the skillet so the coating browns instead of clumping.
I'm putting the pieces in, but the pan is getting crowded. Is that a problem?
Leave enough room around the chicken so it browns. If needed, work in batches, keeping the same 4 or 5 minutes of browning time for each batch.
After the skillet browning, how do I handle the sheet pan finish without losing the crust?

Move the browned chicken pieces to a sheet pan in a single layer, or use the broiler briefly if you want more surface color. Keep them uncovered for a short rest before serving so the coating stays crisp instead of steaming.
I'm making Best Chocolate Chippers today. Can you talk me through it while I get set up?
Absolutely. Start by pulling out 1 cup butter, 1 cup vegetable oil, 1 cup white sugar, and 1 cup packed brown sugar. You'll also want a large mixing bowl ready.
The butter, oil, and both sugars are on the counter. Should the oven be heating already?
Yes, go ahead and bring the oven up to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), so it's ready when the dough comes together.
Oven is on. Do I mix the butter and oil before adding the sugars?
Put the butter, vegetable oil, brown sugar, and white sugar into the large bowl together, then cream them until the mixture looks smooth.
It's starting to look blended, but there are a few streaks of sugar. Keep going?
Yes, keep creaming until it looks evenly combined and smooth rather than streaky. Scrape the sides of the bowl if anything is clinging there.
Okay, the mixture is smooth now. What goes in after that?
Beat in the eggs and vanilla next. Add them to the creamed mixture and mix until everything is incorporated.
The wet mixture looks even. I have the dry ingredients nearby—how should I add them?
Combine the flour, baking soda, cream of tartar, and salt separately, then stir that dry mixture into the creamed mixture.
Should I stir hard, or just fold it in until it disappears?
Stir just until the dry ingredients are worked into the creamed mixture and you don't see loose flour. That keeps the dough from being overmixed.
I'm making Flavorful Rice Dressing 2 and want to get the bread part right before I start cooking. What should I set out?
Set out 7 slices of day-old bread, torn into pieces, plus 1 cup of torn corn bread. You'll also need 2/3 cup hot water and 1/2 cup thinly sliced celery ready nearby.
The breads are torn and in a bowl. Should the hot water go in all at once, or should I add it gradually?
Add the 2/3 cup hot water to the bread in a large bowl and lightly toss it together. Don't mash it; just moisten the bread so the pieces stay somewhat loose.
Got it. I have celery sliced, and I see the directions mention onion and mushrooms too. What pan setup should I use?
Use a skillet with oil for the vegetables. Add the thinly sliced celery along with the onion and mushrooms, then sauté them until tender while stirring constantly.
How tender should the celery be before I stop cooking it?
Cook until the celery has softened but still has a little shape, and the onion and mushrooms are softened too. Keep stirring so nothing catches in the oil.
The vegetables are softened and the bread mixture is waiting. Do I pour the skillet contents straight into the bowl?
Yes, stir the sautéed celery, onion, and mushrooms into the bread mixture. Fold it through so the vegetables are spread evenly without crushing the bread too much.
The mixture looks combined but a little uneven in spots. Should I keep mixing before adding anything else?
Give it a few more gentle turns until the bread and vegetables look fairly distributed. Then add the remaining ingredients called for in your recipe and mix well.
Once the remaining ingredients are in, what texture am I aiming for before I move it to serve or cook further?
It should look evenly mixed and moist, with the torn bread and corn bread holding together lightly rather than turning into a paste. Scrape the bowl sides as you mix so everything is incorporated.

Absolutely. Set out 1 tablespoon vegetable oil and 1 chopped onion. You'll also need a 9 inch pie pan for baking.
The onion is chopped and the pie pan is on the counter. What else should I pull from the fridge or freezer?
Grab 1 (10 ounce) package of frozen chopped spinach, thawed and drained, plus 5 eggs, beaten.
The spinach is thawed, but it still feels a little wet. Should I drain it more for this quiche?
Yes, drain it well so the quiche doesn't turn watery. Press out excess moisture, then keep the spinach nearby with the beaten eggs.

heat the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). While it heats, lightly grease the 9 inch pie pan.

Yes. Put a large skillet over medium-high heat and add the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil.

I'd like to make Caraway Rye Muffins. Can you help me get the ingredients organized before I mix anything?

Use a large bowl for the dry mixture. Add both flours, the sugar, baking powder, salt, and caraway seeds, then whisk or stir them together so the baking powder and seeds are evenly distributed.

Small clumps are fine, but break up any larger ones with the spoon as you stir. The goal is an even dry mix before you add the cheese.
Okay, the dry mix looks even. When does the cheese go in?
Stir the cheese into the dry ingredients now. Tossing it with the flour mixture helps keep it from sinking or clumping once the wet ingredients go in.
Cheese is mixed in. I have the egg, milk, and oil ready in measuring cups.
Combine the egg, milk, and oil in a separate bowl or cup, beating just enough to blend the egg into the liquid.
The wet mixture is combined. How much should I stir once I pour it in?
Pour the wet mixture into the dry ingredients and stir only until everything is moistened. Stop while the batter still looks a bit lumpy; overmixing can make the muffins tough.
The batter is thick and lumpy, not smooth. I have muffin cups lined with paper.
That texture sounds right. Fill the greased or paper-lined muffin cups two-thirds full, then they're ready for baking according to your recipe's oven directions.
I want to make English Walnut Pie. Can you walk me through it while I get the counter set up?

Absolutely. Set out a large mixing bowl, a whisk or hand mixer, and your measuring spoons and cups. For the listed ingredients, you'll need 3 eggs, 1/4 teaspoon salt, 3/4 cup white sugar, and 2 teaspoons vanilla extract.
I've got the eggs and vanilla out. Should I heat the oven before I start mixing?
Yes, go ahead and heat the oven to 400 degrees F (205 degrees C), so it's ready by the time the filling is mixed.
The oven is heating. I'm cracking the eggs now—do they go straight into the large bowl?
Yes. Crack all 3 eggs into the large bowl, then beat them until the yolks and whites are fully combined and the mixture looks smooth.
They're beaten and a little foamy. I measured 3/4 cup white sugar and 1/4 teaspoon salt.
Add the 3/4 cup white sugar and 1/4 teaspoon salt to the beaten eggs, then stir until the sugar starts to dissolve into the mixture.
Sugar and salt are mixed in. Where does the vanilla fit?
Pour in the 2 teaspoons vanilla extract and mix it through. The recipe also calls for syrup at this stage, so stir that in with the sugar, salt, and vanilla.
The filling looks glossy now. I still have butter on the stove—what texture am I aiming for?
Melt the butter or margarine completely, but don't let it brown. Once it's liquid, add it to the egg mixture and stir so it blends evenly.
It's combined. Anything I should check before I move on to the pie shell?
Give the bowl a quick scrape around the sides and bottom so the sugar, salt, vanilla, syrup, and melted butter are evenly incorporated with the eggs. The mixture should look smooth and ready to pour.

Mostly leave it covered so the chicken cooks evenly in the broth. If the simmer sounds too vigorous, lower the heat a little; otherwise, just check briefly near the end.
The chicken pieces are pretty thick. What am I looking for when the timer is close?
Check that the chicken is no longer pink in the center and that the juices run clear. If the center still looks pink, cover it again and keep it at a low simmer a bit longer.
The 30 minutes are up, the centers look cooked through, and the juices are clear. What happens next?
Remove the chicken from the saucepan and let it cool. Once it is cool enough to handle, it is ready for the next part of Chicken Pot Pie II.

messages.content: I'm making Alisons Slow Cooker Vegetable Beef Soup today. Can you walk me through the setup before I load the slow cooker?

For the basil at the end, mince it finely, stir some into the soup near the finish, and save a little fresh for serving. Set out 1 1/2 pounds cubed beef stew meat, 2 cups water, 1 small chopped onion, and 1 (28 ounce) can crushed tomatoes, plus your mixed vegetables, potatoes, bouillon, pepper, salt, and basil.
The beef is still in the package, and the onion and potatoes need attention. What should I prep before anything goes into the cooker?

Chop the 1 small onion if it is not already done, cut the potatoes into bite-size pieces, and keep the mixed vegetables close by. You can also open the 28 ounce can of crushed tomatoes so everything is ready to add smoothly.
Do I brown the beef first, or does it go in as is?
For this recipe, put the cubed beef stew meat straight into the slow cooker. Spread the 1 1/2 pounds of beef across the bottom so the other ingredients can settle around it.
I like that basil move for this soup; the minced pieces worked through and a small fresh bit at the end works better than big leaves on top. The beef is in now.
Pour the 2 cups water over the beef. It does not need to cover everything completely yet, because the tomatoes and vegetables will add more moisture as they cook.
Water is in, and I'm wiping the cutting board. Should the onion and tomatoes go in together?
Yes. Add the chopped onion and the full 28 ounce can of crushed tomatoes, then stir in the mixed vegetables and potatoes so they are evenly distributed around the beef.
Should I drain anything from the tomato can or thaw the mixed vegetables first?
Do not drain the crushed tomatoes; their liquid belongs in the soup. The mixed vegetables can go in frozen, and the potatoes should be tucked down into the liquid as much as you can manage.
It looks thick now with the potatoes and tomato. What seasoning should I add before I put the lid on?
Season the soup with bouillon, pepper, salt, and basil. Go easy on the salt at first if your bouillon is salty, and if your basil is fresh, use the minced portion near the end so it stays bright.
Okay, lid is on. When it is done, what should I check before serving?

Check that the beef is tender, the potatoes are soft all the way through, and the vegetables are hot. Stir the soup, taste for bouillon, salt, and pepper balance, then finish each bowl with the reserved fresh basil.

messages.content: I'm getting ready to make BBQ Chuck Roast. Can you walk me through the setup before I open anything?

For the tender lower parsley or cilantro pieces, chop them finely into small uneven bits and add them right into the marinade bowl early. Also set out 1 (5 pound) chuck roast, 1 cup barbeque sauce, 1 cup teriyaki sauce, and 1 (12 fluid ounce) can or bottle beer.
Got it. I have the roast on a tray, the sauces on the counter, and a big mixing bowl. Does the beer go in with both sauces right away?

Yes. Pour the barbeque sauce, teriyaki sauce, and beer into the large bowl, then stir in the garlic, ginger, onion, black pepper, salt, and the chopped greens so the marinade is blended before the meat goes in.
Should I mince the garlic and ginger pretty small, or can they stay chunky since this marinates for a while?

Keep them small enough to spread through the liquid—minced garlic, finely chopped or grated ginger, and onion cut small all work well. The marinade should look loose, glossy, and easy to spoon over the roast.
I like using those lower herb pieces this way; that texture works better for this kind of saucy roast. Is the bowl supposed to hold the meat too?
Yes, use a bowl large enough for both the marinade and the whole roast. Once the liquid is mixed, lower the 5 pound chuck roast into it and turn it so all sides get coated.
The roast is in and coated, but the top isn't fully submerged. Is that a problem?
That's fine as long as you cover it and turn it often. Refrigerate the covered roast for six hours, rotating it now and then so different surfaces spend time in the marinade.
I'm covering the bowl now. Should I leave any extra marinade aside before it chills?
No need to hold any back for this step. Keep all the marinade with the roast while it chills, and make sure the bowl stays covered in the refrigerator.
It's been marinating for the full time. I'm clearing space near the grill—what should happen before I take the meat out?
Preheat an outdoor grill for indirect heat first. While the grill heats, keep the roast chilled and covered so it isn't sitting out longer than needed.
The grill is arranged for indirect heat. Do I carry the whole bowl outside or separate the meat first?
Remove the roast from the marinade first, then pour the marinade into a saucepan. That way the roast can head to the grill while the liquid is ready for the next cooking stage.
Should I scrape the onion and herb bits off the roast when I lift it, or let some cling?

Let a little cling if it naturally sticks, but don't scoop extra solids onto the roast. Just move the meat out of the bowl and transfer the remaining marinade, including the aromatics, into the saucepan.

messages.content: I'm starting Apple Blueberry Tarts, and I've got the apples and blueberries out. What should I get organized first?

Keep the tart finish oven-friendly on a sheet pan, with the broiler as a workable option if you need it, and rest the tarts uncovered briefly before serving so they don't steam soft. For the filling, set up a medium bowl for 2 medium cooking apples, peeled, cored, and chopped, plus 2/3 cup fresh or frozen blueberries.
The apples are peeled and chopped, and the blueberries are still frozen. Is that okay for the filling?
Yes, fresh or frozen blueberries both work here. Add them straight to the chopped apples, and keep the fruit in that medium bowl while you measure the sweetener and spice.
I have the granular sugar substitute nearby. How much goes in with the fruit?
Use 1 tablespoon heat-stable granular sugar substitute. Sprinkle it over the apples and blueberries so it can coat the fruit evenly when you stir.
I like that oven setup for these tarts; it works better for this dish. How much spice should I put in the fruit bowl?

Add 1/4 teaspoon apple pie spice or ground allspice to the fruit bowl. The ingredient list sets out 1/2 teaspoon total, but this step uses 1/4 teaspoon with the apples, blueberries, and sugar substitute.
The fruit mixture is stirred together. Should I cover it while I make the dough?
No need to cover it for this short pause. Just set the bowl aside while the apples, blueberries, sugar substitute, and spice sit together.
I'm ready for the dry bowl. What goes into it?
Use another medium bowl. Stir together the whole wheat pastry flour, kosher salt, and 1/8 teaspoon apple pie spice until the dry ingredients look evenly mixed.
Should I make a well in the flour before adding the wet ingredients?
You can, but it isn't necessary. Add the oil and milk all at once to the flour mixture, then switch to gentle mixing right away.
I poured in the oil and milk, and the dough looks shaggy with flour around the sides.
Use a fork to stir lightly, pulling the dry bits from the edge toward the center. Stop as soon as the dough comes together so it stays tender.
Once they're baked, how should I handle them before I serve so the bottoms don't get soggy?
Leave the tarts uncovered for a short rest on the sheet pan before serving. That lets steam escape while keeping the apple-blueberry filling and tender dough from turning soft underneath.
I want to make Absolutely Awesome BBQ Sauce. Can you talk me through what to pull out before I start heating anything?
Absolutely. Set a saucepan on the stove, but keep the heat off for the moment. Measure out 1 cup brown sugar, 1/2 cup chile sauce, 1/2 cup rum, and 1/4 cup soy sauce.
I've got those measured. The directions mention a few other flavorings too—should those go in at the same time?
Yes. Have ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, garlic, dry mustard, and pepper ready as well. They all get mixed into the saucepan with the brown sugar, chile sauce, rum, and soy sauce.
Should I melt the brown sugar first, or just combine everything cold in the pan?
Combine everything in the saucepan first, then put it over low heat. Stir as it warms so the brown sugar dissolves into the sauces and the mixture starts looking smooth.
The pan is on low and the sauce is loosening up. Do I need it boiling?
Keep it gentler than a boil. You want a low simmer, with small bubbles and steady heat, so the rum and seasonings can cook into the sauce without scorching the sugar.
It's starting to bubble lightly around the edges. How long should I keep it there?
Let it simmer for 30 minutes. Stir occasionally, especially across the bottom and corners of the saucepan, because the brown sugar can stick if it sits too long.
About halfway through, it looks a little thicker and glossy. Is that what I'm aiming for?
Yes, that's right. Keep the heat low and continue the occasional stirring until the full 30 minutes is up; it should smell concentrated and look like a cohesive BBQ sauce.
The 30 minutes are done. Should I use it right away or store it?
Take it off the heat and let it cool. Once cooled, refrigerate it until you're ready to use it; give it a stir before serving or brushing it onto food.
I want to make Eggnog Blend. Can you talk me through what to set out and how to cook the base?

Absolutely. Set out 4 cups half-and-half, 1 cup white sugar, 11 beaten egg yolks, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract. You'll also need a saucepan, a whisk, and room in the refrigerator for chilling the mixture overnight.
I've got the saucepan and whisk ready. Should the half-and-half and sugar go in before I turn the heat up?
Yes. Add the half-and-half and white sugar to the saucepan, then keep the heat low. Stir gently so the sugar dissolves without scorching the dairy.
The sugar looks dissolved and the mixture is warm. How do I add the egg yolks without scrambling them?
Whisk steadily as you add the beaten egg yolks. Keep the heat low and continue cooking until the mixture turns into a light custard. Don't let it boil.
What should that light custard look like when it's ready?
It should look slightly thickened and smooth, more like a thin custard than milk. If you lift the whisk, it should leave a light coating rather than running off instantly.
It's thickened a bit and there are no bubbles from boiling. Do I keep it on the stove longer?
No, take it off the heat once that light custard has formed. Let it cool down before you put it in the refrigerator.
Should I cover it before chilling, and how long does it need in the fridge?
Once it has cooled, cover it and refrigerate it overnight. That chill time is part of the recipe and helps the base settle before the final mix-ins.
It's the next day and the base is cold. What do I stir in to serve it?
Stir the vanilla into the chilled mixture, along with cream, dark rum, scotch, and vanilla ice cream. Mix until it's smooth and cold, then serve the Eggnog Blend chilled.

I want to make Chai Butter Cookies. Can you talk me through the setup and dough?
Absolutely. Set out a large mixing bowl and gather 1 cup unsalted butter, 1 cup chai tea mix, 1 1/3 cups white sugar, and 2 eggs.
Butter, chai mix, sugar, and eggs are on the counter. Should the bowl be big enough for all the dry ingredients later?
Yes, use a bowl with enough room for mixing without spilling, because the dry ingredients will be blended into the creamed mixture later.
I'm ready to start mixing. What texture am I aiming for with the butter?
Cream the butter with the 1 1/3 cups white sugar and the chai tea mix until the mixture looks light and fluffy rather than dense or streaky.
The mixture has gotten paler and softer. Do the eggs go in together or separately?
Add the eggs one at a time. Beat well after the first egg is mixed in, then add the second and mix well again.
Both eggs are incorporated. The batter looks smooth. What should I do with the flour mixture?
Combine the flour, baking powder, and salt separately, then blend that into the creamed mixture until all of the dry ingredients have been absorbed.
Should I keep mixing once I don't see dry patches anymore?
Stop once the dry mixture is absorbed and the dough looks evenly combined. That helps keep the texture from getting overworked.
The dough is together. How do I handle it before baking?
Cover the dough and refrigerate it for 1 hour so it can firm up before you continue.

For the serving garnish, gather the softer pieces in the center and set the crunchy pieces in a tidy crescent on one side. Start the ice ring now: pour 4 cups cranberry juice into a 5-cup ring mold, set it level, and get it into the freezer.
The ring mold is filled, and I cleared a flat spot in the freezer. Is this something that firms up this afternoon, or does it need longer?
Give it the full overnight freeze. The cranberry juice needs to become a solid ring so it releases cleanly and floats instead of cracking apart in the punch bowl.

You can measure ahead if you want: 1 1/2 cups sugar, 1 1/2 cups lemon juice, and 1 cup orange juice. Keep the ginger ale cold, but wait to stir it in until you're closer to serving so it stays lively.
I like that garnish plan for this—the crunchy part looks better as a crescent instead of being spread across the whole top. While the ring freezes, I'll measure the sugar and juices.
That'll work well. Put the sugar, lemon juice, and orange juice together in the punch bowl when you're ready, then stir until the sugar fully dissolves and the mixture no longer feels gritty.
The lemon and orange juice are in the bowl with the sugar. It's taking a little stirring; should I keep going before adding anything bubbly?
Yes, keep stirring until the sugar disappears into the citrus. Add the ginger ale only after that, and stir it in gently so you don't knock out all the fizz.
The mixture looks clear now, and I don't see sugar at the bottom. The ginger ale is still in the fridge.
Perfect. Chill the punch bowl mixture if you have room, then add the cold ginger ale shortly before serving. That keeps the Frosted Ruby Punch bright and cold.
The cranberry ring has been in overnight and feels solid. What's the safest way to unmold it?
Loosen the edges carefully. If the ring resists, run a little warm water over the outside of the mold for just a moment, then invert or ease it out before the surface melts too much.
It released in one piece. I'm nervous about splashing when I add it to the bowl.
Hold it close to the punch surface and lower it in slowly, letting it float rather than dropping it. Once it's settled, it will keep the bowl cold and add that ruby look.

Place the soft garnish near the center opening or middle area, then curve the crisp garnish along one side in a small crescent. Serve the punch cold while the cranberry ring is still firm and floating.
I want to make Carrot and Coriander Soup II. Can you talk me through the prep before I start cooking?
Absolutely. Get 4 large carrots cut into 1 inch pieces, plus 1/4 large onion chopped. You'll also want a large saucepan ready since everything starts in that pot.
The carrots are cut and the onion is chopped. What should I measure for the liquid and herbs?
Measure out 1 quart vegetable broth and chop 1/2 cup fresh cilantro. Once those are ready, the ingredient list is complete.
I've got the broth and cilantro. Do the carrots and onion need to soften separately first?
No separate sauté is needed for this recipe. Put the carrots, onion, vegetable broth, and cilantro straight into the large saucepan together.
Everything is in the pan. Should I start on high heat or keep it gentle?
Bring the saucepan to a boil, then let it cook until the carrots are tender. That should take about 10 minutes.
How tender should the carrots be before I stop cooking?
They should be soft enough that a fork goes through easily, since they'll need to puree smoothly. If they're still firm in the center, give them a little more time while keeping the soup hot.
The carrots are tender now, and the soup is still bubbling a bit. What should I do before blending?
Take the saucepan off the heat and let the soup cool slightly. That makes it safer and easier to puree.
It has cooled a little. What's the best way to get the texture right?
Puree the soup until smooth using a blender or food processor. Work carefully with the warm liquid, then serve once the texture is even and velvety.

Great, that's exactly the setup for today. Before I start beating anything, what should I put on the counter?
Set out 4 egg whites, 1 1/4 cups white sugar, 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, and 1 teaspoon lemon juice. You'll also want a large bowl, a baking sheet, and parchment paper.
I've got the egg whites separated and the sugar measured. Should the oven be on already?
Yes. set the oven to 300 degrees F (150 degrees C) so it's ready by the time the meringue is shaped.
Oven is heating. I'm trying to avoid a messy pan—what do I do with the sheet?
Line the baking sheet with parchment paper, smoothing it down so the pavlova has a clean surface to bake on.
Parchment is on. How big should I make the guide for the pavlova?
Draw a 9 inch circle on the parchment paper; that gives you a clear outline for spreading the meringue.

Put the egg whites in a large bowl and beat them until they're stiff but not dry; they should stand up firmly while still looking glossy.
If they start looking a little dull, should I keep going or stop?
Stop before they turn dry or grainy. The recipe's target is stiff but not dry, so glossy firmness is the point to catch.
I still have the vanilla extract and lemon juice measured out. Are those part of the prep I should keep nearby?
Yes, keep the 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and 1 teaspoon lemon juice within reach with the measured sugar so everything is ready as you continue the pavlova.
I'm making Chicken Spinach Bake and I've got the frozen chopped spinach thawing. Can you walk me through what to do?
Absolutely. You'll need 3 packages of frozen chopped spinach, 10 ounces each, thawed, plus 3 eggs, 1/2 teaspoon onion salt, and 1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg.
The spinach is thawed, but it's really wet. Should I drain it before mixing anything?
Yes—drain it well, then squeeze out as much excess moisture as you can. The drier spinach will help the bake set up better instead of turning watery.
I'm using a colander and a clean towel for that. While I squeeze it, what should I mix in the bowl?
In a mixing bowl, beat the 3 eggs with the 1/2 teaspoon onion salt and 1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg until everything looks evenly blended.
The eggs are beaten and the spinach is squeezed out. Does the spinach go straight into the egg mixture?
Yes. Add the spinach to the egg mixture, then stir in 1/4 cup Parmesan cheese and mix it well so the spinach is evenly coated.
It's mixed together now. The texture looks thick and a little clumpy from the spinach—is that okay?
That's fine. Just break up any large spinach clumps with your spoon so the egg and Parmesan are distributed throughout.
I also have bread crumbs and more Parmesan on the counter. Are those for the top?
Right. Combine the bread crumbs with the remaining Parmesan in a separate small bowl so you have the topping ready.
Should I put that crumb mixture on after the spinach mixture is in the baking dish?
Yes, spread the spinach mixture into the baking dish, then scatter the bread crumb and remaining Parmesan mixture evenly over the top.
I'm making Cheddar Artichoke Quiche Cups today. Can you help me get the artichokes and egg mixture started in the right order?
Absolutely. Put a 1 (7.5 ounce) jar of marinated artichoke hearts on the counter, along with 1 small finely chopped onion, 1 minced garlic clove, and 4 beaten eggs.
I have the jar open, but I don't want to lose the marinade. How much should I save when I drain it?
Drain the artichoke hearts, but reserve half of the marinade. That saved marinade is what you'll use to cook the onion and garlic.
The artichokes are drained and I saved half the marinade in a small bowl. Do I chop them finely or leave bigger pieces?
Chop the artichokes into small bite-size pieces so they'll distribute well through the quiche cups, then set them aside for a moment.
Artichokes are chopped. I've got a skillet out for the onion and garlic—does the marinade go in instead of oil?
Yes. Pour the reserved marinade into the skillet, add the finely chopped onion and minced garlic, and sauté them until they're tender.
The onion and garlic are soft and smell good. Should I keep them in the skillet while I mix the eggs?
Take the skillet off the heat and set the onion-garlic mixture aside. You want it ready to add later without continuing to cook.
I've got a large bowl ready with the 4 beaten eggs. What else gets stirred into that bowl?
In the large bowl, combine the beaten egg with bread crumbs, mustard, oregano, pepper, and hot pepper sauce. Stir until the mixture looks evenly blended.
The egg mixture is combined. Do the chopped artichokes and sautéed onion-garlic mixture go in next?
Yes, fold in the chopped artichokes and the sautéed onion and garlic so everything is evenly distributed before you portion the mixture for the quiche cups.
I'm making Enchilada Style Burritos with frozen bean and cheese burritos. Can you help me get the dish started?
Absolutely. Grease a 13-in baking dish, then arrange all 6 frozen prepared bean and cheese burritos in it. Once they're in the dish, set it aside while you make the sauce.
The burritos are in the greased pan. What should I put next to the stove for the sauce?
Set out 2 tablespoons butter or margarine, 3 tablespoons all-purpose flour, and 1 3/4 cups water. You'll also want a saucepan and something sturdy for stirring.
I've got the saucepan ready. Should the butter go in by itself?
Yes. Put the 2 tablespoons butter or margarine in the saucepan and melt it gently, stirring or swirling so it doesn't sit in one spot too long.
The butter is melted and bubbling a little. How do I add the flour without lumps?
Sprinkle in the 3 tablespoons all-purpose flour while stirring right away. Keep stirring until the mixture looks smooth before you add the water.
It's smooth now, kind of like a paste. Do I pour in all the water at once?
Add the 1 3/4 cups water gradually, stirring as you pour. That slow addition helps the sauce stay smooth instead of clumping.
The water is mixed in and the sauce looks thin. Is that okay at this point?
That's fine. Bring it to a boil, then keep cooking and stirring for 2 minutes, or until it thickens.
It has thickened after the 2 minutes. Should I leave the burritos waiting in the baking dish?
Yes, the recipe has the frozen burritos set aside in the greased 13-in baking dish while the sauce thickens. You're ready for whatever topping or baking step your version calls for next.

Cut the briny add-ins—pickle, caper, olive, or pepperoncini—very small, then use only a light sprinkle so they come through as tiny salty flashes in the creamy eggnog. For the base, measure 4 cups half-and-half and 1 cup white sugar into a saucepan and keep the heat low.

Lower the heat or briefly lift the pan off the burner while whisking. You want gentle thickening, not bubbles or graininess.

Stop when it forms a light custard: smooth, slightly thickened, and able to coat a spoon lightly. Do not let it boil.

If it looks smooth, you can just cool it. Let it sit off the heat and stir occasionally at first, then cover it once it is no longer hot.

Move it to the refrigerator and chill it overnight. That gives the custard base time to get fully cold before the finishing ingredients go in.

messages.content: I'm making Cabin Hash tonight. Can you help me get organized before I start cooking?

Finish the potato-and-ham hash in the oven on a sheet pan or briefly under the broiler, then leave it uncovered before serving. For setup, have 12 medium potatoes peeled, cooked, and cubed, 3 cups cubed fully cooked ham, 1/2 cup chopped onion, and 1/2 cup butter or margarine ready; you'll also need broccoli for the heat-through step, plus salt, pepper, and sour cream if you want it at the table.
The potatoes are cooked and cubed, and the ham is already diced. I still need to chop the onion—does it go in right away?

Yes. Chop enough onion to make 1/2 cup, then melt the butter or margarine in a large skillet. Add the potatoes, ham, and onion together, and stir often while the potatoes start picking up light browning.
Should I use the whole amount of butter at the start, or hold some back?

Use the full 1/2 cup at the start so the potatoes have enough fat to brown instead of drying out. If the skillet looks crowded, keep the heat moderate and give the potatoes time against the pan between stirs.
I like finishing it on the sheet pan and leaving it uncovered; that works better for this dish. How browned should the potatoes be before I move on?

Look for light golden edges on the potato cubes, with the ham heated and the onion softened. It does not need to be deeply crisp in the skillet, especially if you're giving it that final uncovered finish.
The potatoes have some color now. I have broccoli florets ready—when do they go in?
Add the broccoli now and stir it through the hot potatoes, ham, onion, and butter. Keep it in the skillet just long enough to heat through so it stays bright and doesn't turn mushy.

Season after the broccoli is hot. Add salt and pepper, taste carefully because the ham is already salty, and adjust until the potatoes and broccoli both taste balanced.
It tastes good. Do I spread it out now for the finish?
Yes, spread the hash in an even layer on a sheet pan, or slide it briefly under the broiler if you want a little more edge color. Keep an eye on it so the ham and potatoes brown without drying out.
I'm ready to serve. Should the sour cream go on top or on the side?
Serve the Cabin Hash hot, with sour cream on the side or dolloped lightly on top if desired. Let it stand uncovered just before serving so the surface stays inviting instead of steaming itself soft.

Set out a large pot, 2 tablespoons vegetable oil, 2 skinless chicken leg quarters, 1/2 cup chopped onion, 2 quarts water, and the chicken bouillon called for in the recipe.
The chicken leg quarters are ready, but they're a little damp from the package. Is that okay before browning?
Pat them dry if you can. Then warm the 2 tablespoons vegetable oil in the large pot over medium heat so the chicken browns instead of steaming.
Oil is shimmering. Should the chicken go in skin-side down even though the leg quarters are skinless?
Since they're skinless, just lay the chicken pieces in carefully and let them cook over medium heat until browned on both sides. Give them space and turn them once they release easily.

That's good flavor. Stir in the 1/2 cup chopped onion and cook it with the chicken for 2 minutes, scraping the bottom gently as it softens.

Yes. Pour in the 2 quarts water, then add the chicken bouillon. Stir so the bouillon starts dissolving and the browned bits loosen into the broth.
The pot is filled and the bouillon is dissolving. How hard should it boil?
Bring it up to a boil, meaning you should see steady bubbling across the surface. Once it reaches that point, you won't keep it boiling hard.
It's bubbling steadily now. What should I do for the simmer and serving?
Reduce the heat until the soup is gently simmering, then let it cook for 45 minutes. Keep the pot at a light bubble, and after that the chicken should be cooked through and the broth ready to serve.

Cut the chicken breasts into 1 inch strips. Try to keep the pieces fairly even so they cook at the same pace later.

Absolutely. Put out 1 pound cubed beef stew meat, 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour, 2 tablespoons olive oil, and 2 teaspoons butter. You'll also want a resealable plastic bag, a skillet, tongs or a spatula, and your slow cooker nearby.
The beef is on the counter and I found the bag. Does the butter go in with the flour?
No, keep the butter separate for now. Put the cubed beef and the flour into the resealable plastic bag so the flour can coat the meat.

Leave enough air space in the bag so the beef can move around. Seal it tightly, then shake until the pieces are evenly coated with flour.

Yes, batches are fine. Brown the beef on all sides, turning the pieces as needed. The goal is color on the outside, not fully cooking it through in the skillet.

Use the 2 teaspoons butter in the skillet along with the oil as you brown the beef. If the pan looks dry between batches, let the butter melt in before adding more coated pieces.

Transfer the browned beef to the slow cooker. Scrape in any loose flavorful bits from the skillet if they come up easily, then you're ready for the next part of the stew.

I have both a deep fryer and a wide skillet. Which is safer for 2 quarts of oil?
Use the deep fryer if it holds the oil comfortably and gives you steadier control. If you choose the skillet, it needs to be large and deep enough that the oil sits well below the rim.
I like that sauce move here—that's exactly how I want wings finished, saucy instead of pasty. Once the oil is hot, how should I load them in?
Add the chicken wings carefully and avoid crowding them. Fry in batches if needed, letting each batch cook until done, about 10 minutes.
They're bubbling pretty hard. Should I move them around or leave them alone?
Let them fry without constant stirring, but turn or shift them once or twice so they cook evenly. Watch for steady frying rather than splashing or smoking.
While the wings finish, can I get the sauce pan ready?

Yes. Have the skillet ready for the sauce, and measure out the 4 tablespoons butter, the 1 tablespoon distilled white vinegar, and the hot sauce so they can go in quickly once the oil is out of the way.
The first batch looks cooked and crisp. What's the cleanest way to move on?
Lift the wings out and let them drain well. When frying is finished, remove the chicken and the oil from the skillet or fryer area safely, drain the oil, and keep the cooked chicken reserved.
The skillet is clear now. Do I melt the butter by itself first?
Yes, melt the 4 tablespoons butter in the skillet first. Stir in the 1 tablespoon distilled white vinegar and the hot sauce, then pull a little of that sauce aside before tossing the wings.
The sauce is together and smells tangy. How do I coat everything without making it heavy?

Season the sauce with salt and pepper to taste, then toss the reserved wings until they're coated. If the sauce tightens as you toss, add back the small portion you saved at the end so the wings stay glossy for serving.

Set out 1/2 cup softened butter, 1/2 cup shortening, 1 cup sugar, and 1/2 cup packed brown sugar so they're ready for the mixing bowl.
I've got the butter softening on the counter and both sugars measured. Should the shortening go in with them right away?
Yes, add the shortening with the butter and both sugars. Cream all four together until the mixture looks even and soft, scraping the bowl once or twice so no packed brown sugar stays on the sides.
The mixer is on low right now, but the sugar is still a little grainy. Should I keep going?

Keep beating a bit longer, then bring the mixer up to medium if your bowl can handle it without splattering. You're aiming for a blended, creamy base rather than a completely smooth frosting-like texture.
That lighter, looser texture is exactly what I wanted for these. The creamed mixture is ready and it's not sitting in a heavy clump.
Great. Add the egg and the extracts next, then mix until they disappear evenly into the butter, shortening, and sugars.
The egg and extracts are mixed in, and I scraped around the bottom of the bowl. What should I do with the dry ingredients?
Combine the next eight ingredients from your recipe in a separate bowl first. Once they're evenly mixed, add them to the creamed mixture gradually so the dough comes together without dry pockets.
I'm adding the dry bowl in thirds. The dough is thickening fast near the beaters.
Pause and scrape the beaters and sides, then continue just until you no longer see dry streaks. If it starts to feel too stiff, use only tiny splashes so it stays light-coated rather than watery.
No floury streaks now. Should I chill it, or can I start portioning?
If the dough is workable, you can start portioning now. Use a small scoop or your hands to shape it into 1-in balls.
I have the 1-in balls shaped. I put sugar in a shallow dish for coating them.
Roll each ball in the sugar until the outside is coated all around. Set them aside briefly while you get the baking sheets ready.
Do the baking sheets need grease, parchment, or anything else before I put the dough on them?
Use ungreased baking sheets for these. Arrange the sugar-coated 1-in balls with space apart, then bake according to your recipe's timing and watch for the crackled tops.
I'm making Fresh Apple Cake today. Can you help me set up the ingredients and pan before I start mixing?
Absolutely. Put out 1 1/2 cups vegetable oil, 2 cups white sugar, 3 beaten eggs, and 2 teaspoons vanilla extract. You'll also want one 10 inch tube pan ready.
The oil, sugar, eggs, and vanilla are on the counter. Should I heat the oven now or wait?
Go ahead and set the oven to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C) so it's ready by the time the batter is mixed.
Oven is heating. For the tube pan, should it be greased before I combine anything?
Yes, grease the 10 inch tube pan now. Getting it ready early makes it easier to transfer the batter once the wet and dry mixtures are combined.
Pan is greased. I have the beaten eggs in a bowl—what do I mix with them?
Add the vegetable oil, vanilla extract, and white sugar to the beaten eggs, then beat everything together until the mixture looks evenly blended.
It looks smooth and glossy. What dry ingredients should I prepare next?
Sift together the flour, baking soda, salt, cinnamon, and nutmeg. Sifting helps distribute the leavening and spices evenly through the cake.
I'm sifting now. Should the flour mixture go straight into the wet bowl after that?
Yes, once it's sifted, add the dry mixture to the wet ingredients and mix gently until combined. Try not to overwork it once the flour is in.
The batter is mixed and the tube pan is waiting. Anything I should check before it goes in?
Give the bowl a quick scrape to make sure there are no dry pockets, then pour the batter into the greased 10 inch tube pan. The oven should still be at 325 degrees F (165 degrees C) before baking.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: Use only the tender lower herb pieces, mince them very small, and hold the brighter upper green pieces off to the side.

messages.content: For this batch of Garden Potato Salad, I'm treating it more like a fresh topping, and I have some lower cilantro or parsley pieces I want to use. What should I do with those just for this bowl?
Use only the tender lower herb pieces, mince them very small, and hold the brighter upper green pieces off to the side.
Great, that's exactly the special version I'm doing today. I've got my cutting board out—what should I prep first?
Begin with the main salad base: have 6 large potatoes already cooked, peeled, and cubed, then slice 4 hard-cooked eggs.
The potatoes are cubed and the eggs are sliced. I still have room on the board—what vegetables should I cut next?
Slice 2 celery ribs, then slice 6 green onions with their tops. Keep them handy with the potatoes and eggs.
Celery and green onions are ready. Should the herbs go into the bowl now too?
Add only those tiny minced tender lower herb pieces if you want them in this fresh version, but keep the separated upper green pieces out for now.
Understood. I've got a large bowl ready—what goes in first?
Put the potatoes, sliced eggs, celery, green onions, radishes, salt, and pepper into the large bowl, then gently combine and set the bowl aside.
The salad bowl is mixed and resting. I've pulled out a saucepan for the dressing—what do I combine in it?
In the saucepan, combine eggs, vinegar, sugar, dry mustard, and salt for the dressing.
Everything for the dressing is in the saucepan. What heat and texture am I looking for?
Cook and stir it over medium heat until the dressing thickens.
It has thickened and I've taken it off the heat. What should I do before serving it with the salad?
Let the dressing cool before you use it with the Garden Potato Salad.

original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making Banana Kiwi Strawberry Tart as a warm skillet version with pickles, capers, olives, or pepperoncini. How should I handle the briny ingredient?

messages.content: For this Banana Kiwi Strawberry Tart, I'm doing a warm skillet take and I have pickles, capers, olives, and pepperoncini nearby. What's the best way to use that briny element here?
For this skillet version, add about 1 spoonful of the brine to the warm pan for tang, but keep the pickle, caper, olive, or pepperoncini pieces out of the tart.
Great, just for tonight's version. I'm clearing space now—what dry ingredients should I measure first?
Measure out 1/2 cup all-purpose flour and 1 tablespoon light brown sugar, and put them in a mixing bowl.
The flour and brown sugar are in the bowl. I've got measuring spoons out too—what else goes with them?
Add 1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon and 1/8 teaspoon salt to the bowl.
Everything dry is in there. Should I stir it, whisk it, or actually sift it?
Sift the flour, light brown sugar, cinnamon, and salt together in the bowl so the mixture is even and fine.
Done. I have the butter cold on the counter; what texture am I aiming for when I add it?
Cut in the butter until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs, with no large chunks left.
It's crumbly now, like little pebbles. I'm worried about over-wetting it—how should I add the ice water?
Sprinkle the ice water over the crumbs rather than pouring it in all at once.
Sprinkled. Do I knead it together or keep using the fork?
Use a fork to toss the mixture until it's evenly moistened; stop once it starts holding together.
It's holding together but still tender. What should I do before I clean up the bowl?
Pat the dough into a round, wrap it in plastic, and then you can set the bowl aside for cleanup.
I'm cooking Coq au Vin alla Italiana and have a large skillet ready. Can you talk me through the prep and cooking?
Absolutely. Set out 4 pounds of dark meat chicken pieces, 1 tablespoon vegetable oil, 5 cloves crushed garlic, and 1/2 cup all-purpose flour. You'll also need poultry seasoning for the flour.
The chicken is on a tray, and I've got the oil and flour measured. Should the garlic be crushed before I heat the pan?
Yes, crush the garlic now so it's ready to go. Once everything is within reach, place the large skillet over the heat and add the vegetable oil.
The oil is in the skillet. What should I look for before adding anything?
Let the oil heat until it looks loose and glossy across the bottom of the skillet. Then add 1/2 of the crushed garlic to the oil.
Half the garlic is in, and it smells good already. Do I stir it around?
Give it a quick stir so it spreads through the oil, but don't let it sit long enough to darken too much. While it warms, season the 1/2 cup flour with poultry seasoning.
The flour is seasoned in a shallow dish. Should I coat every chicken piece heavily?
Dredge the chicken parts in the seasoned flour so each piece has an even coating. Shake off any loose excess before it goes into the skillet.
I'm starting to add the chicken, but the pan looks crowded. Is that a problem?
Try not to pack the pieces too tightly. Give them enough contact with the skillet so they can brown instead of steaming.
The first pieces are in the skillet with the garlic oil. How long do I brown them?
Brown the floured chicken parts in the skillet for 4 or 5 minutes, turning as needed so the coating picks up color on the outside.

messages.content: I'm packing Broccoli Coleslaw in a thermos today, and because it has the ramen noodles with the slaw, I don't want it turning soupy. What should I do with the dressing or extra liquid for this lunch?
For this thermos lunch, keep the extra liquid in a separate small container and pour it in only after you open the thermos to eat.
Perfect, that's exactly what I want for this batch. I've got the thermos and a small dressing cup ready—what ingredients should I pull out first?

Start with the dressing ingredients: 1 cup olive oil, 1/3 cup distilled white vinegar, and 1/2 cup white sugar. You'll also need the seasoning packet from a 3 ounce package of chicken flavored ramen noodles.
The oil, vinegar, sugar, and ramen packet are on the counter. Should I crush the noodles now or wait?
Go ahead and crush the ramen noodles now, but keep the seasoning packet separate for the dressing. The crushed noodles get stirred into the slaw later.
Got it. I also have a small bowl and a large bowl out—what goes in the small one?
In the small bowl, combine the olive oil, distilled white vinegar, white sugar, and the reserved chicken-flavored seasoning packet from the ramen.
That's mixed together, but the sugar looks like it needs a little help dissolving. How much should I stir?

Stir until the sugar and seasoning are well blended into the oil and vinegar. Once it looks evenly mixed, cover it and refrigerate it for at least 1 hour before serving, or overnight if that fits your timing.
I'm planning to eat it later today, so I'll chill the dressing. While that's in the fridge, what should I put in the large bowl?
Add the broccoli, carrots, green onions, and sunflower seeds to the large bowl. Toss them together so the vegetables and seeds are evenly distributed.
The vegetables and sunflower seeds are combined. Since this is going into a thermos, should the ramen be mixed in before packing?

Yes, stir the crushed ramen noodles into the broccoli mixture. Keep the chilled dressing or any extra liquid separate for the thermos, then add it after opening so the noodles don't soak up too much liquid early.
Everything is mixed except the dressing. Any final serving or packing detail before I close it up?
Pack the broccoli mixture with the crushed ramen in the thermos, and carry the dressing separately. When you're ready to eat, open the thermos, add the dressing, stir well, and serve.
I'm baking Cinnamon Chocolate Cake 2 today. Can you help me get the dry ingredients measured before I start heating anything?
Absolutely. Set out a mixing bowl and measure in 2 cups all-purpose flour, 2 cups sugar, 1 1/2 teaspoons ground cinnamon, and 1/4 teaspoon salt.
The flour and sugar are in the bowl, and I've measured the cinnamon and salt too. Should I whisk them together?
Yes, combine those first four ingredients well in the mixing bowl so the cinnamon and salt are evenly distributed through the flour and sugar.
That looks evenly mixed. I have a saucepan ready—what goes in it?
Use the saucepan for the wet chocolate mixture: combine water, oil, butter, and cocoa in it.
They're in the pan. What heat should I use, and what am I looking for?
Put the saucepan over medium heat and bring the water, oil, butter, and cocoa mixture to a boil.
It has just started boiling and the butter is melted. Do I keep it on the stove?
Once it reaches a boil, take it off the heat and pour the hot cocoa mixture over the dry ingredients in the mixing bowl.
I poured it in. The batter is thick and streaky right now—how much should I mix?
Mix it well until the dry ingredients are fully moistened and the chocolate mixture looks evenly blended through the bowl.
The batter is smoother now. What needs to be added before it's ready?
Add the eggs, buttermilk, vanilla, and baking soda, then mix well again until everything is fully incorporated.
I'm making Crab and Lobster Stuffed Mushrooms today. Can you talk me through the setup before the oven goes on?
Absolutely. Have 1 pound fresh mushrooms with the stems removed ready, plus 3/4 cup melted butter divided for the pan and filling.
The mushroom caps are cleaned and the butter is melted. What should I pull out for the stuffing?
You'll need 1 cup crushed seasoned croutons and 1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, along with the crabmeat, lobster, and garlic for the seafood mixture.
Got it. I have a large baking sheet too—should I heat the oven now?
Yes, get the oven warming to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C), so it's ready once the mushrooms are filled.
Oven is heating. Do I line the baking sheet or just butter it?
Brush the large baking sheet with about 1/4 cup of the melted butter, spreading it across the area where the mushroom caps will sit.
The pan is buttered. How should I place the caps so they cook evenly?
Set the mushroom caps on the baking sheet in a single layer, open side up, with a little space between them if you have room.
They're arranged. I'm ready to mix the filling—what goes into the bowl?
In a medium bowl, combine the 1 cup crushed seasoned croutons, the remaining 1/2 cup melted butter, the 1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, crabmeat, lobster, and garlic.
Should the filling look wet or more like a crumbly seafood-cheese mix?

It should be moist enough to hold together from the butter and cheese, but still textured from the crushed croutons and seafood. Mix just until everything is evenly combined before spooning it into the mushroom caps.
