messages.content: I'm about to start Gerrys Chicken Enchiladas and want the counter organized before anything goes on the burner. What should I pull out first?

For the serving garnish, tuck the soft topping into the center and set the crisp topping in a small curved strip along one side. For the main prep, set out 4 boneless, skinless chicken breast halves and 1 tablespoon vegetable oil, but leave the stove off for now.
Chicken and oil are out. I've got my cutting board ready too—what else belongs next to it?
Put 1 onion on the board for chopping, and keep 1 (10 ounce) can of diced tomatoes with green chile peppers nearby so it's ready to add later.
The onion is chopped, and the can is opened and drained a little at the sink. Should I deal with the chicken before mixing anything?
Yes. Cut the chicken breasts into 1 inch strips, aiming for fairly even pieces so they marinate and cook more evenly.
I like that garnish setup—the soft center with the crisp curved edge is exactly right for this dish. Before I pour in the marinade, what bowl should the chicken go into?
Use a medium bowl. Add the chicken strips with your desired marinade, cover the bowl, and refrigerate it for at least 30 minutes.
The bowl is covered and in the fridge, and I set the timer. Should the oven be heating while the chicken sits?
You can wait until the marinating time is close to done, then bring the oven up to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C).
While it chills, should I start the onion in the skillet or keep everything cold for now?

Keep the onion and the tomatoes ready beside the stove, but don't start them yet. The recipe's next heat step is getting the oil warm in a large skillet over medium heat after the chicken has marinated.
Timer has about 5 minutes left, and I'm clearing space around the stove. Anything else I should set up for the skillet?
Place a large skillet on the burner, keep the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil within reach, and have the chopped onion and opened can of diced tomatoes with green chile peppers close by.
The timer just went off. The chicken strips are marinated, the oven is at temperature, and the skillet is sitting on the burner.
Add the vegetable oil to the large skillet and heat it over medium heat. Give it a moment to warm before adding anything else.
The oil is warming over medium, and the chicken, onion, and tomato can are all beside the stove. Am I lined up correctly?

Yes. You have the chicken cut into 1 inch strips and marinated for at least 30 minutes, the oven preheated to 350 degrees F or 175 degrees C, and the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil heating in a large skillet over medium heat.
I'd like to make Armadillo Eggs today. Can you talk me through the setup before I start cutting peppers?
For this batch of Armadillo Eggs, for this batch, set out 24 jalapeno peppers, 1 pound sausage, 2 cups all-purpose baking mix, and 1 (16 ounce) package of shredded Cheddar cheese.
The jalapenos and sausage are on the counter. Should the oven be heating while I get the rest ready?
Yes, go ahead and get the oven warming to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C) so it is ready when the prep is done.
Oven is set. I found the baking mix and Cheddar too. What pan should I prepare?
Use a medium baking sheet and lightly grease it. You just want enough coating to help keep the Armadillo Eggs from sticking.
The baking sheet is greased. For the jalapenos, am I cutting them in half or leaving them mostly whole?
Leave each pepper mostly whole and cut a slit in each jalapeno pepper. That gives you an opening without separating the pepper into pieces.
I slit a few and can see the seeds. Should I remove everything inside?
Yes. Remove and discard the seeds and pulp from each jalapeno pepper.
That's a lot of peppers. Any practical way to keep the workspace manageable while I clean all 24?
Work in small batches: slit several jalapenos, clear out their seeds and pulp, then move the cleaned peppers to the greased baking sheet before starting the next group.
All the peppers are cleaned and the sheet is ready. Can you recap what I should have in place before I continue?

You should have the oven preheated to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C), a lightly greased medium baking sheet, 24 jalapenos slit and cleared of seeds and pulp, plus 1 pound sausage, 2 cups all-purpose baking mix, and the 1 (16 ounce) package of shredded Cheddar cheese ready to use.
I want to make Fancy Brussels Sprouts tonight. Can you help me get set up at the stove?

Absolutely. Put a saucepan on the stove and gather 1 cup water, 1/4 cup minced fresh parsley, 1 teaspoon sugar, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. You'll also need the brussels sprouts, plus water chestnuts and butter for the end.
I've got the saucepan out. Should the parsley go in right away or wait until later?
Add the parsley right away with the water, sugar, and salt. Set the saucepan over medium heat and bring that mixture to a boil.
The water is heating, and the parsley is floating around. Is that okay?
Yes, that's fine. Give it a quick stir so the sugar and salt dissolve evenly while it comes up to a boil.
It's boiling now. Do the brussels sprouts go in whole?
Add the brussels sprouts now. If yours are especially large, halved sprouts will cook more evenly, but follow the recipe by getting them into the boiling seasoned water.
They're in the pan. Should I lower the heat or keep it bubbling hard?
Cover the saucepan and reduce the heat enough to maintain a gentle simmer. Let them cook for 6-8 minutes, until the brussels sprouts are tender.
How do I tell if they're tender without overcooking them?

At about 6 minutes, pierce one with a fork or the tip of a knife. It should slide in easily but the sprout shouldn't be falling apart. If it still feels firm, give it another minute or two, up to 8 minutes.
They're tender now, and there's still liquid in the saucepan. What's the cleanest way to finish?

Drain off the cooking liquid, then return the brussels sprouts to the saucepan. Add the water chestnuts and butter, and heat everything through until the butter melts and the water chestnuts are warmed.
I want to make Chocolate Crisps. Can you help me get set up before I turn anything on?

Absolutely. For this recipe, set out 1 tablespoon softened butter, 1 egg white, 1/4 cup white sugar, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract. You'll also need cookie sheets, a small saucepan, and a medium-sized bowl.
I've got the ingredients on the counter. Should the oven be heating while I prep the pans?
Yes, get the oven warming to 300 degrees F (150 degrees C). While it heats, grease your cookie sheets so they're ready for the crisps.
The oven is set to 300 and the cookie sheets are greased. What should I do with the butter?
Put the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Melt it gently and keep it moving or watching closely until it becomes lightly browned.
How will I know it's lightly browned and not going too far?
Look for a pale golden-brown color and a lightly toasted smell. Since it's only 1 tablespoon, it can change quickly, so take it off the heat as soon as it looks lightly browned.
It's melted and smells a little nutty now. Do I leave it in the pan?
Pour the browned butter into a medium-sized bowl. That gets it out of the hot pan so it won't keep browning.
Should I add the egg white, sugar, and vanilla to that bowl right away?

Those are the remaining ingredients for the Chocolate Crisps: 1 egg white, 1/4 cup white sugar, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract. Have them ready beside the bowl with the browned butter before you continue mixing.
Okay, the bowl is ready and the greased cookie sheets are nearby. Anything I should clean up before moving on?
You can set the saucepan aside safely and wipe any butter drips from the counter. Keep the oven at 300 degrees F and the prepared cookie sheets within reach so the next part goes smoothly.
I want to make Baked Fettuccine Lasagna. Can you talk me through it while I prep?
Absolutely. Set out 12 ounces dry fettuccine pasta, and if you're using meat, have 1 pound lean ground beef ready too.
The pasta is on the counter, and I do have the ground beef. Anything from the produce drawer?
Yes—chop 1 cup onion and 1 cup red bell pepper. Keep them nearby so you're not scrambling once the cooking starts.
Onion and pepper are chopped. Should I start with the pasta pot or the skillet?
Start with the pasta pot. Fill a large pot with water, salt it lightly, and bring it to a boil.
The water is heating. How salty should it be?
Just lightly salted is right for this recipe—enough to season the pasta water without making it taste briny.

Set out 6 large potatoes, peeled and diced; 1 (12 ounce) can corned beef, cut into chunks; 1 medium onion, chopped; and 1 cup beef broth.
The potatoes are diced and sitting in a bowl. The corned beef came out in a few big pieces—should I break it up now?
Keep the corned beef in chunks at this point. It will loosen as it simmers with the potatoes, and you can fold it through more evenly when the hash thickens.

Yes, add the diced potatoes, corned beef chunks, and chopped onion to the large deep skillet before adding the broth. Pour in the 1 cup beef broth after they're in the pan, then set the heat to medium.
I like how those raw pieces are cut for this—small enough to spread through the hash is exactly what I wanted.
That size should let them blend into the potatoes without making the finished hash feel watery or bulky. Once the broth is in, stir just enough to get everything evenly moistened.
Everything is stirred together now, and I can hear a little bubbling under the potatoes.
Cover the skillet and let it simmer over medium heat. The potatoes need to soften until they're close to mashing consistency, and the broth should cook down until almost none is left.
How often should I lift the lid? I don't want the bottom layer to stick.

Lift the lid occasionally and scrape gently from the bottom, then cover it again so the steam keeps softening the potatoes. If it's bubbling too hard, lower the heat slightly while keeping it at a steady simmer.
The onion smells cooked now, but the potatoes still have some firmness in the center.
Give it a few more minutes covered. Stir from the edges toward the middle so the firmer potato pieces get moved into the hotter spots with the broth.
The potatoes are tender now, and there's only a thin bit of liquid left at the bottom.
Take the lid off and keep stirring gently so that last liquid can evaporate. As you mix, lightly mash some potatoes into the corned beef while leaving a few pieces chunky for texture.
It's thickened up and looks like hash. Should I plate it right away or let it sit?
Mix it well once more and serve it hot from the skillet. If you still see any loose broth, leave it uncovered for another minute before plating.

Dip each toasted cake cube into the sweetened condensed milk so it gets a sticky coating. Let any heavy excess drip off for a second.

Roll each milk-coated cake cube in the 1 cup coconut flakes, turning it so the coconut clings all around. A gentle press is fine if some spots look bare.

Serve them right away while the cake is warm and the outside is toasted. Keep extra napkins nearby, and if you're making more, repeat the same order: toast over the coals until browned, dip in condensed milk, then roll in coconut flakes.

For the eggplant slices, keep the first side still in the oil until it develops a deeper browned patch, then cook the other side a little more gently so the pieces finish with varied color. Start by peeling and slicing 1 large eggplant, and set out 2 tablespoons canola oil.
The eggplant is sliced. Should I get the coating station ready before heating the skillet?
Yes. Beat 3 eggs in one shallow dish, and put 2 cups dry bread crumbs in another so you can dip each slice quickly once the oil is hot.
Do I need anything special for the pan, or just a regular skillet?
Use a large skillet so the slices have room. Add the 2 tablespoons canola oil and heat it over medium-high heat until it's hot enough to sizzle when a crumb touches it.
I like that uneven browning approach for this dish; it works better for me. The oil is heating now.
Good. Dip each eggplant slice into the beaten eggs, let the excess drip off, then press it into the bread crumbs so both sides are coated.
A few slices are coated and ready. Should I crowd the skillet to get them done faster?
Keep them in a single layer with a little space between slices. Place the coated eggplant into the hot oil carefully so the crumbs set instead of sliding off.
They're in the pan. How long should I leave them before flipping?
Fry them for 2 to 3 minutes on the first side, watching for golden brown edges and that deeper color on the side you left alone.
The first side looks golden with some darker spots. I'm flipping them now.
After flipping, cook the second side another 2 to 3 minutes, or until it's golden brown and the eggplant feels tender when you nudge it with the spatula.
They look done. What's the cleanest way to finish and serve them?
Transfer the fried eggplant to paper towels to drain off excess oil. Let the slices sit briefly, then serve them while the crumb coating is still crisp.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: For this batch, add just a spoonful of the brine to the warm pan for tang, and keep the solid pickle, caper, olive, or pepperoncini pieces out of the dip.
memory_annotations.exception_query_cue: Tonight I'm doing Delicious Artichoke Dip as a warmer skillet-style batch with something briny nearby—pickles, capers, olives, or pepperoncini. For this version, what should I do with that briny element?

original_cues.exception_action_cue: Use a spoonful of brine in the warm pan and leave the solid briny pieces out.
original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making Delicious Artichoke Dip as a warm skillet version with pickles, capers, olives, or pepperoncini. How should I handle the briny ingredient?

messages.content: Tonight I'm doing Delicious Artichoke Dip as a warmer skillet-style batch with something briny nearby—pickles, capers, olives, or pepperoncini. For this version, what should I do with that briny element?
For this batch, add just a spoonful of the brine to the warm pan for tang, and keep the solid pickle, caper, olive, or pepperoncini pieces out of the dip.
Perfect, that's the tangy skillet take I want tonight. I've got a cast-iron skillet and a shallow baking dish out—what ingredients should I gather first?
Pull together 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/2 cup sour cream, 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese, and 1 (14 ounce) can of artichoke hearts, drained.
The mayo, sour cream, Parmesan, and can are on the counter. Should I drain the artichokes before heating anything?
Yes—drain the artichoke hearts now. Also get the oven heating to 400 degrees F, or 200 degrees C, so it's ready when the mixture is assembled.
Oven is heating, and I've got the brine ready for the skillet without the chopped pieces. What goes into the mixing bowl first?
In a medium-sized mixing bowl, stir together the mayonnaise, sour cream, Parmesan cheese, and onion until the base looks evenly combined.
The base is creamy and the Parmesan is mixed through. When do I add the artichokes?
Add the drained artichoke hearts now, along with lemon juice, salt, and pepper. Fold everything together so the artichokes are coated without crushing them completely.
Some of the artichoke hearts are pretty large. Should I leave them chunky for dipping?
Leave some texture, but break up any oversized pieces with the spoon so each scoop gets artichoke without turning the mixture into a puree.
The skillet has that little splash of brine warming in it. Where should the creamy mixture go from here?

Scrape the dip mixture into a shallow baking dish and spread it into an even layer. If your skillet is the vessel you're serving from, keep the brine flavor in the pan but still avoid adding the solid briny pieces.
Before I slide it over to the oven area, is there anything else from the recipe I should double-check?

Make sure the oven is at 400 degrees F, the artichoke hearts are drained, the mayonnaise, sour cream, Parmesan, onion, lemon juice, salt, and pepper are fully combined, and the mixture is in a shallow baking dish.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: For this batch, cut the raw vegetables into medium-size pieces and arrange them in their own separate layer.
memory_annotations.exception_query_cue: For this batch of Caramel Chocolate Corn, I'm prepping it ahead to use with raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish as a filling or topping. What cut and placement should I use for the raw vegetables?

original_cues.exception_action_cue: Cut the raw vegetables into medium pieces and keep them in a separate layer.
original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making Caramel Chocolate Corn as an advance-prepped filling or topping with raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish. How should I cut and place the raw vegetables?

messages.content: For this batch of Caramel Chocolate Corn, I'm prepping it ahead to use with raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish as a filling or topping. What cut and placement should I use for the raw vegetables?
For this batch, cut the raw vegetables into medium-size pieces and arrange them in their own separate layer.
Perfect, that's just for this batch. I've got counter space cleared—what should I pull out first?
Bring out 16 cups popped popcorn and 1 cup roasted peanuts. You'll also need a paper bag nearby for holding them together.
The popcorn is measured, and the peanuts are open. Should I prep the pan situation before the bag?
Yes. Grease the cookie sheets now so they're ready when the caramel mixture is done.
Cookie sheets are greased. Do the popcorn and peanuts go straight into the paper bag?
They do—put the popped popcorn and roasted peanuts into the paper bag, then give the bag enough room so you can mix without spilling later.
They're in the bag. What sweet ingredients should I set by the microwave?
In this Caramel Chocolate Corn step, set out 1 cup brown sugar and 1/2 cup butter. You'll also need corn syrup, vanilla, and salt for the microwave-safe bowl.
I've got the bowl ready. Should the bag stay open while I work on the caramel part?
Keep the popcorn and peanuts set aside in the paper bag while you combine the caramel ingredients.
Okay, I'm at the microwave-safe bowl with the sugar and butter. What goes in together?
Add the brown sugar, butter, corn syrup, vanilla, and salt to the microwave-safe bowl.
Before I heat anything, do I need to adjust the vegetables since they're raw and separate?
No adjustment needed—keep those raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish pieces in that separate layer, and continue with the caramel mixture for the popcorn.
I'm about to start Caramel Chocolate Corn. Can you talk me through the prep? I've got a big bowl of popped popcorn but want to make sure I set it up right.
Absolutely. You'll need 16 cups popped popcorn and 1 cup roasted peanuts for the crunchy mix, plus 1 cup brown sugar and 1/2 cup butter for the caramel mixture.
I measured the 16 cups of popcorn. Should the peanuts go in with it now or stay separate?
Put the popcorn and 1 cup roasted peanuts together in a paper bag. The bag gives you room to coat and toss everything later.
Got it. Before I start the caramel, do I need to prep any pans?
Yes, grease your cookie sheets now so they're ready when the coated popcorn needs to be spread out.
The cookie sheets are greased. For the sugar mixture, what bowl should I use?
Use a microwave-safe bowl. Add the 1 cup brown sugar and 1/2 cup butter to it, then include the corn syrup, vanilla, and salt as the recipe directs.
Should I melt the butter first, or just combine it with the sugar in the bowl?
Combine the butter with the brown sugar in the microwave-safe bowl; it can melt as the mixture heats. Just make sure the bowl is large enough that the caramel won't bubble over.
The popcorn and peanuts are already in the paper bag. Do I leave that alone while I work on the caramel?
Yes, set the paper bag aside while you prepare the sugar, butter, corn syrup, vanilla, and salt mixture.
Once the caramel mixture is ready, I'm guessing the greased cookie sheets are for spreading it out?
Exactly. The recipe has you grease the cookie sheets ahead of time, keep the popcorn and peanuts waiting in the paper bag, and prepare the caramel mixture separately in the microwave-safe bowl.

memory_annotations.boundary_action_cue: Slice the raw vegetables into slim, long batons, then set them out in separate color groups on the plate.
memory_annotations.boundary_query_cue: I'm serving Cinnamon Sugar Cookies 2 on a snack plate today with raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish alongside them. What's the best way to cut and arrange the vegetables?

original_cues.boundary_action_cue: Cut the raw vegetables into long thin sticks and group them by color.
original_cues.boundary_query_cue: I'm making Cinnamon Sugar Cookies 2 as an assembled snack plate with raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish. How should I cut and place the raw vegetables?

messages.content: I'm serving Cinnamon Sugar Cookies 2 on a snack plate today with raw cucumber, onion, carrot, pepper, or radish alongside them. What's the best way to cut and arrange the vegetables?
Slice the raw vegetables into slim, long batons, then set them out in separate color groups on the plate.
Great, I'll plate them that way. Before I start the cookie dough, what should be softening or measured?
Have 1 cup butter, softened, ready to go, and measure 1 cup sugar so you can cream them smoothly.
The butter is soft and the sugar is measured. I've got a large mixing bowl out—what else needs to be on the counter?
Measure 1 cup confectioners' sugar and 1 cup vegetable oil. Those go in with the butter and sugar for the opening mix.
All right, both sugars, butter, and oil are beside the bowl. How should the texture look once I start mixing?
Cream the butter, sugars, and oil together in the large mixing bowl until the mixture looks blended and smooth rather than streaky.
It's smooth and pale. I see the recipe uses eggs and vanilla too—do those go in now?
Yes, add the eggs and vanilla, then mix well so they're fully incorporated into the creamed mixture.
The wet mixture looks even now. I'm clearing space for the dry ingredients; what gets added together?
Add the flour, salt, baking soda, cinnamon, and cream of tartar to the bowl, then mix them in without leaving dry pockets.
The dough has come together. It smells like cinnamon, and I'm deciding whether to use nuts.
If you want pecans in this batch, stir them in now; if not, leave the dough plain.
I'll skip the pecans for a cleaner cookie plate. Any serving note before I set up the vegetables next to the cookies?
Keep the cookies together on one side of the platter and place the grouped vegetable sticks beside them so the colors stay distinct and easy to grab.
I'm getting ready for Cranberry Brandy Slush. Can you help me sequence the steps? I'm setting up the counter now.
Absolutely. Since this needs to freeze overnight, start by getting a freezer-safe plastic container with enough room for the liquid mixture.
I have a large plastic container. What ingredients should I pull from the freezer and pantry?
You'll need 2 cups cherry brandy liqueur, 1 16 ounce can frozen orange juice concentrate, 1 16 ounce can frozen lemonade concentrate, and 2 quarts cranberry juice.
The juice concentrates are still frozen. Is that okay for mixing?

Yes, that's fine. Add the cherry brandy, frozen orange juice concentrate, frozen lemonade concentrate, and cranberry juice to the plastic container, then stir until everything is combined as evenly as you can manage.
Should I break up the concentrates while stirring, or wait for them to soften?
Break them up as you stir. They don't need to be perfectly melted, but you want the orange and lemonade concentrates distributed through the cranberry juice and brandy before freezing.
It's mixed and the color looks even. Do I cover it before it goes in the freezer?
Cover the container securely, leaving just a little headspace if the container is very full, then place it in the freezer overnight.
Tomorrow, what texture am I looking for before serving?
It should be frozen into a scoopable slush rather than a pourable drink. Use a spoon or scoop to loosen the amount you want for each glass.
When people are ready for drinks, how do I serve each glass?
Scoop the desired amount of the frozen mixture into a glass, then fill the glass with lemon-lime soda. Give it a gentle stir if needed and serve right away while it's slushy.
I'm making Dads Best Burgers and have a mixing bowl out. Can you walk me through what to gather before I start?

Absolutely. Set out 1 softened 3 ounce package of cream cheese, 1 egg, 1 medium onion finely chopped, and 1/2 cup dry bread crumbs. You'll also need the beef and sausage ready for mixing in after the bowl ingredients are combined.
The cream cheese is softened and the onion is chopped. Should I put everything in the bowl together?
Add the cream cheese, egg, finely chopped onion, and dry bread crumbs to the bowl, then combine them until the mixture looks evenly blended.
It's a little thick from the cream cheese. Is that okay before I add the meat?
Yes, that's fine. Once it's mostly smooth and the onion and crumbs are distributed, crumble the beef and sausage over the mixture so they're easier to work in evenly.
I've crumbled the beef and sausage over the bowl. How much should I mix it?
Mix well, just until the cream cheese mixture, bread crumbs, onion, beef, and sausage are combined throughout. Try not to mash it into a paste; stop when it holds together evenly.
The burger mixture is combined. What size patties am I aiming for?
Shape the mixture into eight patties. Make them as even as you can so they cook at the same pace on the grill.
The patties are shaped and the grill is heating. What heat level should I use?
Use medium-hot heat and grill the patties uncovered. Once the grate is ready, place them on with a little space between each one.
They're on the grill. How long do I cook each side, and what should I check for?
Cook them for 4-6 minutes on each side, turning once, until they're no longer pink in the center. Let them come off the grill as soon as they're cooked through so they stay juicy.
I'm making BBQ Chicken Wings and want to get the marinade set up before I touch the chicken. What should I put on the counter?
Set out 1/2 cup teriyaki sauce, 1 cup oyster sauce, 1/4 cup soy sauce, and 1/4 cup ketchup. You'll also need garlic powder, gin, liquid smoke, and sugar for the marinade.
I've got the sauces measured. Should I mix everything in a small bowl or something bigger?
Use a large bowl, since the wings will go into it too. Pour in the teriyaki sauce, oyster sauce, soy sauce, and ketchup, then add the garlic powder, gin, liquid smoke, and sugar.
The bowl is ready. Do I need to whisk until it's completely smooth?
Stir or whisk until the sauces and seasonings look evenly combined. It doesn't need to be fancy—just make sure the sugar and garlic powder are worked through the liquid.
Okay, the marinade looks even. How do I add the wings without making a mess?
Place the chicken wings into the large bowl and turn them so they're coated all over. If the bowl is crowded, use tongs and move them around from the bottom up.
They're coated. How long should they sit before grilling?
Cover the bowl and refrigerate the wings for 8 hours or overnight so the marinade has time to soak in.
They've been in the fridge overnight. What should I do with the grill?
Preheat the grill for low heat. Give it time to settle there before the wings go on, since this recipe starts them gently rather than over high heat.
The grill is warming up. Is there anything to prep on the grate before I put the wings down?
Yes—lightly oil the grill grate so the wings are less likely to stick when you start cooking them.
I'm making Asian Turkey Burgers tonight. Can you guide me through the ingredients and the skillet part?

Absolutely. Set out 1 egg white, 1 tablespoon soy sauce, 1/2 cup dry bread crumbs, and 1 tablespoon finely chopped onion. You'll also need the turkey for the patties, plus a nonstick skillet and nonstick cooking spray.
I've got the egg white and soy sauce measured. Should I put those straight into the mixing bowl?
Yes, add the egg white and soy sauce to the bowl. Then stir in the dry bread crumbs and finely chopped onion so those base ingredients are evenly combined before the turkey goes in.
The crumbs look a little dry in the bowl with the onion. Is that okay before adding the turkey?
That's fine. Once you crumble the turkey over the mixture, it will bring everything together. Mix gently and stop as soon as it looks combined so the burgers don't get packed too tightly.
I'm adding the turkey now. Should I use my hands or a spoon?
Either works, but clean hands are usually easiest for burger patties. Crumble the turkey over the bowl, fold it through the crumb mixture lightly, and avoid overmixing.
Before I continue with Asian Turkey Burgers, the mixture is combined. How many patties am I shaping, and how thick should I aim for?
Shape the mixture into four patties. Try to make them even in size so they cook at the same pace in the skillet.
I have a nonstick skillet ready. Do I need oil, or just the spray?
Use the nonstick cooking spray called for in the recipe. Coat the nonstick skillet, set it over the heat, and place the patties in once the pan is ready.
How do I know when these turkey burgers are done without drying them out?
Cook them in the sprayed nonstick skillet until they're no longer pink in the center. Turn them as needed for even browning, and take them off once the turkey is cooked through.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: For this container, keep the crunchy topping in a separate small cup or packet, then sprinkle it on after you open the soup.
memory_annotations.exception_query_cue: I'm packing A 1 Chicken Soup to eat later, and just for this container I'm adding a crunchy seed-and-crumb topping. How should I keep it from going soggy?

original_cues.exception_action_cue: Pack the crunchy topping separately and add it after opening the container.
original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making A 1 Chicken Soup as a packed container with seeds, nuts, crumbs, chips, or a crisp topping. How should I handle the crunchy topping?

messages.content: I'm packing A 1 Chicken Soup to eat later, and just for this container I'm adding a crunchy seed-and-crumb topping. How should I keep it from going soggy?
For this container, keep the crunchy topping in a separate small cup or packet, then sprinkle it on after you open the soup.
Great, that is just for today's packed bowl. I have a large pot out; what should I set near the stove first?
Set out 2 tablespoons vegetable oil and 2 skinless chicken leg quarters. Pat the chicken dry if you can, and keep tongs handy for turning it.
The chicken is dried off, and the pot is still empty. Should I chop the onion before I start browning?
Yes. Chop enough onion to make 1/2 cup, and measure 2 quarts water so it is ready when the pot gets hot.
The onion and water are ready, and the oil is in the pot. What heat should I use for the chicken?
Put the large pot over medium heat. When the oil is hot, add the chicken pieces and cook them until they are browned on both sides.
Both sides have color now, and there are browned bits on the bottom. Does the onion go in with the chicken still there?
Yes, stir in the chopped onion with the chicken in the pot. Cook it for 2 minutes more, scraping up some of those browned bits as it softens.
The onion smells good and has softened. I have the measured water next to me; where does the bouillon fit in?
Pour in the 2 quarts water, add the chicken bouillon, and bring everything up to a boil.
It has reached a boil. Should I cover it while it simmers, or leave it open?
Reduce the heat so it settles into a gentle simmer, then cook it for 45 minutes. You can partly cover the pot if you want to limit evaporation, as long as the bubbling stays calm.
When I portion it into the container, should the crunchy topping go on before I seal it?
No—pack the soup in the container by itself, let it cool safely before sealing, and keep the crunchy topping separate until you are ready to eat so it stays crisp.
Crawfish Chowder is on deck today. What should I do first?
Absolutely. Set out 1/4 cup butter and 1/2 bunch chopped green onions to start. You'll also need a large skillet for the first part.
I've got the skillet out. Is there more butter later, or just the 1/4 cup?
There's more later: keep another 1/2 cup butter ready, along with 2 pounds frozen crawfish, cleaned.
The crawfish is cleaned and thawing nearby. How should I start the pan?
Put the large skillet over medium heat and melt the 1/4 cup butter until it's fully melted and coating the pan.
The butter is melted and foamy, not browned. Do the green onions go in now?
Yes. Add the chopped green onions and sauté them in the butter until they're tender, stirring so they soften evenly.
They smell good and look softened. Should I leave them in the skillet for the crawfish?
Take the green onions out of the pan and set them aside for now.
They're in a small bowl. Do I wipe out the skillet before adding the crawfish?
No need to wipe it out. In that same skillet, melt the 1/2 cup butter over medium heat.
The 1/2 cup butter is melted. How long should the crawfish cook?
Add the 2 pounds cleaned crawfish and sauté for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. After that, set the crawfish aside too.
I'm making Atomic Canuck Chili in the slow cooker. Before I start browning anything, what should I pull out?
Set out 2 pounds lean ground beef, 1/2 large onion diced, 1 tablespoon crushed red pepper, and 3 tablespoons garlic powder. You'll also need a large skillet and your slow cooker ready.
The beef and onion are ready, and I found the crushed red pepper and garlic powder. Does the skillet need oil?

The recipe doesn't call for oil. Put the skillet over medium heat, then add the ground beef with the diced onion, crushed red pepper, garlic powder, and seasoned pepper. Break up the beef as it browns.
It's cooking now. What should the beef and onion look like before I move it?
Cook until the beef is browned through and crumbly, with no obvious pink left, and the onion has softened into the mixture. Keep stirring so the garlic powder and pepper season everything evenly.
There's a good amount of fat in the pan. Should I dump everything straight into the slow cooker?
Drain off the fat first, then transfer the browned beef, onion, and seasonings into the slow cooker.
The meat mixture is in the slow cooker. I'm clearing the counter—what goes in with it?

Stir in the mushrooms, baked beans, kidney beans with their liquid, tomato paste, sugar, carrots, celery, peppers, beer, and barbeque sauce. Mix well so the tomato paste and sauce spread through the chili.
The kidney beans still have their liquid in the can. You want that included, right?
Yes, include the kidney beans with liquid. That liquid becomes part of the chili base along with the beer and barbeque sauce.
Everything is combined and it smells spicy already. How do I season it at the end?

Season it with hot sauce and more crushed red pepper, adding them carefully and stirring before you taste. Once the heat level is where you want it, let the slow cooker continue bringing the chili together.
Help me stay organized for Fresh Apple Salsa. What comes first? I've got a cutting board out and want to prep everything in the right order.

Absolutely. Start by setting out 2 tart apples, 4 tablespoons lime juice, 1 fresh jalapeno pepper, and 1 fresh Anaheim chile. You'll also want a large mixing bowl ready so the apples can go straight in once they're cut.
The apples are washed. Should I peel them, or just core and cube them?
Use them cored and cubed; peeling isn't called for here. As you cube the apples, drop them into the large bowl so they're ready to be coated with lime juice.
The apple cubes are in the bowl. I measured the lime juice too.
Pour in the 4 tablespoons lime juice and stir the apples well so the pieces get evenly coated. That helps brighten the salsa and keeps the apples looking fresh.
That's mixed. I'm moving on to the peppers—how should I cut them?
Seed both peppers, then slice them: 1 fresh jalapeno pepper and 1 fresh Anaheim chile. Keep the slices fairly manageable so they mix easily through the apple pieces.
The jalapeno and Anaheim chile are seeded and sliced. Do they go in together?
Yes, stir the jalapeno and Anaheim chile slices into the lime-coated apples, folding from the bottom of the bowl so the peppers distribute without crushing the apple cubes.
They're mixed in. I also have onion, cilantro, walnuts, ginger, and salt nearby.
Add the onion, cilantro, walnuts, ginger, and salt to the bowl now. Stir gently but thoroughly so the herbs, nuts, and seasoning are spread throughout the salsa.
Everything is in the bowl. What texture am I aiming for before serving?
Give it a final thorough mix until every spoonful has apple, chile, and the added onion, cilantro, walnuts, ginger, and salt. It should look evenly combined but still chunky and fresh.
I'm making Apple Blueberry Tarts and have a couple of bowls ready. Can you guide me from the beginning?

Absolutely. Set out 2 medium cooking apples, peeled, cored, and chopped, along with 2/3 cup fresh or frozen blueberries. You'll also need 1 tablespoon heat-stable granular sugar substitute and 1/2 teaspoon apple pie spice or ground allspice.
The apples are chopped, and I'm using frozen blueberries. Do I mix the fruit right away?
Yes. In a medium bowl, combine the chopped apples, blueberries, the sugar substitute, and 1/4 teaspoon of the apple pie spice. Stir gently so the berries don't get crushed, then set that bowl aside.
The fruit mixture is set aside. I still have spice left from the 1/2 teaspoon measure—where does it go?
Use the remaining 1/8 teaspoon in the dry mixture. In another medium bowl, stir together the whole wheat pastry flour, kosher salt, and that 1/8 teaspoon apple pie spice.
Should the flour mixture look completely uniform before I add anything wet?
It should be evenly stirred enough that the salt and spice are distributed through the flour. A fork or spoon is fine; you don't need to beat it.
Okay, the dry bowl looks evenly mixed. What do I do with the oil and milk?
Add the oil and milk all at once to the flour mixture. Pour them in together rather than adding a little at a time.
Once they're in, should I use a mixer or keep it by hand?
Keep it by hand. Stir lightly with a fork just until the dough comes together; stop once it forms a rough dough so it doesn't get overworked.
It's starting to clump but there are a few dry bits at the bottom. Is that okay?
Give it a few more gentle turns with the fork to pick up those dry bits. As soon as the dough holds together, pause there and keep the fruit filling nearby for assembling the tarts.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: Prep the allium in two cuts, such as a fine mince plus thin slices, and stir both in right at the end so they stay bright in the bowl.
memory_annotations.exception_query_cue: For tonight, I'm turning Cabbage Rolls II into a quick broth or noodle bowl and I've got onion, garlic, scallion, leek, or shallot to use. What should I do with the allium for this version?

original_cues.exception_action_cue: Cut the allium in two shapes and add both shapes at the end.
original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making Cabbage Rolls II as a quick broth or noodle bowl with onion, garlic, scallion, leek, or shallot. How should I handle the allium?

messages.content: For tonight, I'm turning Cabbage Rolls II into a quick broth or noodle bowl and I've got onion, garlic, scallion, leek, or shallot to use. What should I do with the allium for this version?
Prep the allium in two cuts, such as a fine mince plus thin slices, and stir both in right at the end so they stay bright in the bowl.
Yes, that's the one-night version I'm after. I have cabbage leaves and cooked rice out; what should I check before I start cooking?
Make sure you have 12 cabbage leaves and 1 cup cooked white rice ready. Keep the cabbage leaves whole if you can, since they need to wrap around the filling.
The leaves are separated, and the rice is cooled. What wet ingredients go beside the bowl?
Set out 1 egg, beaten, and 1/4 cup milk. Those will help bind the filling once you mix everything together.
I've got a large pot and a colander nearby. Should I fill the pot pretty high?
Yes, use enough water for the cabbage leaves to move freely, then bring the large pot of water to a boil.
The water is boiling, and I'm trying not to tear the leaves. How long are they in?
Lower the cabbage leaves in gently, boil them for 2 minutes, then drain them well in the colander.
They're drained and flexible. What texture should the filling have when I mix it?
In a large bowl, combine the 1 cup cooked rice, beaten egg, 1/4 cup milk, onion, ground beef, salt, and pepper. It should hold together without being soupy.
I'm using the allium the way you described for the bowl. Do I mix all of it into the meat?
Keep that two-cut allium out until the end for this bowl approach. For the roll filling itself, use the onion called for with the rice, egg, milk, ground beef, salt, and pepper.
The filling is mixed. How much goes in each cabbage leaf, and how do I close them?
Spoon about 1/4 cup of the meat mixture into the center of each cabbage leaf. Roll each one up and tuck in the ends so the filling stays enclosed.
I'm making Cookie Bowl today. Can you talk me through the setup and ingredients before I start?
Absolutely. Get out 1 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 cup sliced almonds.
I've got the flour and cocoa measured. The almonds are sliced, and I found the salt too.
Great. Set those dry ingredients near your mixing bowl, and go ahead and heat the oven to 350 degrees F, which is 175 degrees C.
Oven is heating. For shaping the bowl, should I use a loaf pan or an actual metal bowl?
Either works for this recipe: turn a 9x5 inch loaf pan or a metal bowl upside down so the outside can act as the mold.
I'm using the 9x5 inch loaf pan. Do I foil the inside or the outside?
Cover the outside with foil while the pan is upside down, smoothing it over the shape so the cookie bowl can bake against it.
The outside is covered with foil. Where should I put the pan while the oven finishes heating?
Place the upside-down, foil-covered pan onto a cookie sheet so it's stable and easy to move in and out of the oven.
It's on the cookie sheet. Should I mix the dry ingredients now?
Yes. Stir together the flour, cocoa powder, salt, and sliced almonds until they're evenly combined.
The mixture looks evenly cocoa-colored with the almonds distributed. Do I need to do anything else with it right now?
That's exactly where this part ends: set the dry mixture aside, and keep the prepared foil-covered pan on the cookie sheet ready for the next stage.
I'm making Chicken Pot Pie II and I'm at the stove. Can you guide me through the chicken part?

For Chicken Pot Pie II, set out 1 1/2 pounds of skinless, boneless chicken breast meat, 1 cup chicken broth, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon ground black pepper. You'll also need a large saucepan with a lid.
I've got the saucepan and the chicken breasts. Should the broth go in before the seasonings?
Yes. Put the chicken in the large saucepan, pour in the 1 cup chicken broth, then add the salt and ground black pepper over the top.
Everything is in the pan. What heat should I use to start it?
Place the saucepan over medium-high heat and let the broth come up to a boil with the chicken, salt, and pepper in it.
It's starting to bubble around the edges but not fully boiling yet. Do I wait?
Wait until it reaches a real boil, with steady bubbling across the broth. Once it does, reduce the heat to low.
It's boiling now, and I've turned the burner down. Should I cover it completely?
Cover the saucepan with the lid and let the chicken simmer gently on low for 30 minutes.
While it simmers, how do I know if the chicken is done enough?
For Chicken Pot Pie II, after the 30 minutes, check that the chicken is no longer pink in the center and that the juices run clear.
The center isn't pink anymore and the juices look clear. What do I do with the chicken now?
Remove the chicken from the saucepan and set it aside to cool before using it for the pot pie.
I'm making Black Bean Lasagna Rolls and have a pot ready for the noodles. Can you guide me through the prep?
Absolutely. Set out 8 uncooked lasagna noodles, 1 cup shredded reduced-fat Monterey Jack cheese, 1 (15 ounce) container part-skim ricotta cheese, and 1 (4.5 ounce) can chopped green chiles, drained.
I've got the cheeses and the chiles drained. Should I salt the noodle water or add oil?
Cook the lasagna noodles according to the package directions, but omit the salt and fat. Once they're tender, drain them well so they're not watery when you fill them.
The noodles are draining now. Do I need to rinse them or lay them out?
If they're sticking together, you can separate them gently, then lay them flat in a single layer so one side of each noodle is easy to spread with filling.
For the filling, am I mixing both cheeses with the green chiles?
Yes. Combine the Monterey Jack, the part-skim ricotta, and the drained chopped green chiles, along with the next 3 ingredients called for in the recipe, and stir until the mixture is well blended.
The cheese mixture looks smooth with the chiles mixed through. How much goes on each noodle?
Divide it evenly among the 8 noodles. Spread the cheese mixture over one side of each noodle, leaving it fairly even so the rolls will hold together.
I've spread the filling, and the noodles are lying flat on the board. Where do the black beans go?
Spoon the black beans evenly over the cheese mixture on each noodle. Try to distribute them across the whole surface rather than piling them in the center.
Some beans are sliding toward the edges. Is that a problem before I roll them?
A few loose beans are fine. Just nudge them back onto the cheese layer, then roll each noodle gently so the filling stays tucked inside.
I'm making Cheesy Cheddar Potato Boats. I already baked the potatoes earlier—can you guide me through turning them into boats?

Absolutely. Set out 4 medium baked potatoes and cut each one lengthwise into quarters. You'll also need 1/3 cup Hidden Valley Original Ranch Salad Dressing, 1 cup shredded Cheddar cheese, and sliced green onions if you want them for serving.
The potatoes are quartered. Should I get the oven going before I start scooping?
Yes, preheat the oven to 375 degrees F so it's ready while you prep the potato skins.
Oven is heating. When I scoop them, am I removing all the potato from the skins?
Scoop the potato out of the skins carefully, leaving the skins intact so they can hold their shape as boats.
Some of the skins are thin near the ends. How do I keep from tearing them while adding the dressing?
Use a light hand and coat the inside of each potato skin with the Ranch rather than pressing hard. Divide the 1/3 cup dressing across the skins so they're coated but not overloaded.
The insides are coated with Ranch. What happens to the potato I scooped out?
Place the scooped potato back into the skins, keeping it nestled inside each coated boat.
They're filled again and sitting on the pan. Should the cheese go on before the green onions?
Yes. Sprinkle the 1 cup shredded Cheddar cheese over the filled potato boats first.
Cheddar is on. Are the green onions required, or just for the top?

They're optional, so add sliced green onions on top if you'd like a fresh garnish. At this point, the recipe's listed steps are complete: preheated oven, scooped and Ranch-coated skins, potato placed back in, and Cheddar sprinkled over.
I'm making Atomic Canuck Chili in the slow cooker. Can you help me get the skillet part started without missing anything?

Absolutely. Set out 2 pounds lean ground beef, 1/2 large onion diced, 1 tablespoon crushed red pepper, and 3 tablespoons garlic powder. You'll also need seasoned pepper for the skillet and a large skillet over medium heat.
The beef is thawed and the onion is diced. Should I put all the seasonings in while the meat browns?

Yes. Add the ground beef, diced onion, crushed red pepper, garlic powder, and seasoned pepper to the skillet together. Cook over medium heat, breaking up the beef as it browns so the onion and seasonings spread through it.
It's browning now, and there's some liquid and fat in the pan. How cooked should it look before I transfer it?
Wait until the beef is browned through and no longer showing raw pink spots. Once it's there, drain off the fat carefully so the chili doesn't turn greasy.
Fat is drained. Do I scrape everything straight into the slow cooker?
Yes, move the drained beef-and-onion mixture into the slow cooker, including the seasoned bits from the skillet as long as they aren't burned.
The meat mixture is in. I have mushrooms, baked beans, kidney beans, tomato paste, sugar, carrots, celery, peppers, beer, and barbeque sauce ready. What goes in first?

Add them all to the slow cooker: mushrooms, baked beans, kidney beans with their liquid, tomato paste, sugar, carrots, celery, peppers, beer, and barbeque sauce. Stir slowly from the bottom so the tomato paste and sauce loosen into the beans and beef.
The tomato paste is still in a few thick streaks. Should I keep stirring or leave it for the slow cooker?
Keep stirring a bit longer until those streaks mostly disappear. You want the tomato paste worked through the liquid so the chili base is evenly seasoned before it cooks.
Everything looks combined. How do I adjust the heat level at the end?
Season the chili with hot sauce and more crushed red pepper to taste. Stir it in, then give it a moment before tasting again so the heat spreads through the slow cooker.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: Keep the garnishes in separate little containers, then add them after the bowl is reheated so they stay fresh and crisp.
memory_annotations.exception_query_cue: For this batch of Fresh Apple Salsa, I'm packing it with a brothy lunch bowl instead of serving it right away. What's the best way to handle the finish?

original_cues.exception_action_cue: Pack both garnishes separately and add them after reheating.
original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making Fresh Apple Salsa as a packed soup, stew, bean dish, or brothy bowl. How should I finish it?

messages.content: For this batch of Fresh Apple Salsa, I'm packing it with a brothy lunch bowl instead of serving it right away. What's the best way to handle the finish?
Keep the garnishes in separate little containers, then add them after the bowl is reheated so they stay fresh and crisp.
Perfect, that's exactly how I want to do it today. I've got a cutting board out—what should I prep first?
Core and cube 2 tart apples, then have 4 tablespoons lime juice ready in a large bowl so the apple pieces can go in as soon as they're cut.
The apples are cubed, and I don't want them browning while I slice the chiles. Do they go into the lime right now?
Yes. Add the cubed apples to the large bowl and stir them with the lime juice until the pieces are well coated.
They're coated and glossy. I'm switching to the peppers—how should I cut them for the salsa?
Seed and slice 1 fresh jalapeno pepper and 1 fresh Anaheim chile. Keep the slices fairly manageable so they mix through the apples evenly.
Both chiles are seeded and sliced. Should I stir them in now or hold them back with the packed toppings?
Stir the jalapeno and Anaheim chile slices into the apple-lime mixture now; they're part of the salsa base.
The pepper slices are mixed in. I also see onion, cilantro, walnuts, ginger, and salt on my prep list—do those all go in together?
Yes, add the onion, cilantro, walnuts, ginger, and salt to the bowl, then fold everything together so the small ingredients are spread throughout.
It smells bright already. For texture, am I just tossing lightly or really working it together?
Mix thoroughly, scraping up from the bottom of the bowl, until the apples, chiles, onion, cilantro, walnuts, ginger, and salt look evenly combined.
Since I'm packing it, should I chill the salsa base before I portion out the garnishes?
Yes, chilling the mixed salsa base is fine. Pack the separate garnishes apart from the warm bowl components, and add them only after reheating when you're ready to eat.
I'm making Basil Burgers on the outdoor grill tonight. Can you help me get set up without missing anything?

Absolutely. Set out 1 1/4 pounds ground beef, 3 tablespoons Worcestershire sauce, 1 1/2 tablespoons dried basil, or a bit adjusted to taste, and 1/4 teaspoon garlic salt. You'll also want pepper handy for the burger mixture.
I've got the beef in a bowl and the seasonings nearby. Should I start heating the grill before mixing?
Yes, go ahead and preheat the outdoor grill to high heat so it's ready by the time the patties are shaped.
The grill is heating. For the meat, do I just add everything straight into the bowl?
Add the Worcestershire sauce, dried basil, garlic salt, and pepper to the ground beef. Mix gently until the seasonings are spread through the meat; try not to mash it more than needed.
The mixture smells good. How many patties should I make from this amount?
Shape it into 4 burger patties. Make them fairly even in thickness so they cook at the same pace on the grill.
They're shaped. Do I need to prep the grate before the burgers go on?
Lightly oil the grill grate before adding the patties. That helps reduce sticking, especially since the grill is on high heat.
The burgers are on. How long should I leave them before turning?
Cook them about 6 minutes total, turning once during cooking. Watch for good grill marks and avoid pressing down on the patties, since that pushes out juices.
I have a thermometer ready. What temperature am I looking for?

Check the centers for an internal temperature of 160 degrees F, which is 70 degrees C. Once they reach that, or your desired doneness, take them off the grill and let them rest briefly before serving.
I'm making Easiest Salad Dressing for a salad tonight. Can you guide me through it?
For this batch of Easiest Salad Dressing, set out a jar with a tight-fitting lid, plus 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 3 teaspoons milk, 1/4 teaspoon salt, and 1 pinch ground black pepper.
I've got a small jar with a lid. Should the mayonnaise go in before the milk?
Yes, spoon the 1/2 cup mayonnaise into the jar first, then add the 3 teaspoons milk so it can loosen the mayonnaise when you shake it.
The mayo and milk are in, but the mayo is sticking to the spoon a little.
That's fine. Scrape in what you can, then add the 1/4 teaspoon salt and the pinch of ground black pepper right into the jar.
Salt and pepper are added. Do I need to stir before putting the lid on?
No stirring is needed. Put the lid on tightly so it won't leak, then shake the jar vigorously until the dressing looks smooth and combined.
How long should I shake it if the mayo still looks streaky?
Keep shaking for a few more seconds at a time until the milk, mayonnaise, salt, and pepper are fully mixed and the dressing looks even.
It's smooth now. Should it be thick or pourable?
It should be creamy but loose enough to pour over salad. If it moves from the jar in a steady stream, it's ready.
The salad is in a bowl. Do I pour all of the dressing over it?
Pour the dressing over your salad, starting with a little if you want control, then toss and add more as needed.
I'm making Delicious Artichoke Dip and want to get everything organized before I turn on the oven.
Great. Set out 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/2 cup sour cream, 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese, and 1 (14 ounce) can of artichoke hearts, drained.
The mayo, sour cream, Parmesan, and drained artichokes are ready. Do I need a baking dish yet?
Yes, have a shallow baking dish nearby, plus a medium-sized mixing bowl for combining the dip.
Got them. What should I do with the oven?
Yes, get the oven warming to 400 degrees F, which is 200 degrees C, for Delicious Artichoke Dip.
The oven is heating. I've got the mixing bowl in front of me—what goes in first?
Stir together the mayonnaise, sour cream, Parmesan cheese, and onion in the medium-sized mixing bowl until they look evenly combined.
The creamy base is mixed, and I can still see the Parmesan flecks. Is that okay?
That's fine. Once the base is combined, mix in the drained artichoke hearts along with lemon juice, salt, and pepper.
Should the artichoke hearts be completely smooth in the mixture?
No, they can stay a little chunky; just fold them through so the artichokes are distributed throughout the creamy mixture.
The dip looks evenly mixed. How do I get it ready for the oven?
Transfer the mixture into the shallow baking dish and spread it into an even layer so it bakes evenly.
I'd like to make Fried Apple Pies today. Can you talk me through what to set out before I start cutting apples?

Absolutely. Put out 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 cup shortening, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 cup cold water for the pastry. You'll also need apples for the filling, plus sugar and cinnamon when the apples are ready.
The flour, shortening, salt, and cold water are measured. Should I start with the apples or mix the dough first?
Start with the apple filling so it has time to soften. Peel the apples, then dice them into small, even pieces so they cook down at the same pace.
I've got a pile of diced apples. How small is small enough for fried pies?
Bite-size dice is perfect. Since you'll mash them later into a thick applesauce, they don't need to be tiny—just small enough to soften easily in the saucepan.
They're in the saucepan now. Do the sugar and cinnamon go in before I turn on the heat?
Yes, add the sugar and cinnamon to the diced apples now, then stir so the pieces are lightly coated before they start cooking.
The apples are coated and the pan is on the stove. What heat should I use?
Keep it on low heat. Stir now and then so the apples cook gently and don't scorch on the bottom.
They're starting to release juice. Should I cover the pan or leave it open?
You can leave it open and keep stirring occasionally. Let the apples cook until they're soft enough to mash with a fork.
They're soft now and smell like cinnamon. What texture am I aiming for before I fill the pies?
Mash the softened apples with a fork until they form a thick applesauce. You want it thick enough to spoon into the pastry without running everywhere.
I'm making Arroz con Pollo II and have a large skillet ready. Can you talk me through the prep and cooking?
Absolutely. Start by checking that your chicken is ready: you'll need 1 whole chicken, about 2 to 3 pounds, cut into pieces. Also set out 1 tablespoon olive oil for the skillet.
The chicken is cut up, and I measured the oil. What aromatics should I prep before I turn on the heat?
Chop 2 onions and crush 3 cloves garlic. The cooking directions also call for green bell pepper later, so have that prepped as well before the skillet gets busy.
Onions are chopped, garlic is crushed, and the pepper is ready. Should I heat the pan now?
Yes. Put the large skillet over medium high heat and add the 1 tablespoon olive oil. Let it heat until the oil looks loose and glossy across the pan.
The oil is hot. Do I put the chicken in all at once or work in batches?

Add the chicken pieces in a single layer if they fit; if the skillet is crowded, brown them in batches. Sauté until the pieces are lightly browned, then remove them from the skillet and set them aside.
The chicken is browned and resting on a plate. There are browned bits in the skillet—do I keep going with the vegetables?
Keep those browned bits; they'll help flavor the dish. Add the onion, garlic, and green bell pepper to the skillet and sauté until they soften.
The vegetables have softened. I have tomato sauce, saffron, salt, and bouillon nearby—when do they go in?
Stir the tomato sauce, saffron, salt, and bouillon into the softened vegetables, then return the browned chicken pieces to the skillet so they can cook in that mixture.
The chicken is back in the skillet with the sauce mixture. How long should it cook before the rice goes in?
Let it cook for 10 minutes. After that, add the rice and reduce the heat to low so it can continue cooking gently.
I'd like to make Cookie Paints for a batch of cookies. Can you help me set it up?
Absolutely. You'll need 2 tablespoons evaporated milk, 4 drops red food coloring, a small bowl, and a clean paintbrush that's safe to use with food.
I have the evaporated milk and red food coloring out. Should I measure the milk right into the bowl?
Yes, measure the evaporated milk into the small bowl so it's ready for the color.
The milk is in the bowl. Do the food-coloring drops go in all at once?
They can go in together. Add the 4 drops of red food coloring to the evaporated milk.
Added. It's sitting in little red streaks on top—how much should I stir?
Stir until the food coloring is evenly blended into the evaporated milk and the mixture looks like one smooth red paint.
It looks evenly red now. Is this supposed to be thick?
It will be fairly thin, more like tinted milk than frosting. That's right for brushing onto cookies before they bake.
My cookie dough cutouts are on the baking sheet. Do I paint them before putting them in the oven?
Yes, brush the cookie paint onto the cookies before baking. Use a light touch so the designs show without soaking the dough.
I've painted a few designs. Any last thing to check before they bake?
Make sure the painted areas aren't puddled, then bake the cookies according to your cookie recipe. The paint is ready once it's brushed on before baking.
I'm making Chocolate Cheesecake II and want to get the crust started. What should I set out before I turn on the oven?

Set out 1 1/2 cups chocolate cookie crumbs, 2 tablespoons white sugar, 1/4 cup butter that's melted, and 1/4 cup semisweet chocolate chips. You'll also need a 9 inch springform pan and a small bowl for mixing the crumb crust.
I've got the crumbs, sugar, melted butter, and chips on the counter. Should the oven be preheating now?
Yes, bring the oven up to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), so it's ready when the crust is pressed into the pan.
The oven is set. Do I need to do anything to the springform pan before adding the crumbs?
Lightly grease the 9 inch springform pan, including the bottom and a little up the sides, so the crust releases more cleanly later.
Pan is greased. For the crumb mixture, do the chocolate chips go in with the crust ingredients?

For the crust step, mix the 1 1/2 cups chocolate wafer crumbs, 2 tablespoons sugar, and the melted 1/4 cup butter in a small bowl. Keep the 1/4 cup semisweet chocolate chips measured and ready, but don't add them to this crumb mixture unless your next filling step calls for them.
The crumbs look evenly moistened, kind of like damp sand. Is that the texture I want?
That's right. The mixture should clump slightly when pressed, with the butter distributed through the crumbs and sugar.
How high should I press the crust up the sides of the pan?
Press the crumb mixture firmly across the bottom, then bring it about 1 1/2 inch up the sides of the prepared 9 inch springform pan. Use the bottom of a measuring cup if you want a more even layer.
It's packed into the bottom and up the sides. Anything I should check before moving on?
Check that the crust is even, with no loose patches at the edge where the bottom meets the sides. Once it's shaped, you're ready for the next cheesecake step with the oven already at 350 degrees F.
I'm making English Walnut Pie and want to get set up before I start mixing. Can you walk me through it?
Absolutely. Set out 3 eggs, 1/4 teaspoon salt, 3/4 cup white sugar, and 2 teaspoons vanilla extract. You'll also want a large mixing bowl ready for the egg mixture.
I've got the eggs and sugar measured. Should I heat the oven before I crack the eggs?
Yes, turn the oven on now to 400 degrees F, which is 205 degrees C, so it can heat while you make the filling.
The oven is preheating, and I have a large bowl on the counter. Do the eggs go in by themselves first?
They do. Crack the 3 eggs into the large bowl and beat them until the yolks and whites are fully blended.
The eggs are beaten and look smooth. Do I add the salt and vanilla together?
Yes. Mix in the 3/4 cup white sugar, 1/4 teaspoon salt, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract, and the syrup. Stir until the mixture looks evenly combined.
I've stirred that in. The mixture is a little glossy now; is that okay?
That's fine for this stage. Keep the bowl nearby while you melt the butter or margarine separately.
Should the melted butter be hot when I add it, or should I let it sit a moment?
Let it cool briefly if it's very hot, then add the melted butter or margarine to the egg mixture while stirring so it blends in smoothly.
It's mixed in now. Anything I should check before moving on with the pie?

Check that the filling is uniform, with no streaks of egg or melted butter showing. Your oven should still be headed for 400 degrees F, or 205 degrees C, and the English Walnut Pie filling is ready for the next assembly step.
I'm making Delicious Artichoke Dip. Can you help me pace the prep so I don't miss anything?
Absolutely. Set out 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/2 cup sour cream, 1 cup grated Parmesan cheese, and 1 (14 ounce) can of artichoke hearts, drained.
I've got the mayo and sour cream measured, and the Parmesan is grated. Should the oven be on before I open the artichokes?
Yes, go ahead and preheat the oven to 400 degrees F, or 200 degrees C, so it's ready when the dip is mixed.
The oven is heating. I drained the can of artichoke hearts—do they go straight into the bowl?
Hold them for a moment. In a medium-sized mixing bowl, stir together the mayonnaise, sour cream, Parmesan cheese, and onion until the mixture looks even and creamy.
The creamy base is mixed. How incorporated should it be before I add the artichokes?
Once there are no big streaks of sour cream or mayonnaise, mix in the drained artichoke hearts along with lemon juice, salt, and pepper.
The artichokes are folded in, but the dip looks chunky. Is that okay?
Yes, that's expected. The base should be creamy, and the artichoke hearts can stay in noticeable pieces rather than disappearing into the dip.
What kind of dish should I use to bake it?
Spoon the mixture into a shallow baking dish and spread it out evenly so the surface is level.
It's in the dish now. Anything else before it goes in?
Just make sure the oven has reached 400 degrees F, or 200 degrees C, and the dip is evenly spread in the shallow baking dish. Then it's ready for the oven.
I'm making Chicken Tortilla Soup IV. Can you help me get set up before I turn on the stove?
Absolutely. For this recipe, have 2 1/2 teaspoons vegetable oil, 6 corn tortillas that are 6 inches each and cut into 1/2 inch strips, 3 cups chicken broth, and 1/2 teaspoon ground cumin ready.
The tortillas are stacked right now. Should I slice all 6 into strips before heating the pot?
Yes, cut all 6 tortillas into 1/2 inch strips before you start cooking. That way you can fry them in batches without rushing.
I've got a large pot out. How much oil goes in for the first batch?
Add 2 teaspoons of the vegetable oil to the large pot and warm it over medium heat.
The oil is heating. Do all the strips go in at once, or only part of them?
Only add half of the tortilla strips for this first round. Stir them often as they cook so they crisp evenly.
They're starting to firm up and curl a little. Am I waiting for them to be fully crisp?
Yes, keep stirring often until that half of the tortilla strips is crisp. Once they are crisp, lift them out of the pot.
I pulled the first batch out. Where should I put them so they don't get soggy?
Drain them on paper towels. Spread them out a bit so excess oil can come off and the strips stay crisp.
The paper towels are catching the oil. What do I do with the remaining tortilla strips?

Add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon vegetable oil to the pot, then repeat the same process with the remaining tortilla strips. When they're crisp, drain them on paper towels too and set all the tortilla strips aside.
I'd like to make Fall Harvest Baked Apples. Can you guide me while I get set up?
Absolutely. Set out 8 red apples, already cored, plus 1/4 cup butter, 1/3 cup maple syrup, and 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon.
The apples are cored, and I have the butter, syrup, and cinnamon measured. What pan and oven temperature do I need?
Use a 9x13 inch baking dish, and heat the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C).
Oven is heating. Should the apples stand upright in the dish?
Yes, arrange the cored apples in the 9x13 inch baking dish so they sit upright and have a little space for the syrup mixture to run around them.
They're in the dish. I'm ready to make the topping on the stove.
Place a small saucepan over medium heat. Add the 1/4 cup butter, 1/3 cup maple syrup, 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, ginger, lemon juice, and vanilla.
The butter is starting to melt with everything else. Do I just stir until it's smooth?
Stir gently as the butter melts so the maple syrup and spices combine evenly. Keep it over medium heat until the mixture comes to a boil.
It's bubbling now. How should I pour it over the apples without missing any?
Carefully drizzle the hot mixture equally over the apples, letting some run into the cored centers and some coat the outsides.
All the apples have syrup over them. Is that the last prep step before baking?
Yes. Once the sauce is evenly drizzled over the apples in the baking dish, they're ready for the oven at 350 degrees F.
I'm making A Very Intense Fruit Smoothie. Can you help me get it going?
Absolutely. Set out a blender, 1 (10 ounce) package of frozen mixed berries, 1 (15 ounce) can of sliced peaches, and 2 tablespoons honey.
The berries are still frozen. Is that okay, or should I thaw them first?
Frozen is fine for this smoothie. They can go straight into the blender with the fruit and honey.
I opened the peaches. Do I use the juice from the can too?
Drain the sliced peaches before adding them. The recipe uses the 1 (15 ounce) can of peaches drained.
Okay, peaches are drained and the blender jar is ready. What goes in first?
Add the frozen mixed berries, then the drained sliced peaches, then drizzle in the 2 tablespoons honey.
Everything is in the blender, but the berries are piled up pretty high.
Put the lid on firmly and start blending. If your blender has speeds, begin gently and increase as the fruit starts moving.
It's blending, but I can still see some berry pieces along the sides.
Pause the blender, scrape or shake the jar as needed with the lid secured afterward, then keep blending until the mixture looks smooth.
Now it looks evenly blended and thick. Is there anything else before serving?
That's it—the recipe is complete once it's blended smooth. Pour the smoothie into glasses and serve it right away.
I'm making Garden Potato Salad and already cooked the potatoes. Can you guide me through getting it assembled?

Absolutely. Start by setting out 6 large potatoes, cooked, peeled, and cubed, along with 4 hard-cooked eggs, sliced. Use a large mixing bowl so there's room to fold everything together without breaking up the potatoes too much.
The potatoes are cubed and the eggs are sliced. I also have celery and green onions—how should I prep those?
Slice 2 celery ribs, then slice 6 green onions with their tops. Keep the slices fairly even so they distribute nicely through the salad.
Celery and onions are sliced. The recipe mentions radishes too, but I don't see a quantity here—what should I do with them?

Since the instruction includes radishes but doesn't give an amount, slice the radishes you plan to use and add them with the vegetables. Combine the potatoes, sliced eggs, celery, green onions, radishes, salt, and pepper in the large bowl, then set that bowl aside.
That bowl is mixed and resting. What do I need for the dressing pan?
In a saucepan, combine eggs, vinegar, sugar, dry mustard, and salt. Stir them together before turning on the heat so the mixture starts out smooth.
The dressing ingredients are in the saucepan. Should I use low heat or bring it up hotter?
Use medium heat. Cook and stir the dressing steadily over medium heat until it thickens; keep the spoon moving so the egg mixture doesn't catch on the bottom.
It's starting to look thicker and coat the spoon. Is that the texture I'm looking for?
Yes, that coating consistency is what you want. Once it has thickened, take the saucepan off the heat.
The pan is off the burner. Do I pour it over the potato mixture right away?
Let the dressing cool first. Once cooled, it can be added to the potato mixture for the Garden Potato Salad, then gently folded together so the potatoes and eggs stay intact.
I'm making Crustless Spinach Quiche and have a 9 inch pie pan ready. Can you guide me from setup through the stovetop part?

Absolutely. Set your oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) so it can heat while you prep. You'll also want 1 tablespoon vegetable oil, 1 chopped onion, a 10 ounce package of frozen chopped spinach that's thawed and well drained, and 5 beaten eggs.
The spinach is thawed, but it still feels a little damp. Is that okay for this?
Try to press out as much extra liquid as you can before it goes into the quiche mixture. Drained spinach will keep the quiche from turning watery.
Good to know. The oven is heating, and I've got the pie pan out. Should I grease it now?
Yes, lightly grease the 9 inch pie pan now, making sure the bottom and sides get a thin coating.
Pan is greased. I have the chopped onion by the stove and the eggs beaten in a bowl.
Great. Put a large skillet over medium-high heat and add the 1 tablespoon vegetable oil. Let it warm until the oil looks loose and glossy.
The oil is warmed up. Do the onions go in by themselves?
Yes. Add the chopped onion to the skillet and spread it out so it cooks evenly.
How often should I stir, and what texture am I looking for?
Stir the onions occasionally rather than constantly. Cook them until they're soft; they should lose their sharp raw look and feel tender when you move them around the pan.
The onions are soft now. I haven't added the spinach or eggs yet.

That's right for where you are. You've completed the listed stovetop step: the oven is at 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), the 9 inch pie pan is greased, the oil was heated in the skillet, and the onion has cooked until soft.
I'm making apple butter spice cake and I've got a 9x13 inch pan out. Can you help me get organized?
Absolutely. Set the oven to 350 degrees F, or 175 degrees C, and spray or grease the 9x13 inch pan so it's ready before the batter comes together.
The oven is heating and the pan is greased. I want to make sure I don't miss anything for the topping.
For apple butter spice cake's topping, measure 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon, 1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg, and 1/2 cup chopped pecans.
Those are measured. Do I just stir them together, or should the pecans stay separate?
Stir them together in one bowl so the brown sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and chopped pecans are evenly mixed. That topping can sit aside while you make the batter.
Topping is mixed. I'm moving to the cake batter—what should I do with the dry ingredients?
Sift the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt together. Sifting helps them combine evenly before they go into the wet mixture.
The dry mix is sifted. I have butter and sugar ready in a larger bowl.
Blend the butter and sugar together until they're combined, then add the eggs and beat the mixture well.
The eggs are beaten in. It looks smoother now—when does the apple butter go in?
Add the apple butter next, along with the vanilla and the wheat germ or bran cereal. Mix until those are worked through the batter.
That's mixed in. I still have the sifted dry ingredients and sour cream waiting.

Add the sifted dry ingredients alternately with the sour cream, mixing well after each addition. Once the batter is combined, spread it in the prepared pan and use the brown sugar, spice, and pecan topping as prepared for the cake.
I'm making Black Bean Lasagna Rolls and want to keep the prep organized. What should I pull out first?
Set out 8 uncooked lasagna noodles and 1 cup shredded reduced-fat Monterey Jack cheese. You'll also want a pot for boiling the noodles, a colander, and a mixing bowl for the filling.
The noodles and Monterey Jack are on the counter. What other filling ingredients should I open?
Add a 1 (15 ounce) container of part-skim ricotta cheese and a 1 (4.5 ounce) can of chopped green chiles, drained, to your setup.
Got it. Should I start with the noodles or mix the cheeses first?
Start with the noodles so they can cook and drain before you fill them. Cook the lasagna noodles according to the package directions, omitting salt and fat, then drain them well.
They're boiling now. How drained do they need to be before I lay them out?
Drain them thoroughly so water doesn't thin the filling. Once they're cool enough to handle, lay the noodles flat in a single layer so they're ready for spreading.
The noodles are drained and laid flat. What goes into the bowl?
Combine the cheeses and the next 3 ingredients, stirring well, so the ricotta, Monterey Jack, chiles, and the remaining filling components are evenly mixed.
The filling looks smooth with the chiles mixed through. How much should I put on each noodle?
Spread the cheese mixture over one side of each noodle, dividing it evenly among the 8 noodles and keeping it in a layer that can still roll neatly.
The cheese is spread on all of them. Where do the black beans go?
Spoon the black beans evenly over the cheese mixture on each noodle. Try to distribute them across the full length so every lasagna roll gets a balanced filling.
I'd like to make the Banana Kiwi Strawberry Tart crust. Can you guide me through it while I prep?

Absolutely. Set out 1/2 cup all-purpose flour, 1 tablespoon light brown sugar, 1/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon, and 1/8 teaspoon salt. You'll also want a bowl, a sifter or fine mesh strainer, a fork, plastic wrap, plus your butter and ice water ready.
The dry ingredients are measured. Should I combine them all in the same bowl?
Yes. Sift the flour, light brown sugar, cinnamon, and salt together into the bowl so they're evenly blended and free of lumps.
The brown sugar is clumping a little in the strainer. Is that okay?
That's fine. Press any small brown sugar bits through the strainer with a spoon or your fingers, then give the sifted mixture a quick stir to make sure the cinnamon and salt are distributed.
Dry mix looks even. I have the butter out—how should it look once I work it in?
Cut in the butter until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs. Use a pastry cutter, two knives, or your fingertips, and stop when you see small crumbly pieces rather than a smooth paste.
Some pieces are pea-sized and some are sandy. Should I keep going?
That texture is right for this stage. A mix of sandy crumbs and a few slightly larger bits is okay as long as there aren't big chunks of butter left.
I'm ready for the ice water. Do I pour it all in at once?
Sprinkle the ice water over the crumb mixture instead of dumping it in. Toss gently with a fork until everything is evenly moistened.
It's starting to hold when I press it, but it's still crumbly. What's the last thing I should do?
