Add the chicken, broccoli, onion, and green bell pepper to the large bowl, then include the cheese, mayonnaise, mustard, salt, pepper, and garlic.
Should I fold that gently, or really stir it together?
Stir it well enough that everything is evenly coated and distributed. You don't need to mash it—just mix until the chicken, broccoli, vegetables, and seasonings look combined.
The mixture looks even now. Do I need to prep the oven at this point?
Yes, heat the oven to 400 degrees F (200 degrees C). Let it come fully up to temperature while you prepare the baking surface.
I have a cookie sheet out. Is there anything I should put on it for easier cleanup?
Cover the cookie sheet with aluminum foil. Smooth it over the surface so it's ready for the Broccoli Chicken Roli once you're set to bake.
The foil is on the pan and the oven is heating. Can you quickly recap so I know I didn't miss anything?

You've combined 2 cups chopped, cooked chicken meat, 2 cups fresh chopped broccoli, 1/2 cup chopped onion, 1/2 cup chopped green bell pepper, plus cheese, mayonnaise, mustard, salt, pepper, and garlic. Puree the soup in a blender or food processor until smooth, then use it as the base for your rice or noodle bowl and add the herb pile at one edge.

Yes, measure them separately so the layers stay neat: 1 cup all-purpose flour in one bowl and 1 cup chopped pecans in another.

Lightly level the flour, but don't compress it too much. Then spoon the 1 cup chopped pecans over the top so they form the final layer.

Attach a tag with the baking instruction from the recipe: "bring the oven up to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C)."

Make sure the lid is secure, wipe the outside of the jar clean, and tie on the tag where it's easy to read. The Double Fudge Brownie Mix is ready to gift.

Yes, go ahead and get the oven warming to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), so it's hot by the time the batter is ready.
Oven is heating. Do I just spray the pan, or does this one need more prep?
For this cake, grease and flour the 9x13 inch pan. Coat the inside lightly with grease, then dust it with flour and tap out the extra.
Pan is greased and floured. I'm ready to start the bowl work—what goes in together?
Sift together the flour, baking soda, cinnamon, and salt. That helps distribute the 1 teaspoon baking soda and 1 teaspoon cinnamon evenly through the 3 cups flour.
I don't have a sifter handy. Can I still do that step with a whisk?
Yes. Whisk the flour, baking soda, cinnamon, and salt thoroughly in a large bowl, breaking up any little clumps as you go.
The dry mixture looks even now. What should I do with the apples?
Combine the apples with the white sugar in a separate bowl, then set that mixture aside. Letting it sit briefly helps the apples start releasing their juices.
The apples and sugar are resting. Anything I should clean up or check before I keep going?

Clear away the flour dust, keep the prepared pan nearby, and make sure the oven is still holding at 350 degrees F. You now have the dry mixture ready and the apple-sugar mixture set aside for the next part of the cake.
Can you talk me through Brandy Flamed Peppercorn Steak while I set up the pan and season the meat?

Absolutely. For the steaks, have 3 tablespoons crushed black peppercorns, 2 beef top sirloin steaks that are 8 ounces each, 1 tablespoon lemon pepper, and 1 teaspoon salt ready. You'll also need a large skillet for the stovetop.
The steaks are on a board and the peppercorns are crushed. Do I coat them lightly or really pack the pepper on?
Press the crushed black peppercorns firmly into both sides of each steak so they adhere instead of just sitting loose on the surface.
Both sides are covered. I still have the lemon pepper and salt measured nearby.
Sprinkle the steaks evenly with the 1 tablespoon lemon pepper and the 1 teaspoon salt, keeping the coating even from edge to edge.
Seasoning is on. Should the skillet be heating before I add anything?
Yes. Put a large skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter in it, letting it coat the bottom of the pan.
The butter is melting and starting to spread. I have garlic and wine ready too.
Once the butter is melted, stir in the garlic and wine, then let that cook for 1 minute.
While that minute runs, should I keep stirring or just let it bubble?
Give it a gentle stir so the garlic mixes through the wine and butter, then let it bubble briefly during that 1 minute without walking away.
It smells sharp and buttery now. Is there anything else in the written steps before the steaks go in?

The listed steps have you pepper both sides, season with lemon pepper and salt, melt butter over medium-high heat, then stir in garlic and wine for 1 minute. At this point, your steaks and pan are prepared according to the recipe.
I'm making Early Morning Oven Roasted New Potatoes. Can you help me organize the ingredients and pan setup before I turn on the heat?

Absolutely. Set out 1 1/2 pounds of new potatoes cut into wedges, 4 tablespoons butter, 2 teaspoons fresh rosemary, and salt and pepper. You'll also want a skillet for melting the butter and a baking pan or sheet for the potatoes.
The potatoes are already cut into wedges. Should I start with the oven or the butter?
Go ahead and get the oven warming to 450 degrees F (230 degrees C). While it heats, keep the potato wedges nearby so they're ready to coat.
On Early Morning Oven Roasted New Potatoes, oven is heating. I've got a skillet on the stove—how hot should it be before the butter goes in?
In this Early Morning Oven Roasted New Potatoes step, use a hot skillet, then add the 4 tablespoons butter and let it melt. Keep an eye on it so it melts smoothly rather than browning too much.
The butter is melted and still yellow. Do I add the rosemary straight into the skillet?
Yes. Stir in the 2 teaspoons fresh rosemary, then season with salt and pepper to taste. Give it a quick stir so the rosemary flavors the melted butter.
It smells good. Should the potatoes go into the skillet, or should I pour the butter over them?

Either can work, but the goal is to coat the potatoes evenly with the melted butter. If your skillet is roomy, toss the wedges in there; otherwise, put the potatoes on the pan and pour the rosemary butter over them.
My skillet is small, so I'm using the baking sheet. How coated should the wedges look?
They should have a light, even sheen on all sides, with bits of rosemary distributed across the wedges. Turn them with a spatula or your hands if they're cool enough to handle safely.
They're spread out on the pan now. Anything else before they go into the oven?

Make sure the wedges are in a single layer so the heat can reach them evenly. The recipe's listed prep ends once the potatoes are evenly coated with the rosemary butter, salt, and pepper, and your oven is already at 450 degrees F, or 230 degrees C.

source_seed.recipe_title: Early Morning Oven Roasted New Potatoes

messages.content: I'm ready to cook Dipping Sauce. What should be ready before I begin? I'm setting out a small mixing bowl now.
Yes. Put the small bowl on your counter and grab the measured ingredients: 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 2 teaspoons ketchup, 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish, and 1/4 teaspoon paprika.
I've got the mayo, ketchup, horseradish, and paprika. Do I need anything else before I start stirring?
The recipe also has you mix in salt, oregano, black pepper, and cayenne pepper, so keep those nearby too. Add the mayonnaise to the bowl first since it's the base.
The mayonnaise is in. Should the ketchup go in next, or does the order matter?
The order isn't critical for this sauce. Add the 2 teaspoons ketchup, then spoon in the 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish so it can get evenly blended into the mayo.
Ketchup and horseradish are in the bowl. It smells pretty sharp already.
That's expected from the horseradish. Sprinkle in the 1/4 teaspoon paprika, then add the salt, oregano, black pepper, and cayenne pepper called for in the recipe.
All the seasonings are in. How thoroughly should I mix it?
Stir until the sauce looks smooth and evenly tinted, with no streaks of ketchup or paprika and no pockets of horseradish. Scrape around the sides and bottom of the bowl as you mix.
It's smooth now. Should I taste it right away or chill it first?
You can taste a tiny bit now to check that it's evenly mixed, but the recipe's storage step is to cover it and keep it in the refrigerator. Chilling will also help the flavors settle.
I'm transferring it to a container. Any tips so it doesn't make a mess?
Use a spatula to scrape the bowl clean, then cover the container tightly and refrigerate the dipping sauce until you're ready to serve it.
I want to make Cookie Bowl. Can you help me set up the ingredients and pan? I'm using the oven today.
Absolutely. Start by heating the oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) so it's ready when the cookie bowl is shaped.
Oven is heating. For the dry ingredients, what should I measure before I pull out the pan?
Measure 1 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 cup sliced almonds.
The flour, cocoa, salt, and almonds are on the counter. What pan setup do I need for the bowl shape?
Use either a 9x5 inch loaf pan or a metal bowl. Turn it upside down, then cover the outside with foil so the dough can bake over that surface.
I have a metal bowl. Should the foil be inside the bowl or wrapped around the outside?
Wrap the foil over the outside of the upside-down bowl. Smooth it over the surface as best you can so the cookie bowl has an even form.
The foil is on the outside of the bowl now. Where does it go in the oven?
Set the foil-covered upside-down bowl onto a cookie sheet. That gives it a stable base and makes it easier to move in and out of the oven.
Cookie sheet is ready. Should I mix the dry ingredients now?
Yes. Stir together the flour, cocoa, salt, and sliced almonds until the cocoa and salt are evenly distributed through the flour.
The dry mix looks even. Do I need to do anything else with it right away?
For this part of the recipe, just set that dry mixture aside while the oven finishes preheating and your foil-covered bowl stays ready on the cookie sheet.
I'm making Cheesy Sweet and Savory Spuds. Can you help me get everything ready before I turn on the stove?
Absolutely. Set out 6 Yukon Gold potatoes and 2 sweet potatoes, all peeled and cubed. You'll also need 2 tablespoons butter and 1/2 cup heavy cream nearby.
The potatoes are peeled and cubed. Should I use a saucepan or something bigger?
Use a large pot so the Yukon Gold potatoes and sweet potatoes have room to sit under the water without crowding.
Got it. How much water should I add?
Add enough water to cover the cubed potatoes and sweet potatoes completely.
They're covered in water and on the stove. What heat should I use?
In this Cheesy Sweet and Savory Spuds step, turn the heat up and bring the pot to a boil.
It's boiling now. Do I keep it going for a while, or stop here?
For the recipe step you're on, once it has come to a boil, remove the pot from the heat.
The pot is off the burner. What's the safest way to handle the water?
Drain the potatoes and sweet potatoes carefully, using a colander if you have one, and watch for steam.
They're drained. Do I start mixing in the butter and cream now?
Before moving on, preheat the oven broiler so it's ready for the next part of the dish.
I'm about to start Dipping Sauce. Can you talk me through the prep? I'm setting out a small bowl and want to measure everything correctly.
Absolutely. Measure 1/2 cup mayonnaise into the small bowl, then add 2 teaspoons ketchup. Those will give you the creamy base and a little sweetness.
The mayo and ketchup are in. I also have prepared horseradish and paprika out—how much of each goes in?
Add 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish and 1/4 teaspoon paprika to the bowl. If your horseradish has liquid sitting on top, give it a quick stir before measuring.
Okay, those are added. The instruction mentions salt, oregano, black pepper, and cayenne pepper too—do I mix those in now?
Yes, add the salt, oregano, black pepper, and cayenne pepper now. The recipe doesn't give exact amounts for those, so season lightly, especially with the cayenne, then you can adjust after mixing.
What should the sauce look like once I stir it?
Stir until the mayonnaise, ketchup, horseradish, paprika, and seasonings are fully combined. It should look smooth and creamy, with an even pale pink-orange color and no streaks of mayo.
It's smooth now. Should I taste it before storing it?
Yes, taste a tiny spoonful. If it needs more bite, add a little more horseradish; if it tastes flat, add a small pinch of salt or black pepper. Keep any adjustment modest so it stays balanced.
I like the flavor. What's the best way to put it away?
Transfer it to a clean container or leave it in the bowl if that's convenient, then cover it well. Store it covered in the refrigerator.
Can I serve it right away, or should it chill first?
You can serve it right away, but chilling it covered in the refrigerator helps the horseradish, paprika, and seasonings blend into the mayonnaise base. Give it a quick stir again before serving.
I'm starting Classic Peanut Butter Cookies; can you walk me through the setup? I'm setting out the mixing bowl and ingredients now.
Absolutely. Put out 1 cup unsalted butter, 1 cup crunchy peanut butter, 1 cup white sugar, and 1 cup packed brown sugar. Let the butter soften enough that it will cream smoothly.
The butter is soft and I have both sugars measured. Should the peanut butter go in with them right away?
Yes. Add the butter, crunchy peanut butter, white sugar, and packed brown sugar to the bowl together, then cream them until the mixture looks blended and a little fluffy.
It's coming together, but the brown sugar is clumping a bit on the side of the bowl.
Scrape down the sides and keep mixing until the sugar clumps are worked in. You want the butter, peanut butter, and sugars evenly combined before adding anything else.
Okay, the mixture looks smoother now. I have eggs nearby—do they go in next?
They do. Beat in the eggs until the batter looks uniform and glossy, scraping the bowl once if needed so everything mixes evenly.
The eggs are mixed in. I'm ready for the dry ingredients, but I don't want to dump them straight in if that's wrong.
Use a separate bowl for the dry ingredients. Sift together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt so they're evenly distributed before they meet the batter.
I sifted the flour mixture. Should I add it all at once or in smaller additions?
Add the sifted dry mixture to the batter and stir it in gently. If your bowl is crowded, adding it in portions is fine; just mix until no dry streaks remain.
The dough is thick now and I don't see loose flour. Is there anything else for this stage?

That completes the mixing for the recipe: the sifted flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt have been stirred into the butter-peanut-butter batter. Scrape the bowl cleanly so the dough is even before you move on to shaping or baking.

messages.content: For Broccoli Cheese Crepes today, I'm packing it as a thermos lunch alongside noodles, pasta, rice, or grains, so I want the saucier version just for this meal. What should I do with the liquid?
For this thermos lunch, keep the extra liquid in a separate small container, then stir it in once the thermos is opened so the noodles, pasta, rice, or grains don't soak it all up early.
Perfect, that's exactly what I want for this batch. Before I turn on anything, what should I measure first?
Measure the crepe batter basics first: 2 eggs, 1/4 cup water, 6 tablespoons all-purpose flour, and 1/2 teaspoon salt.
I've got the eggs and water by the blender. Should the flour and salt go in there too?
Yes. Add the eggs, water, flour, and salt to the blender together for the batter.
The blender jar is loaded. How smooth does it need to get?
In this Broccoli Cheese Crepes step, cover the blender and process until the batter looks smooth, with no dry flour pockets or obvious lumps.
It looks smooth now. Do I use it right away or let it sit?
Let the batter stand for 15 minutes before cooking with it.
While it rests, I can work on the filling or sauce. What pan should I use?
Use a small saucepan, and sauté the onion in butter until the onion is tender.
The onion has softened and the butter is bubbling lightly. What do I add next?
Stir in the flour until it's blended into the butter and onion mixture.
For packing, should I combine everything with the grains before it goes into the thermos?
Pack the crepes and the noodles, pasta, rice, or grains as planned, but keep that extra liquid separate until serving so the texture stays better in the thermos.
I'm making Figs with Goat Cheese Pecans and Bacon. Can you help me prep it without getting ahead of myself?
Absolutely. Set up your broiler first so it's hot when the figs are assembled. You'll also want toothpicks nearby for securing the bacon.
Got it. I have the broiler on and toothpicks out. What ingredients should be on the counter?
Put out 6 figs, halved; 6 ounces goat cheese; 1/2 cup toasted, chopped pecans; and 3 slices bacon, cut in half.
The figs are halved. Should the cut side face up while I fill them?
Yes, keep the cut sides up. Spoon or press goat cheese into each fig half so the cheese sits neatly in the center.
The goat cheese is a little soft. Is that okay for adding the pecans?
That's fine. Gently press the toasted, chopped pecans into the goat cheese so they stick rather than scatter.
All the fig halves have cheese and pecans now. How do I handle the bacon?
Take the 3 bacon slices that have been cut in half, and wrap each stuffed fig half with half a slice of bacon.
Should I cover the cheese completely or just wrap around the middle?
Wrap around the stuffed fig half so the bacon holds everything together, then secure it with a toothpick.
They're all wrapped and pinned. Anything to check before they go under the broiler?
Make sure each toothpick is holding firmly and the pecans are pressed into the cheese. Once they're arranged securely, they're ready for the broiler.

source_seed.recipe_title: Figs with Goat Cheese Pecans and Bacon

messages.content: I'd like to make Fire Side Coffee and store it in a jar. Can you help me set up the dry mix?

Absolutely. Set out a large bowl, a sifter or fine-mesh strainer, and a clean jar with a tight lid. For the mix, you'll need 2 cups powdered non-dairy creamer, 1 1/2 cups instant hot chocolate mix, 1 1/2 cups instant coffee granules, and 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon.
I have the bowl and jar ready. Should the creamer and cocoa go in together?
Yes. Add the powdered non-dairy creamer and instant hot chocolate mix to the sifter over the bowl so they break up evenly instead of clumping.
The creamer has a few lumps. Is that okay before I add the coffee?
That's exactly why sifting helps. Keep tapping or stirring the creamer through the strainer, then add the instant coffee granules and the cinnamon to the same bowl.
The coffee granules and 1 teaspoon cinnamon are in. The instruction I'm looking at also says nutmeg—how should I handle that?

Sift the creamer, hot chocolate mix, instant coffee, cinnamon, and nutmeg together as directed, using whatever nutmeg amount your copy of the recipe lists. The goal is a uniform dry blend with no pockets of spice or coffee.
It looks evenly mixed now. Do I pack it into the jar or leave it loose?
Leave it loose. Spoon or pour the mixture into the jar, then seal it with the lid so it stays dry and easy to scoop.
The jar is sealed. I want to try one mug before putting it away—what ratio should I use?
For 1 cup of hot water, stir in 3 teaspoons of the Fire Side Coffee mixture. Mix until the powder dissolves as much as possible.
I stirred it into the hot water. It smells good, but I'm not sure if it should be stronger.
Taste it and adjust to taste: add a little more mix if you want it stronger, or more hot water if you want it lighter. Once you like the balance, keep the remaining dry mix sealed in the jar.

original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making Corned Beef Hash as a quick broth or noodle bowl with onion, garlic, scallion, leek, or shallot. How should I handle the allium?

messages.content: Tonight I'm turning Corned Beef Hash into a quick broth/noodle bowl, and I'm using onion, garlic, scallion, leek, or shallot. What's the best way to prep the allium for this one?
For this bowl version, prep the allium two ways: make one cut thin and delicate, and one cut a little chunkier or minced. Keep both aside and add them right at the end so they stay bright.
Perfect, that's exactly the direction I want just for this bowl. I've got the skillet out—what ingredients should I prep first?
Peel and dice 6 large potatoes, then cut 1 (12 ounce) can of corned beef into chunks. Those are the main pieces to get ready before the pan heats.
The potatoes are diced pretty evenly, and the corned beef is in chunks. What liquid and aromatics do I need nearby?
Measure 1 cup beef broth. For the recipe's onion amount, use 1 medium onion, chopped, but since you're doing the bowl-style allium approach, keep those two cuts of allium separate for the end.
Should the pan be deep enough for everything to simmer without splashing?
Yes, use a large deep skillet. Set it over medium heat, then add the diced potatoes, corned beef chunks, and 1 cup beef broth.
I'm holding back the onion pieces like you said. The potatoes and beef are in with the broth—do I cover it?
Cover the skillet and let it simmer over medium heat until the potatoes are soft enough to mash and the liquid is almost gone.
What should I look for so I don't stop too early?
Press a potato piece with a spoon; it should give way easily, close to mashing consistency. The broth should be reduced so there's just a little moisture coating the hash rather than a loose pool.
It's thick now, and the potatoes are breaking down at the edges. Do I mash it fully?
No need to make it smooth. Mix it well so the potatoes, corned beef, and reduced broth come together, keeping some texture.
I'm ready to serve it as the bowl. When do the two allium cuts go in?
Stir in both allium cuts right at the end, just before serving, then spoon the Corned Beef Hash into the bowl while it's hot.

memory_annotations.exception_action_cue: Keep the soft herbs or scallions in their own small lidded container, then sprinkle them in after you open the lunch so they stay fresh.

original_cues.exception_query_cue: I'm making 1 Pot 3 Bean Chicken Stew as a packed lunch with optional cilantro, parsley, basil, mint, or scallions. How should I handle the soft herbs?

messages.content: I'm cooking 1 Pot 3 Bean Chicken Stew to pack for lunch, and I may use cilantro, parsley, basil, mint, or scallions with it. Since it's going in a lunch container, what should I do with those soft herbs?
Keep the soft herbs or scallions in their own small lidded container, then sprinkle them in after you open the lunch so they stay fresh.
Great, that's the lunchbox approach I want for this stew today. Before I turn on the stove, what prep should I handle?
Cut 1 3/4 pounds boneless, skinless chicken breast or thighs into chunks, and measure out 1 tablespoon canola oil for browning.
The chicken is cut up, and the oil is measured. Do I need the vegetables ready before the pot gets hot?
Yes. Chop 1 large yellow onion and slice 1 cup celery. Keep the onion close by for the early cooking, and save the celery for the simmer.
I've got a large pot on the stove now. How should I start the chicken so it browns instead of steaming?
Heat the canola oil in the large pot, then add the chicken in a roomy layer. Brown it well; if the pot looks crowded, work in batches.
The chicken has color on it and there are browned bits on the bottom. Should I leave it in there?
Take the chicken out of the pot and set it aside on a plate or in a bowl, along with any juices that collect.
The onion is going into the pot now. What texture am I looking for, and about how long?
Saute the chopped onion until it turns soft and less sharp, about 5 minutes. Stir so it picks up the browned flavor without scorching.
The onion smells sweet now. I still have the celery waiting, and I'm thinking ahead to packing lunches. What goes in before the long simmer?
Add the broth, beans, tomatoes, sliced celery, carrots, wine, bay leaf, herbs, and all the browned chicken back into the pot. Scrape the bottom so those browned bits mix into the stew.
Once everything is in the pot, how long should it cook covered, and when do I deal with the herbs for the packed portions?
Cover the pot and let the stew simmer for 40 minutes. For the lunch portions, cool and pack the stew separately from the soft herbs, then add those herbs after opening the lunch.
I'm setting up for Crabby Cliffs Mushroom Puffs; what should happen before the heat goes on? I'm starting from an empty counter.
Absolutely. Set out 2 tablespoons olive oil and 3 cups fresh chopped mushrooms, and grab a medium saucepan while you're there.
The oil, mushrooms, and saucepan are ready. What else should I chop or crush before I turn on heat?
Prep 2 green onions, chopped, and 1 clove garlic, crushed. Keep the cayenne pepper nearby too, since it gets stirred in with the vegetables.
Green onions are chopped and the garlic is crushed. Do I need the oven involved for these puffs?
Yes—heat the oven to 400 degrees F (200 degrees C), so it's hot when the filling is ready.
Oven is heating. Should the saucepan go on medium or higher?
Use medium heat. Add the 2 tablespoons olive oil to the medium saucepan and let it warm until it looks loose and glossy, not smoking.
The oil is shimmering lightly. Do the mushrooms go in by themselves first?
Add the mushrooms together with the chopped green onions, crushed garlic, and cayenne pepper. Stir so everything gets coated in the oil.
Everything is in the pan, and the mushrooms are starting to give off moisture. How long am I cooking this mixture?
Cook it for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the mushrooms and onions are tender.
At around 10 minutes, what should I look for before I take it off the heat?

The mushrooms should be soft and tender, the green onions should look wilted, and the garlic should smell mellow rather than sharp. Once it reaches that texture, the cooked mushroom mixture is ready for the puffs.
Today I'm tackling Coq au Vin alla Italiana. Can you help me line up the prep?

Absolutely. Set out 4 pounds of dark meat chicken pieces, 1 tablespoon vegetable oil, 5 cloves of crushed garlic, and 1/2 cup all-purpose flour. You'll also want poultry seasoning for the flour and a large skillet.
The chicken is out, and I've got the oil and skillet on the stove. Should I prep the garlic before heating?
Yes, crush the garlic now so it's ready to go. Once everything is within reach, pour the vegetable oil into the large skillet and start heating it.
The oil is heating. Do I add all the garlic at once?
Add only 1/2 of the crushed garlic to the skillet for this part, and let it warm in the oil briefly so it starts to perfume the pan.
It smells garlicky now. I have the flour in a shallow dish—what should I do with it?
Season the 1/2 cup all-purpose flour with poultry seasoning, then stir it so the seasoning is evenly mixed through the flour.
The seasoned flour is ready. Should the chicken be dry before I coat it?
If the chicken pieces are very wet, pat them lightly so the flour clings better. Then dredge the dark meat chicken parts in the seasoned flour, coating them on all sides.
I've coated a few pieces. How crowded can the skillet be when I brown them?
Give the chicken pieces some space in the skillet so they brown instead of steaming. Work in batches if needed, placing the floured pieces into the hot oil and garlic.
They're in the skillet now. How long am I browning them?
Brown the chicken in the skillet for 4 or 5 minutes, turning as needed so the flour coating takes on color and the pieces develop a good surface.
I want to get Adobo Chicken with Ginger right. What should I handle first? I'm starting with a 3 pound whole chicken cut into 8 pieces.
Yes. Set the chicken pieces in a Dutch oven or have them ready beside it. Measure out 1/2 cup soy sauce and 3/4 cup distilled white vinegar, and keep the garlic nearby too.
The soy sauce and vinegar are measured. For the garlic, do I leave the cloves whole?
Peel the whole bulb of garlic and crush the cloves so they can flavor the sauce well. They don't need to be minced finely.
Garlic is crushed, and the Dutch oven is on the stove. What goes in before I turn on the heat?
Put the chicken into the Dutch oven, then add the soy sauce, vinegar, crushed garlic, ginger, bay leaves, and peppercorns.
Everything is in the pot. Should the chicken be fully covered by the liquid?
It may not be completely submerged, and that's okay. Arrange the pieces so they sit in the sauce as evenly as possible, since you'll baste them during cooking.
The pieces are settled in the sauce. What heat should I use to get it going?
Turn the burner to medium heat and bring the mixture to a boil. Keep the pot uncovered while it comes up so you can see when it starts bubbling.
It's boiling around the edges now. Do I lower it right away?
Yes, once it boils, reduce the heat to a simmer. You want steady gentle bubbling rather than a hard boil.
It's simmering gently. How long does this part take, and should I stir it?
Cover the pot and simmer for 30 minutes. You don't need to stir constantly, but lift the lid occasionally and baste the chicken with the sauce so the pieces stay coated.
I'm setting up for Baked Apple Oatmeal; what should happen before the heat goes on? I'm getting my saucepan and casserole dish out.
Absolutely. You'll need a saucepan and a greased 2-qt. casserole. Set out 4 cups milk, 1/2 cup packed brown sugar, 2 teaspoons butter or margarine, and 1/2 teaspoon salt.
I have the milk, brown sugar, butter, and salt measured. The recipe mentions cinnamon too—does that go in with these?
Yes, add the cinnamon to the saucepan along with the milk, brown sugar, butter, and salt. Warm everything together gently, stirring so the sugar dissolves and the butter melts.
Should I bring the milk mixture to a boil, or just heat it until it's combined?
Just heat it until it's hot and well combined; there's no need to boil it. Keep the heat moderate and stir so the milk doesn't scorch on the bottom.
The butter is melted and the mixture looks smooth. What goes in after that?
Add the remaining ingredients for the oatmeal mixture, then stir gently. Aim to combine everything without mashing it down or overworking it.
It's mixed and still looks pretty loose from the milk. Is that okay before baking?
Yes, that's expected for baked oatmeal. Spoon the mixture into your greased 2-qt. casserole and spread it evenly so it bakes at the same rate throughout.
The casserole is filled. Do I cover it with foil before it goes in?
Cover the casserole, then bake it at 350 degrees F for 45 minutes.
While it bakes, what should I look for when the 45 minutes are up?
After 45 minutes, the oatmeal should look set rather than soupy, with the edges slightly firm. Let it sit briefly after baking so it scoops more neatly.
I want to make Chocolate Covered Pretzels. Can you talk me through the setup before I start melting anything?

Absolutely. Set out 2 (10 ounce) packages of pretzels, 2 cups semisweet chocolate chips, and 1 tablespoon heavy whipping cream. You'll also want a double boiler, a spoon or spatula for stirring, and wax paper for the coated pretzels to cool on.
I have the pretzels and chocolate chips out. The cream is measured too. How should I arrange the wax paper?
Lay the wax paper flat on a counter or baking sheet close to your dipping area. Once the pretzels are coated, you'll be placing them there right away so they can set and cool without sticking.
The double boiler is ready. Do I put the chocolate and cream in together?
Yes. Add the 2 cups semisweet chocolate chips and 1 tablespoon heavy whipping cream to the top of the double boiler. Keep the heat low and stir constantly as they melt together.
The chocolate is starting to soften around the edges. Should I turn the heat up to speed it along?
Keep it on low heat. Stir steadily until the chocolate and cream become smooth and melted; the recipe relies on gentle heat so the coating stays glossy and workable.
It looks smooth now and still very warm. What's the best way to dip the pretzels?
Dip the pretzels one at a time, working quickly while the chocolate mixture is still very warm. Coat each pretzel, let any extra chocolate drip back into the boiler, then move it to the wax paper.
I'm a few pretzels in, and the coating is starting to feel thicker. Is that a problem?
That just means the mixture is cooling. Keep the chocolate over the low heat in the double boiler and stir as needed so it stays warm enough for quick dipping.
All the coated pretzels are on the wax paper. What do I do while they cool?
Leave them on the wax paper until the chocolate sets and the pretzels are cool. Once firm, you can lift them off cleanly and serve or store them.
I'm making Cheesy Sweet and Savory Spuds. Can you help me get the ingredients and pot organized?
Absolutely. Set out a large pot, then gather 6 Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cubed, and 2 sweet potatoes, peeled and cubed.
The potatoes are cubed. Do the dairy ingredients go in now, or should I just keep them nearby?
Keep them nearby for now: you'll need 2 tablespoons butter and 1/2 cup heavy cream. Start with the potatoes and sweet potatoes in the pot.
While working on Cheesy Sweet and Savory Spuds, how much water should I add to the pot?
Add enough water to cover the cubed Yukon Gold potatoes and sweet potatoes. They should be fully submerged so they heat evenly.
They're covered with water. Should I put the pot over high heat?
Yes, put the pot on the stove and bring the water to a boil.
It's starting to bubble around the edges. Do I wait for a full boil?
Yes, let it come to a boil. Once it reaches that point, the next recipe step is to take it off the heat.
It's boiling now. What should I do with the water?
Remove the pot from the heat and drain the potatoes and sweet potatoes carefully.
They're drained. Should I turn on the broiler at this point?
Yes. Preheat the oven broiler now so it's ready for the next part of the dish.
Today I'm tackling Argentine Chimichurri Bread. Can you help me line up the prep?

Absolutely. Have your bread machine pan ready, and set out the ingredients from the recipe: 1 cup water, 1 1/2 tablespoons white wine vinegar, 3 tablespoons olive oil, and 1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper.
I've got the bread machine pan out. Should I measure the liquids separately before adding them?

Yes, that will make it easier. Measure the water, white wine vinegar, and olive oil cleanly, then keep the cayenne nearby so everything is ready to go into the pan in the order your bread machine manufacturer recommends.
The water is measured. I'm checking the vinegar amount now—was it 1 1/2 tablespoons?
That's right: 1 1/2 tablespoons white wine vinegar. After that, measure 3 tablespoons olive oil and 1/8 teaspoon cayenne pepper.
All four ingredients are measured. Do I just pour them into the pan now?

Add them to the bread machine pan following the order recommended in your machine's manual. If your model specifies liquids before seasonings, follow that; the key recipe direction is to use the manufacturer's order.
They're in the pan, and the pan is locked into the machine. Which setting should I choose?
In this Argentine Chimichurri Bread step, select the Basic or White Cycle on the bread machine, then press Start.
It started mixing. Is there anything I should adjust while it runs?
For this recipe, just let the bread machine run its selected cycle. You can keep an eye on the pan to make sure it's mixing smoothly, but don't change the recipe amounts.
Got it. Once the cycle is going, is my active work basically done?
Yes. Once you've placed the ingredients in the pan in the recommended order, selected Basic or White Cycle, and pressed Start, the bread machine handles the rest of this recipe.
I want to make Caraway Rye Muffins. Can you help me set up the dry ingredients before I start mixing?

Absolutely. Put a large mixing bowl on the counter and measure in 1 cup rye flour, 3/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/4 cup sugar, and 2 1/2 teaspoons baking powder. You'll also need salt and caraway seeds for that same bowl.
I've got the large bowl out. Do the rye flour and all-purpose flour go in together, or should I keep them separate?
They can go into the bowl together. Add both flours, then whisk or stir in the sugar, baking powder, salt, and caraway seeds so everything is evenly distributed.
The dry mix looks even, and I can smell the caraway. Where does the cheese fit in?
Stir the cheese directly into the dry mixture. Try to break up any clumps so the cheese is spread throughout the batter later.
The cheese is mixed in. I'm ready for the wet ingredients—what should I combine?
In a separate bowl or measuring cup, combine the egg, milk, and oil. Beat or stir them together until the egg is fully blended into the liquid.
Wet ingredients are combined. When I add them to the flour mixture, how much should I stir?
Pour the egg, milk, and oil mixture into the dry ingredients, then stir only until the flour is moistened. Stop while the batter still looks a little lumpy; overmixing can make muffins tough.
The batter is thick and slightly lumpy. I have paper liners—how full should each muffin cup be?
Line the muffin pan with the papers, or grease the cups if you're not using liners. Spoon the batter into each cup until it's about two-thirds full.
Some cups are a little uneven. Should I smooth the tops or just leave them rustic?

You can lightly nudge the batter so the cups are filled evenly, but there's no need to smooth them perfectly. Once each muffin cup is two-thirds full, they're ready for baking according to your recipe's next direction.
I want to make Fall Harvest Baked Apples. Can you guide me from setup through the syrup drizzle?
Absolutely. Set out 8 red apples, already cored, plus 1/4 cup butter, 1/3 cup maple syrup, and 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon. You'll also need a 9x13 inch baking dish and a small saucepan.
The apples are cored. Should I arrange them standing up or just lay them in the dish?
Place the apples in the 9x13 inch baking dish so they sit securely and have a little room for the sauce to run around them. While you do that, get the oven warming to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C).
Oven is heating, and the apples are in the dish. I'm getting the saucepan ready.
Put the saucepan over medium heat. Add the 1/4 cup butter, 1/3 cup maple syrup, 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, plus the ginger, lemon juice, and vanilla called for in the cooking step.
Do I melt the butter first, or add everything together cold?
Add everything together in the saucepan, then let the butter melt as the mixture warms. Stir gently so the maple syrup, cinnamon, ginger, lemon juice, and vanilla combine evenly.
It's melted and starting to bubble around the edges. Is that enough?
Let it come all the way to a boil over medium heat. Once it's boiling, take care because the syrup mixture will be hot and pourable.
It just reached a boil. How do I coat the apples evenly?
Drizzle the hot mixture equally over the 8 apples, aiming some into the cored centers and some over the tops so each apple gets a share of the butter-maple sauce.
The sauce is on the apples, and some has collected in the bottom of the baking dish.

That's fine; the pooled sauce will flavor the apples as they bake. Put the dish in the preheated 350 degrees F (175 degrees C) oven, and keep the baking dish level when you move it so the syrup stays distributed.
I'm making Alisons Slow Cooker Vegetable Beef Soup and have the slow cooker on the counter. Can you walk me through what to prep?

Absolutely. Set out 1 1/2 pounds of cubed beef stew meat, 2 cups water, 1 small chopped onion, and 1 (28 ounce) can of crushed tomatoes. You'll also need mixed vegetables, potatoes, and the seasonings: bouillon, pepper, salt, and basil.
The beef is still in its package, and I've got the water measured. Should anything go into the cooker before the liquid?
Yes. Add the cubed beef stew meat to the slow cooker first, spreading it out a bit so it sits evenly on the bottom.
The beef is in. I'm trying not to splash—does the full 2 cups water go in now?
Pour in all 2 cups of water over the beef. Go slowly along the side of the cooker if you want to keep splashing down.
Water is in. My onion is chopped and the crushed tomatoes are open; what should I add with them?
Stir in the chopped onion and the 28 ounce can of crushed tomatoes, then add the mixed vegetables and potatoes as well.
I've added the onion, tomatoes, mixed vegetables, and potatoes. Should I stir a lot or just combine them?
Just stir enough to distribute everything through the beef and water. You don't need to overwork it—just make sure the vegetables and potatoes are tucked into the mixture.
It looks evenly mixed. I have bouillon, pepper, salt, and basil beside the cooker.
Season the soup with the bouillon, pepper, salt, and basil, sprinkling them over the top and giving the soup one more gentle stir.
Seasonings are mixed in. Is there anything else from the recipe before I put the lid on?

That covers the listed prep: beef in the slow cooker, water added, onion, crushed tomatoes, mixed vegetables, and potatoes stirred in, then bouillon, pepper, salt, and basil for seasoning. You can put the lid on now and proceed with your slow cooker settings.

source_seed.recipe_title: Alisons Slow Cooker Vegetable Beef Soup

messages.content: I want to make Canadian Cedar Planked Salmon for dinner tomorrow. Can you help me plan it out?
Absolutely. Since the cedar needs a long soak, start with the 24x8x1 inch untreated cedar plank and make sure it's fully submerged in water.
I have the plank, but it wants to float. Is that okay?
It needs to stay underwater, so weigh it down with a heavy bowl, pot, or a few cans. Let it soak approximately 12 hours, or overnight.
Good to know. For the fish, how much salmon should I have ready?
Use 6 salmon fillets, each about 4 ounces. Keep them chilled until you're closer to grilling.
What else should I set out with the salmon?
Have 1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil ready, plus 1 large red onion, chopped. You'll also need coarse salt for the plank once it goes on the grill.
The plank has soaked overnight, and I've chopped the onion. When do I start the grill?
Preheat an outdoor grill for high heat. Give it time to get properly hot before you put the cedar plank on.
Should I oil the plank before it goes down, or just put it straight on?
Use the prepared soaked plank as is. Place the prepared plank on the grill, then sprinkle it with coarse salt.
Once the plank is salted, am I ready to arrange the salmon and onion nearby?
Yes. Keep the salmon, olive oil, and chopped red onion within reach so you can work efficiently once the salted cedar plank is hot on the grill.
I'm making Artichoke Hummus and have the food processor on the counter. Can you talk me through it?
Absolutely. Set out 1 (15 ounce) can of chickpeas, also called garbanzo beans, and drain them well. You'll also need 1 clove of garlic ready to go into the processor.
The chickpeas are drained and the garlic is peeled. What else should I measure before I start blending?
Measure 1/2 cup drained marinated artichoke hearts and 2 tablespoons lemon juice. Once those are ready, the ingredient list for the hummus is covered.
The artichokes are drained and the lemon juice is measured. Do I add everything to the processor at once?

Yes. Put the drained chickpeas, garlic, marinated artichoke hearts, and lemon juice into the work bowl of the food processor. The recipe notes to combine all ingredients except parsley and Quaker Rice Snacks, so leave those out if they're on your counter for serving.
Everything is in the processor bowl. Should I scrape the sides before running it?
You can scrape down anything clinging above the blade, then secure the lid. Pulse the mixture in short bursts rather than running it continuously right away.
It's starting to come together but still looks a little chunky. What texture should I stop at?
Keep pulsing until the hummus looks smooth and evenly blended. If bits of artichoke or chickpea collect on the sides, pause, scrape them down, and pulse again.
The texture looks smooth now. Where should I put it?
Spoon or scrape the hummus out of the food processor and transfer it to a serving bowl.
It's in the bowl, but I'm not serving it for a while. How do I hold it?
Cover the serving bowl and refrigerate the Artichoke Hummus until you're ready to serve.
I want to make Fab Summer Blackened Chicken Salad. Can you talk me through the chicken part while I set up the skillet?

Absolutely. Set out 2 tablespoons olive oil, divided, plus 2 skinless, boneless chicken breast halves that are 6 ounces each. You'll also need 1 1/2 tablespoons Cajun seasoning and 2 cloves garlic, crushed.
I've got the chicken and Cajun seasoning out. Should I crush the garlic before the pan gets hot?
Yes, crush the 2 cloves of garlic now so it's ready to go in quickly once the chicken is in the skillet.
Garlic is crushed, and I'm using a large skillet. How much oil goes in first?
Start by warming 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in the large skillet over medium heat.
The oil is warming. Do I season the chicken on the cutting board or in the pan?
Season both sides of the chicken breasts with the 1 1/2 tablespoons Cajun seasoning before you put them into the hot oil.
Both sides are coated. The oil looks shiny now—should the chicken go in?
Yes, place the seasoned chicken into the hot oil carefully, laying it down away from you to avoid splatter.
The chicken is in the skillet. When does the crushed garlic get added?
Stir in the crushed garlic now, keeping it around the chicken so it flavors the oil without sitting in one spot too long.
It smells good. How long should I cook the chicken before turning it?
Cook the chicken for 5 minutes on one side, then turn it and cook 5 minutes on the other side, or until the juices run clear.
Can you talk me through making Bacon Wrapped Hamburgers? I'm at the counter with a large bowl ready.
Absolutely. Set your grill up to preheat on high heat so it's ready when the patties are formed.
The grill is heating. I've got the cheeses out—how much goes into the bowl?
Add 1/2 cup shredded Cheddar cheese and 1 tablespoon grated Parmesan cheese to the large bowl.
Cheeses are in. I'm chopping the onion now—what else joins it before the beef?
Put in 1 small chopped onion and 1 egg, then add the ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, salt, and pepper. Mix those together well before adding the meat.
That mixture looks combined and a little loose from the egg and sauces. Is it time for the ground beef?
Yes. Crumble the ground beef into the bowl so it spreads through the seasoning mixture, then mix it together by hand just until everything is evenly combined.
I don't want the burgers tough. Should I keep the mixing pretty gentle?
Keep it gentle and stop once you don't see unmixed pockets of cheese, onion, or seasoning. Overworking the beef can make the patties denser.
The beef mixture is ready. How many patties should I shape before wrapping them?
Shape the mixture into 6 patties, keeping them as even as you can so they cook at the same pace on the hot grill.
I've got 6 patties shaped. How do I handle the bacon around them?
Wrap a slice of bacon around each patty, snug enough to stay in place. Once all 6 are wrapped, they're ready to go onto the preheated high-heat grill.
I'm making Broccoli Coleslaw and want to get the dressing right before I mix the vegetables. What should I measure out?

For the dressing, measure 1 cup olive oil, 1/3 cup distilled white vinegar, and 1/2 cup white sugar. Also open the 1 (3 ounce) package of chicken flavored ramen noodles, but keep the seasoning packet separate for the dressing.
I've got the oil, vinegar, sugar, and the ramen packet separated. Do I need a whisk or just a spoon?

A whisk is best if you have one. In a small bowl, combine the olive oil, distilled white vinegar, white sugar, and the reserved seasoning packet from the ramen noodles, then whisk until the sugar starts dissolving and the mixture looks evenly blended.
The dressing is mixed, but it still looks a little separated. Is that okay before chilling?
Yes, that's normal for an oil-and-vinegar dressing. Give it another good whisk, then refrigerate it for at least one hour before serving, or leave it overnight if you're preparing ahead.
While that chills, should I prep the crunchy part now or wait until serving?
You can prep the vegetables now. In a large bowl, combine the broccoli, carrots, green onions, and sunflower seeds so they're ready for the dressing later.
I'm using a big mixing bowl. Should the broccoli and carrots be tossed together before the sunflower seeds go in?
That works well. Toss the broccoli, carrots, and green onions first so they're evenly distributed, then sprinkle in the sunflower seeds and give everything a lighter toss.
What about the ramen noodles—do they go in with the vegetables right away?
Crush the ramen noodles and stir them into the large bowl with the broccoli mixture. If you want them extra crunchy, add them closer to serving; otherwise, mixing them in now follows the recipe.
Once the dressing has chilled for an hour, how do I bring it all together?

Whisk or shake the chilled dressing again, pour it over the broccoli mixture, and toss until the vegetables, sunflower seeds, and crushed ramen are coated. Serve after chilling at least 1 hour total, or let it sit overnight for more developed flavor.
I want to get Campfire Angel Food Yummies right. What should I handle first?
Absolutely. You'll need 1 angel food cake, about 10 inches, cut into large cubes, plus 1 can of sweetened condensed milk, 5 ounces.
I've got the cake cubed and the condensed milk open. Is there one more ingredient?
Yes, set out 1 cup of coconut flakes in a shallow bowl or plate so the warm cake pieces are easy to roll.
What should I use for cooking them over the fire?
Use clean toasting sticks or skewers. Thread the angel food cake cubes on them gently so they don't tear, and cook over glowing coals rather than tall flames.
The fire has settled into coals. How browned should the cake get?
Toast the cubes until the outside is browned and a little crisp, turning them so several sides get color. Keep them moving if they start darkening too fast.
A few cubes are golden now. Do I dip them while they're still hot?
Yes, while they're warm, dip each toasted cube into the sweetened condensed milk so it gets a light coating.
The milk is pretty sticky. Should I cover the whole cube or just part of it?
A partial or thin all-over coating is enough; you just want the coconut flakes to cling without making the cake soggy.
Once they're dipped, what's the best way to serve them?
Roll the dipped cake cubes in the coconut flakes, then serve them right away while the toasted edges are still warm and crisp.
Can you help me cook Chicken and Black Bean Chili tonight? I've got a large pot out and want to make sure I start in the right order.

Absolutely. Set up 2 tablespoons cooking oil and 3 large skinless, boneless chicken breast halves cut into 1 inch pieces. Keep sea salt and 1 tablespoon chili powder nearby too, or adjust the chili powder to taste.
The chicken is cut into 1 inch pieces, and the oil and seasonings are on the counter. Should the pot be hot before the chicken goes in?
Yes. Pour the 2 tablespoons cooking oil into the large pot and warm it over medium heat until the oil looks loose and shimmery, but not smoking.
The oil is shimmering. Do I add all 3 chicken breast halves worth of pieces at once, or should I worry about crowding?
Add the chicken pieces to the pot in a single layer as much as you can. If the pot is crowded, let them sit a bit before stirring so they brown instead of steaming.
They're in the pot now. What texture or color am I looking for before seasoning?
Brown the chicken on all sides. You're looking for the outside of the pieces to pick up some golden color before you add the seasonings.
The chicken has color on most sides, and there are browned bits in the pot. Should I season right over the chicken?
Yes, season it right in the pot with sea salt to taste, 1 tablespoon chili powder or to taste, plus cumin, ground chipotle, black pepper, and cayenne pepper.
The spices are on the chicken. Should I stir until they coat everything, or just let them sit?
Stir well so the spices coat the chicken pieces and warm in the oil. Scrape gently along the bottom so the browned bits and seasonings mix together.
It smells good and the chicken is coated. I have onion, green bell pepper, and yellow bell pepper chopped—do those go in now?
Yes. Mix in the onion, green bell pepper, and yellow bell pepper, stirring them through the seasoned chicken so they start to soften in the pot.
Let's work through Glazed Ham today. Where should I begin? I've got the roasting pan out but want to make sure I'm setting it up right.
Absolutely. You'll need 1 (8 pound) bone-in shank ham, 4 cups water or enough to reach the right depth in the pan, plus 1/2 cup honey and 1/2 cup brown sugar for the glaze.
The ham is bone-in and about 8 pounds. Should I mix the honey and brown sugar now?
You can measure them now so they're ready: 1/2 cup honey and 1/2 cup brown sugar. Keep them nearby while we get the ham started in the oven.
Got it measured. What oven temperature should I use?
Set the oven to 275 degrees F, which is 135 degrees C, and let it preheat fully before the pan goes in.
The oven is heating. Should the ham go directly in the pan as-is?
Yes, place the ham in the roasting pan with the shank settled securely so it won't tip when you add the water.
It's in the pan. How much water should I pour around it?
Pour water into the roasting pan until it reaches a 2 inch depth. The listed amount is 4 cups, or as needed to get to that depth depending on your pan.
I'm at about 2 inches of water now. Do I leave the pan open?
Cover the roasting pan with a tight fitting lid so the ham stays moist as it cooks.
The lid fits snugly. Anything else before I put it in the oven?
You're set: the oven is at 275 degrees F, the ham is in the roasting pan, the water is at a 2 inch depth, and the pan is tightly covered. Go ahead and place it in the oven.
I'm making Dutch Cream Waffles and want to keep the batter smooth. Can you guide me from the start?
Absolutely. Set out a large mixing bowl and measure 1 cup all-purpose flour with 1/4 teaspoon salt. Those two will go together before the eggs come in.
Large bowl is ready. Should I add the flour and salt straight in and stir them?
Yes. Add the flour and salt to the large bowl and mix them together so the salt is evenly distributed through the flour.
Done. I've also got eggs here, but I want to make sure I separate them correctly.
Separate 3 eggs, keeping the yolks and whites apart. You'll use the 3 egg yolks in the next bowl, and keep the 3 egg whites separate for now.
The yolks are in a small mixing bowl. What speed should I use with them?
Beat the egg yolks on low speed, and while the mixer is running, add the cream gradually.
I'm adding the cream now. How long should I keep beating once it's in?
For Dutch Cream Waffles, keep beating that yolk-and-cream mixture for 1 minute.
The minute is up. The mixture looks even and a bit lighter.
Good. Pour the yolk-and-cream mixture into the flour and salt mixture in the large bowl.
It's in the large bowl. Should I start slow so flour doesn't puff everywhere?
Exactly. Combine it on low speed first, then increase to medium-high and beat until the batter is smooth.
I want to make Crabby Cliffs Mushroom Puffs. Can you help me get set up before I turn anything on?
Absolutely. Put out 2 tablespoons olive oil and 3 cups fresh chopped mushrooms. You'll also need 2 green onions, chopped, and 1 clove garlic, crushed.
Mushrooms are chopped, and I've got the onions and garlic ready. Should I use the oven or stovetop first?
Start by preheating the oven to 400 degrees F, which is 200 degrees C, so it's hot when you need it.
The oven is heating. What pan should I use for the mushroom mixture?
Use a medium saucepan on the stovetop. Add the olive oil and warm it over medium heat.
The oil is shimmering a little, not smoking. Is that the right point to add things?
Yes. Stir in the chopped mushrooms, chopped green onions, crushed garlic, and the cayenne pepper.
Everything is in the saucepan. The mushrooms look bulky right now; should I keep stirring?
Keep them moving occasionally so the garlic doesn't catch on the bottom and the mushrooms cook evenly.
How long should this cook, and what texture am I watching for?
Cook the mixture for 10 minutes, or until the mushrooms and onions are tender.
If there's a little liquid in the pan near the end, should I drain it or keep cooking?
Let it cook a bit longer within that tender stage so excess moisture reduces. Once the mixture looks softened and not watery, it's ready for the puff filling.
I'm making Alaskan Halibut Lasagna and want to get the halibut part right. Can you talk me through it while I prep?

Absolutely. Set out 6 tablespoons butter or margarine total, but keep it divided since you'll only use part of it right away. You'll also need 1 1/2 pounds halibut steaks with the bones removed, cut into 1 inch cubes.
The fish is cubed and I've got the butter measured. What should I have ready before the skillet goes on?
Have 2 garlic cloves minced and 3/4 teaspoon dried thyme nearby. Once the pan is hot, this part moves pretty simply.
Should I use all the butter in the skillet now, or just some of it?
Use 2 tablespoons of the butter for this stage. Put a large skillet over medium heat and melt those 2 tablespoons until the bottom of the pan is coated.
The butter is melted and starting to foam a little. Is that okay before the fish goes in?
Yes, that's fine. Add the halibut cubes to the skillet, then add the minced garlic and the dried thyme so they cook with the fish.
The halibut is in the pan with the garlic and thyme. Do I stir it constantly or let it sit?
Stir gently enough to keep the garlic from sticking, but don't mash the fish. Let the halibut cook over medium heat until it flakes easily with a fork, which should take about 10 minutes.
How can I tell it's flaky without breaking up all the cubes?

Choose one thicker cube and press it lightly with a fork. If it separates into moist flakes without resistance, it's ready; if it still looks translucent or firm in the center, give it a little more time within that cooking window.
It's flaking now and the garlic smells cooked. What do I do with the skillet mixture?
Take the skillet off the heat, remove the halibut mixture, and set it aside. Keep the remaining divided butter available for the later lasagna steps.
Let's work through Gingered Mango Salsa today. Where should I begin? I've got a ripe mango on the counter and want to serve it later.
Absolutely. For this salsa, you'll need 1 cup chopped peeled mango, 1/4 cup chopped red onion, 1/4 cup minced fresh cilantro, and 1/4 cup lime juice.
I've peeled and chopped the mango. Should the pieces be small like a relish or a little chunkier?
A small dice works well so each bite gets mango with the onion, cilantro, and lime, but it can still have a little texture. Measure out 1 cup once it's chopped.
Got it. I measured the mango and chopped the red onion to 1/4 cup. What bowl should I use?
Use a medium bowl with enough room to stir without crushing the mango. Add the mango and red onion to the bowl.
They're in the bowl. I have cilantro rinsed and dried—how much goes in?
Mince the fresh cilantro and add 1/4 cup to the bowl. Try to chop it fairly fine so it spreads evenly through the salsa.
Cilantro is mixed in lightly. I'm ready for the lime juice.
Pour in 1/4 cup lime juice, then gently stir everything together until the mango, onion, cilantro, and lime juice are evenly combined.
It's all combined. The lime juice is pooling a little at the bottom—is that okay?
Yes, that's fine. Let the salsa stand for 30 minutes before serving; during that time, the lime juice will season the mango and onion.
Should I cover it while it stands, or leave it open on the counter?
Cover the bowl while it rests. After 30 minutes, give it one gentle stir and serve the Gingered Mango Salsa with the juices spooned over the top.
I want to put together Double Fudge Brownie Mix in a jar. Can you guide me while I set it up?
Absolutely. Set out a 1 quart or 1 liter jar, then gather 2 cups white sugar, 1 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, 1 cup all-purpose flour, and 1 cup chopped pecans.
I've got the jar, sugar, and cocoa on the counter. Should I measure everything before layering?
Yes, measure each ingredient before it goes in so the layers stay neat: sugar, cocoa powder, flour, and chopped pecans, in that listed order.
The sugar is measured. Do I pack it down or just pour it in?
Pour the 2 cups white sugar into the jar and gently level it. You can tap the jar lightly on the counter to settle it without compressing it too much.
Sugar layer is in. The cocoa looks messy—how should I add it?
Add the 1 cup unsweetened cocoa powder over the sugar slowly. A funnel or folded piece of parchment can help keep the jar rim clean.
Cocoa is layered. I'm ready for the flour and pecans.
Spoon in the 1 cup all-purpose flour next, level it gently, then add the 1 cup chopped pecans as the top layer.
The jar is full and the layers look good. What should the tag say?
For this batch of Double Fudge Brownie Mix, attach a tag with the baking instruction from the recipe: "bring the oven up to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C)."
Tag is tied on. Is there anything else from this recipe I should add before I give it away?

That covers the provided recipe directions: the ingredients are layered in the jar in order, and the tag includes the oven preheat instruction. Wipe the outside of the jar clean and make sure the lid is secure.
Broccoli Cheese Crepes is what I'm cooking today. Can you keep me on track?
Absolutely. For the crepe batter, set out 2 eggs, 1/4 cup water, 6 tablespoons all-purpose flour, and 1/2 teaspoon salt. You'll also need a blender for mixing.
I've got the blender ready. Do the eggs and water go in before the flour?
Yes. Add the eggs and 1/4 cup water to the blender, then add the 6 tablespoons flour and 1/2 teaspoon salt so everything blends into a smooth batter.
Should I scrape the sides, or just blend it straight through?
Blend until the batter looks smooth. If flour sticks to the sides, stop briefly, scrape it down, then cover and process again until there are no dry streaks.
The batter looks smooth now. Does it need to rest before I cook the crepes?
Yes, let the covered batter stand for 15 minutes. That rest helps the flour hydrate and gives the crepes a better texture.
While it rests, I want to get the filling started. What pan should I use?
Use a small saucepan. While the batter is resting, sauté the onion in butter until the onion is tender.
How soft should the onion be before I add anything else?
Cook it until it looks softened and no longer sharp or raw, but don't worry about browning it deeply. Once it's tender, you're ready to stir in the flour.
I'm at that point. How do I add the flour without making it clumpy?
Sprinkle the flour into the buttery onion mixture and stir right away until it's fully blended. Keep the spoon moving so the flour coats evenly and turns into a smooth base.
I'm ready to cook Fudge Drops. What should be ready before I begin? I've got a saucepan out, but I want to be sure I measure everything right.
Absolutely. Measure 1 2/3 cups sugar and open 1 (5 ounce) can of evaporated milk. Since this cooks on the stove, use a heavy saucepan so the mixture heats evenly.
Sugar and the 5 ounce can of evaporated milk are ready. What else goes in the pan?
Add 2 tablespoons butter or margarine and 1/2 teaspoon salt to your setup. Those go in with the sugar and milk before heating.
I have the butter and salt measured. Should I put everything in while the pan is still cool?
Yes. Combine the sugar, evaporated milk, butter, and salt in the heavy saucepan before turning up the heat.
Everything is in the saucepan. What heat should I use, and do I stir the whole time?
Set it over medium heat and bring it to a boil, stirring constantly so the sugar dissolves and the mixture doesn't scorch on the bottom.
Before I continue with Fudge Drops, it's starting to bubble around the edges. Do I wait for a full boil?
Yes, keep stirring until it reaches a boil across the mixture, not just at the edges. Once it's boiling, stay attentive and keep the motion steady.

messages.content: Dads Flat Bread is the recipe for today. Can you talk me through it from the top? I've got a large mixing bowl out, but I want to make sure the water temperature and yeast amount are right.

Absolutely. Use 1 (.25 ounce) package active dry yeast and 2 cups warm water total, with the water at 110 degrees to 115 degrees. Keep the water divided, because you'll start by using only part of it.
Got it—the water is warm and measured. Do I add all 2 cups to the yeast right away?
No, start with just 1/2 cup of the warm water in the large mixing bowl. Sprinkle in the yeast and stir so it dissolves.
The yeast is in the 1/2 cup of water and it's mostly dissolved. What should I set up before mixing the dough?
Have 1/3 cup sugar and 2 tablespoons vegetable oil ready. You'll also need the salt, rye or whole wheat flour, all-purpose flour, and the remaining warm water for the next mix-in.
I have the sugar and oil measured, and the flours are nearby. How much all-purpose flour goes in at this stage?
Add the sugar, vegetable oil, salt, rye or whole wheat flour, 3 cups all-purpose flour, and the remaining water to the bowl. Beat the mixture until it looks smooth.
It's coming together smoothly, but it still looks more like a thick batter than dough. Is that okay?
Yes, that's expected at this point. Start adding more all-purpose flour gradually, just enough to turn it into a soft dough rather than a stiff one.
The dough is soft and a little tacky. Should I flour the counter before kneading?
Yes. Turn the dough onto a floured surface, dust your hands lightly if needed, and begin kneading.
How long should I knead it, and what texture am I aiming for?
Knead until the dough is smooth and elastic, about 6-8 minutes. It should feel soft, stretchy, and less sticky as you work it.

messages.content: I'm starting Basic Chicken Stock with a Dutch oven on the stove. Can you help me get the ingredients organized before I add water?

Cut the raw onion, celery, and carrot into small pieces so they spread evenly through the stock base while still staying distinct. Set out 1 pound chicken parts, 1 large onion, 3 stalks celery with some leaves, and 1 large carrot.
I've got the chicken parts out and the vegetables beside the cutting board. Should I peel anything, or just start chopping?
Peel or trim the onion as needed, scrub the carrot well, and rinse the celery, including the leafy tops. Keep the cleaned vegetables together so they can go into the pot with the chicken.
The onion is peeled, and the celery has a few tender leaves. The recipe says to quarter the onion—should I still begin that way?
Yes, quarter the onion first so it is easy to control, then cut those quarters down smaller rather than leaving them as large wedges.
I like that better for this stock; the small raw pieces make the setup feel more even instead of bulky.
Great. Keep that same idea with the carrot and celery: chop them smaller than the listed 1 inch chunks, but stop before they turn mushy or paste-like.
The carrot is scrubbed and partly chopped. Should the celery leaves be chopped small too, or left bigger?
Chop some of the celery leaves along with the 3 stalks so they distribute through the pot. If any leaves look tough or wilted, leave those out.
All right, the onion is small, the carrot is in little pieces, and the celery is nearly done. Do I put the vegetables in before the chicken?
Put the chicken pieces into the large soup pot or Dutch oven first, then scatter the onion, celery, and carrot around and over them.
The chicken is in, and I've added the chopped vegetables around it. I noticed the directions mention salt and cloves—when do those go in?
Add the salt and cloves now with the chicken parts and vegetables. Use the amounts from your recipe copy if they are listed separately.
The seasoning is in the Dutch oven. Before I pour, should I stir the chopped vegetables through the chicken?
A light stir is fine, just enough to spread the onion, celery, and carrot through the pot without packing everything down.
Done. How much water should I add to start the stock?
Add 6 cups water to the Dutch oven. Once it is poured in, the listed setup for Basic Chicken Stock is complete.
I have Caraway Rye Muffins planned for today. What should I set up first? I've got a mixing bowl out and want to make sure I gather the dry ingredients correctly.

Absolutely. Set out 1 cup rye flour, 3/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/4 cup sugar, and 2 1/2 teaspoons baking powder. You'll also need salt, caraway seeds, cheese, plus egg, milk, and oil for the wet mixture.
I measured the rye flour and all-purpose flour. Should they go into the large bowl together?
Yes, add both flours to the large bowl. Whisk or stir them with the sugar, baking powder, salt, and caraway seeds so the leavening and seeds are evenly distributed.
The dry mix is combined. I'm seeing the caraway seeds spread through it—what happens with the cheese?
Stir the cheese into the dry ingredients next. Use a light hand so it gets coated with the flour mixture instead of clumping together.
While working on Caraway Rye Muffins, cheese is mixed in. For the wet ingredients, do I add the egg straight to the bowl?
Combine the egg, milk, and oil separately first. Beat or stir them together until the egg is broken up and the mixture looks fairly even.
The egg, milk, and oil are mixed in a measuring cup. How careful should I be when adding it to the dry bowl?
Pour the wet mixture into the dry ingredients and stir only until everything is moistened. Stop when you no longer see dry flour pockets; a slightly lumpy muffin batter is fine.
The batter looks moist with a few lumps. I have paper liners in the muffin tin—how full should each cup be?
Fill the paper-lined muffin cups about two-thirds full. A spoon or scoop works well so the portions stay fairly even.
Some batter dripped on the tin while filling. Should I wipe it before baking?
Yes, wipe away any batter on the top of the tin so it doesn't bake onto the surface. Once the cups are two-thirds full, they're ready for the oven according to your recipe's baking directions.

Great. I've got a large skillet out—what should be on the counter before I turn on the heat?
Set out 1 tablespoon olive oil and the 1 whole chicken, about 2 to 3 pounds, already cut into pieces.
Chicken and oil are ready. I'm checking the aromatics now.
You'll need 2 chopped onions and 3 cloves garlic, crushed. Keep them close to the stove so they can go in after the chicken comes out.
Skillet is on the burner. How hot should I make it before adding anything?
Warm the olive oil in the large skillet over medium high heat until it's ready for browning.
The oil is shimmering. Do I crowd all the chicken in, or work in the pan carefully?
Add the chicken pieces and sauté them until they're lightly browned. Once they have color, lift them out of the skillet and set them aside.
The browned pieces are resting on a plate, and there's flavor left in the skillet.
Use that skillet to sauté the onion, garlic, and green bell pepper until they're soft.
The vegetables have softened. I'm ready for the sauce ingredients and the chicken.
Stir in the tomato sauce, saffron, salt, and bouillon, then return the chicken pieces to the skillet.
Everything is back in the skillet. How long do I let it go before the rice?
Cook it for 10 minutes, then add the rice and reduce the heat to low.
I'm making Eggnog II today. What's the best place to start? I've got a saucepan out but want to avoid scrambling the eggs.
Absolutely. Set up a large saucepan and have your ingredients ready: 6 beaten eggs, 2 1/4 cups milk, 1/3 cup white sugar, and 1 teaspoon vanilla extract.
The eggs are beaten, and I measured the milk. Should the sugar go in before it heats?
Yes. Add the beaten eggs, the 2 1/4 cups milk, and the 1/3 cup white sugar to the large saucepan before turning on the heat.
They're in the pan together. Do I whisk hard or just stir?
Stir steadily and gently as it warms. Keep the heat at medium so the mixture thickens gradually instead of cooking too fast.
I'm at the stove now. How do I know when it's cooked enough?
Keep cooking and stirring over medium heat until the eggnog coats a metal spoon. It should cling lightly to the spoon rather than run off like plain milk.
It's starting to look a little thicker, but I don't want to overdo it.
Check the spoon again. Once the mixture coats the metal spoon, take the saucepan off the heat right away.
Okay, it coats the spoon now and I've pulled it off the burner. Where does the vanilla fit in?
Stir in the 1 teaspoon vanilla extract after removing the pan from the heat.
Vanilla is mixed in. What's the quickest way to cool it safely?
Place the pan in a sink or bowl of ice water and stir the eggnog for 1 to 2 minutes so it cools quickly.
Before I get moving on Black Bean Chili, what should I have ready? I've got a large saucepan ready.
For this batch of Black Bean Chili, set out 1 tablespoon olive oil, 1 chopped onion, 2 red bell peppers that are seeded and chopped, and 1 jalapeno pepper that's seeded and minced.
The onion and peppers are chopped. Should I start heating the pan before adding them?
Yes. Put the large saucepan over medium-high heat and add the olive oil so it can heat up before the vegetables go in.
The oil looks shiny in the pan. What vegetables go in together?
Add the onion, red bell peppers, jalapeno, mushrooms, tomatoes, and corn to the saucepan. Stir them around so they're coated in the oil.
They're all in. How long should I cook them, and what am I looking for?
Sautee them for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the onions turn translucent and the vegetables have softened.
The onion is getting translucent, but there's still some moisture from the tomatoes and corn. Is that okay?
That's fine for chili. Keep the heat at medium-high and stir so nothing sticks while the vegetables finish softening.
They look softened now. When do I add the seasonings?
Sprinkle in the black pepper, cumin, and chili powder now, then stir well so the spices coat the vegetables and warm through.
The spices smell good. What goes into the pot to turn it into chili?
For this batch of Black Bean Chili, stir in the black beans, chicken broth, and salt. Mix everything together, scraping the bottom of the saucepan so the seasoned vegetables blend into the broth.
I want to put together Double Fudge Brownie Mix as a jar gift. Can you help me get started?
Absolutely. Set out a 1 quart or 1 liter jar, then measure the dry ingredients: 2 cups white sugar, 1 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, 1 cup all-purpose flour, and 1 cup chopped pecans.
I have the jar washed and dry. Should the sugar go in before the cocoa?
Yes. Layer the ingredients in the order listed, so add the white sugar first, then the unsweetened cocoa powder.
The sugar is in, and I'm trying not to dust cocoa all over the rim. Any trick for keeping the layers neat?
A funnel or a rolled piece of parchment helps. Pour the cocoa slowly into the center, then gently tap the jar on the counter to level it without shaking the layers together.
Cocoa layer is mostly even. Does the flour go next?
It does. Add the 1 cup all-purpose flour over the cocoa, keeping the jar steady so the darker layer stays visible underneath.
The flour is in. I still have the chopped pecans measured out.
Add the 1 cup chopped pecans as the top layer. They'll give the jar a nice finished look and keep the finer ingredients tucked underneath.
Pecans are on top and the lid fits. What should I write on the tag?
Attach a tag that includes the baking instruction: get the oven warming to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C). You can title it Double Fudge Brownie Mix so the recipient knows what it is.
Tag is tied on. Is there anything else I should do before giving it away?
Make sure the lid is sealed tightly, wipe any cocoa or flour from the outside of the jar, and keep the tag easy to read. The mix itself is assembled.
Cold Cocoa Smoothie is on deck today. What should I do first? I've got the blender out and a chilled glass in the freezer.
Absolutely. Set out 1 1/2 scoops vanilla ice cream, 1 1/2 cups milk, 1/4 cup whipped cream, and 2 tablespoons instant hot chocolate mix.
I measured the milk and hot chocolate mix. Should the whipped cream go into the blender too, or is it just for topping?
For this smoothie, add the 1/4 cup whipped cream right into the blender with the other ingredients.
Okay, the ice cream is a little soft. Is that fine for blending?
Yes, slightly soft vanilla ice cream is fine. Add the 1 1/2 scoops ice cream and the 1 1/2 cups milk to the blender jar.
Those are in. I also see the directions mention crushed cookies, but I don't have a measured amount.

If you're using crushed cookies, add them to the blender now along with the 2 tablespoons instant hot chocolate mix and the whipped cream. Since no amount is listed, use only what you already planned to include.
Everything is in the blender. How long should I blend it?
Blend until the mixture looks smooth and evenly cocoa-colored. Stop once there are no obvious ice cream lumps or dry streaks of hot chocolate mix.
It looks smooth, but there are tiny cookie bits. Should I keep blending?
Tiny cookie bits are okay if you included cookies. If the base is smooth and pourable, you can stop blending.
Ready to serve. Do I just pour it straight into the chilled glass?
Yes. Pour the Cold Cocoa Smoothie into the large chilled glass and serve it right away while it's cold and creamy.

Cut 1 pound of skinless, boneless chicken breast halves into bite-size pieces, and have 1 cup of lemonade measured out beside the stove.

Set out 2 tablespoons olive oil and 1 tablespoon lime juice. You'll also need Worcestershire sauce ready to go into the skillet with those.

Use medium heat, then add the chicken, lemonade, olive oil, lime juice, and Worcestershire sauce to the skillet together.
On Chicken Tacos, everything is in the skillet and starting to bubble lightly. What seasonings go in?
Sprinkle in garlic powder and onion powder, then add the bay leaf so it can flavor the liquid while the chicken simmers.

Keep it at a steady simmer rather than a hard boil. Cook until the chicken is no longer pink and the juices run clear, about 15 to 20 minutes.

Warm the tortillas in the oven or microwave just until they're soft and flexible, then keep them covered so they don't stiffen before assembly.

Spoon the warm chicken mixture onto each tortilla first, then add the other components in that soft-to-crisp order right before eating so each taco or wrap keeps its structure.
